Israeli soldiers patrol after a settler attack during an olive harvest in the West Bank over the weekend. (AP: Leo Correa)

Israeli police say they have arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in the West Bank over the weekend.

The United States, France, Belgium and Poland called on Israel to take action after diplomats and a photojournalist were attacked.

Police said the suspects were arrested in a pre-dawn operation on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction.

Israeli police say they have arrested 10 people in the West Bank after settler attacks on an American photographer and a French mayor.

The arrests were made after calls from the United States to crack down on settler violence and for the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist to be jailed.

France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, have also called on Israel to take action.

The police said that they raided several locations across the West Bank and also seized potential evidence related to the attacks, which have stepped up as settlers disrupt Palestinians' annual olive harvest.

"Following the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians, an arrest operation was conducted before dawn," said Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander.

"Suspects were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the violent incidents, violating a military commander's order concerning a closed military zone, and illegal construction."

The attacks come after global outrage over mounting settler violence in the West Bank.

Masked Israeli settlers were filmed on Friday assaulting Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank.

Levine was hospitalised after sustaining a number of injuries in the attack and underwent surgery on a finger.

On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank.

The settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, 78, the mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, an advocate of the Palestinian cause who had come on a goodwill visit and was helping harvest olives.

A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats.

However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more circumspect.

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and journalists in the occupied West Bank, using slingshots to hurl rocks from hilltops.

He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations" and without coordinating with the military.

He has also said that the facts ​of the attack on Levine were "unclear".

Levine has said she was attacked by settlers and Israel President Isaac Herzog has apologised.

Settler attacks ​on the Palestinians ⁠are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group.

Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

Benjamin Netanyahu is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a tight race for a new mandate in October 27 elections, has tried to shore up his right-wing base and had cast doubt on the circumstances behind the recent settler attacks.

The opposition described the attacks on Westerners as a stain on Israel's image and accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of allowing the violence to happen.

Rights groups note that Israel rarely prosecutes settlers when the victims are Palestinian.

Settler attacks against Palestinians, including killings, beatings, vandalism and arson, averaged six a day in the first half of the year, according to the United Nations.

When Belgian American particle physicist Francis Halzen was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” it was a reminder that for more than a century, scientists have treated Antarctica’s environments as windows onto worlds beyond Earth.

Antarctica has offered scientists a means of reaching and researching beyond Earth without leaving it. Various harsh and challenging Antarctic environments have served as testing sites for equipment destined for the Moon, Mars and beyond. Its ice has collected meteorites that arrive from extraterrestrial sources. And it is one of the best places on Earth from which to observe the universe.

Since the start of the 20th century, scientists have drawn parallels between Antarctic environments and those that can be found beyond our planet.

In 1901, the Australian physicist Louis Bernacchi compared being in Antarctica to what he thought it would be like on the Moon: “a dead silent world above you, and a dead silent world at your feet.”

By the mid-20th century, Antarctic environments were frequently used as approximations of extraterrestrial worlds. NASA officials traveled to the Antarctic “because this was as close to lunar conditions as we could get here on Earth,” as one of them, Ernst Stuhlinger, put it in 1968.

In preparation for the Viking mission to Mars in 1975-76, several microbiologists conducted research in the McMurdo Dry Valleys, convinced that this region of Antarctica closely resembled Mars. This type of research continues today.

Scientists continue to test technologies created for space exploration in the Antarctic, including spacesuits, robotics, and food production facilities, hoping that success in the Antarctic environment will translate into success in the more extreme environments of space.

Likewise, Antarctic workers have been studied to learn about the psychological aspects of long-term isolation and small-group dynamics in stressful situations, another key aspect of space exploration. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 was even modeled after the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, agreeing among nations how to share special spaces for scientific research.

While some critics have said Antarctica’s conditions are too different to serve as a terrestrial stand-in for outer space, the idea of Antarctica as a practice or training ground for space exploration remains a fertile ground for the imagination, both for scientists and the general public.

Antarctic meteorites offer scientists access to materials from the Moon, Mars and beyond without leaving Earth. The men of the 1911-1914 Australasian Antarctic Expedition, led by geologist Douglas Mawson, collected the first meteorite discovered in Antarctica.

Modern meteorite science in Antarctica can be dated to the 1970s, following the 10th Japanese Antarctic Research Expedition’s 1969 discovery of nine meteorites in the Yamato Mountains.

Meteorites come down all around the planet, but Antarctica’s blue-ice areas, which comprise about 1% of Antarctica’s surface ice, often in mountainous regions, are among the best places to look. In those areas, strong katabatic winds flowing fast downhill remove snow, exposing hard, translucent ice. Dark-colored meteorites are easily spotted in contrast with the light-blue ice. And blue-ice areas contain unusually high concentrations of meteorites, as rocks from outer space either land on the surface or emerge from within the ice after being transported by glacial movement.

In 1976, geologist William Cassidy established the United States’ formal efforts to search for meteorites in Antarctica. Geologist Ursula Marvin, a member of one of the program’s earliest expeditions, credited Antarctic environments with providing a special look at planetary geology: “While waiting for future space missions we have found an elegant means of significantly extending the range of planetary samples by making our yearly expeditions to Antarctica.”

That effort has yielded, for example, the first recognized meteorite from the Moon, as well as a meteorite from Mars, which sparked a media firestorm in the mid-1990s when some scientists suggested that it bore evidence of fossilized microbial life.

Despite one early physicist complaining that “taking Astronomical observations” in Antarctica’s weather was “positively painful,” astronomical work has been conducted in Antarctica for over a century. The central regions of the Antarctic ice sheet have low winds, long winter darkness and an exceptionally clear, stable atmosphere. Those conditions give Earth-based instruments unusually favorable access to signals coming from the cosmos.

Since the 1990s, the continent has been a major center for astronomy research, hosting a wide range of sensors and telescopes.

In 2007, the U.S. began operating the South Pole Telescope, which measures cosmic microwave background radiation and the dark energy driving the acceleration of the expansion of the universe, and which helped make the first image of a black hole in 2019. In subsequent years, research stations operated by Japan, China, France and Italy have also constructed increasingly large optical telescopes to observe astronomical objects, including stars and planets.

Scientists also use a constellation of other instruments on the Antarctic Plateau, such as the Antarctic PENGUIn magnetometer array, initially installed in the 1990s, to study extreme space weather events and advance understanding of the near-Earth space environment.

Closer to the coast, Antarctica also hosts a suite of other astrophysical research programs, such as the long-running “CosRay” observatory. Starting in 1960 at McMurdo, a neutron monitor measured low-energy cosmic rays – charged particles from outside the solar system. The project is still running, having moved to a nearby South Korean station in 2017.

Based at the University of Wisconsin, IceCube is a major international collaborative project that involves “450 physicists from 58 institutions in 14 countries,” its website reports.

The project began in 1987 when Halzen conceived of the Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array, known as AMANDA. That project tested the ability to use the ice of the polar plateau as a key element of a telescope to see neutrinos. Those elementary particles, first detected experimentally in 1956, travel through space, interacting only rarely with electrons and atomic nuclei.

Constructed at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station starting in 1993, AMANDA was made up of 677 optical sensors deployed on 19 strings embedded deep in the polar ice. The strings were installed by drilling holes with hot water, lowering the modules into the ice and allowing the holes to refreeze.

The sensors wait for these rare occasions when a neutrino collides with a proton or neutron and produces charged particles that emit a faint flash, known as Cherenkov radiation. After AMANDA successfully detected neutrinos, Halzen and others in 2001 made the case to expand the array to place sensors throughout roughly a cubic kilometer of the Antarctic ice sheet. That project, IceCube, was originally deployed between 2004 and 2011, funded largely by the National Science Foundation.

With the larger group of sensors, scientists can not only detect neutrinos, but they can also determine their direction, energy and type. This allows them to trace some neutrinos back to their sources far away in the universe.

IceCube helps scientists gain insights into questions regarding supernova events, galaxy formation, the Big Bang, dark matter and the properties of the neutrino itself.

As Halzen and countless other scientists have found over the years, Antarctica’s extreme conditions serve as a crucial gateway to understanding some of the greatest mysteries of the cosmos.

horror-biz-blumhouse-scratch:
By

Ryan Benk

,

Ayesha Rascoe

Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Virginia.
                
                    
                    Ryan Benk/NPR News
                    
                
                hide caption

The horror biz is booming, as recent Weekend Edition reporting has made clear. But not everyone wants to be up close and personal the with the IRL frights of a haunted house or spooky corn maze. Many would rather experience nightstalkers, goblins and witches that can't escape the theater or TV screen, or zombies and werewolves that won't lunge off the pages of a book.

Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Va. It's a bookstore devoted exclusively to horror and the supernatural. It's been doing business for just over a month and Harris says she already has steady traffic from both genre stalwarts and first-timers.

"You know, I think people are looking for things that they wouldn't normally find in a lot of other places. I've had people comment about the curation and how they're finding something unexpected," Harris says. "And I'm also surprised at how many people are trying to dip their toe into horror."

Harris is no newbie herself: books and horror have been constant companions.

"My love of horror started from an early age. And I joke, but I do truly blame my parents because my dad was a[n] avid reader. He probably takes responsibility more for my fantasy/sci-fi love, but my mother always loved horror," Harris says.

"To me it was completely normal. I didn't think of it as a spooky thing."

So after a career in aviation, Harris decided to follow her passion and open Long Dark House.

"It's exceeded my expectations and, you know, could be the season. But I just am so appreciative that people are as excited about these genres and this experience as I am. And so anytime someone walks through the door, I'm a little surprised and happy and grateful," she says.

The numbers say Chanthal Harris shouldn't be very surprised. Market research by Nielsen says profits from the genre have jumped almost 26-percent year over year.

And the numbers are good for films as well.

Last May, Backrooms — about a horrifying liminal space that exists beyond our own reality — smashed box office records.

With just a $10 million budget, petty cash for Hollywood, it grossed over $400 million worldwide. The feature film started as a short on YouTube. And It's just one title from the newly-merged studio Blumhouse Atomic Monster.

Actor Chiwetel Umeadi Ejiofor portraying Clark in Backrooms.
                
                    
                    A24/Blumhouse Atomic Monster
                    
                
                hide caption

Abhijay Prakash and Michael Clear head up the studio. Prakash is Blumhouse Atomic Monster's president and CEO. Clear is the president of Atomic Monster and leads the studio's emerging directors program.

"We're drawn like moths to a flame to things that are scary," Clear says. "We reached out to Kane Parsons who had created the short and at the time he was 15 or 16; he was still in high school."

Despite the headlines Blumhouse Atomic Monster garnered for hiring Parsons, Clear adds it's not really all that new for them.

"We've always kind of scoured a variety of sources, particularly for filmmakers who have a sense of how to scare people. Going all the way back to one of the first movies we produced, Lights Out, David Sandberg, the director of that film, was actually himself a YouTube creator," Clear says.

"They say it's hard to describe what scary is but I know it when I see it."

A post-COVID reanimation?

Abhijay Prakash says the COVID-19 pandemic had an outsized impact on the horror film industry.

"Horror as a share of the box office…pre-COVID, was never more than 10% of the box office. Then after COVID though, it's occupying a much larger share. It's over 15%, almost 20% last year and this year. And inside of that we are over half of that box office," Prakash says.

"So our market share is over 50% of the horror box office. And that's where we're focused. We live and breathe it."

Our friends over at the Recreational Fear Lab theorize people are flocking to fear more these days because the real world has been just so darn scary.

But Michael Clear thinks it could be a bit more complicated than that.

"I agree it's part of it, but I also think that one of the things that shifted [is] the bar has been rising for what people need or what draws people to the theatres. It's been rising consistently over the last 10, 15 years," Clear says.

"Maybe all the isolation has just driven people towards more social activities," he adds. "People are craving collective experiences. We're finding more now than before the pandemic that people are going to movies in larger groups. And it just so happens that our genre, because it's participatory — if we do our jobs right, we're getting reactions, audible reactions from the audience — and it can be more fun to experience that with your friends."

"Scary stories in the dark," Abhijay Prakash underlines. "[It] has delivered for thousands of years."

It has to be "real"

While Blumhouse Atomic Monster makes its bid to reign supreme in theaters, many scream queens and kings are finding bite-sized horror scrolling social media. And often, those scary shorts are the products of AI.

"Personally, I think that, you know, anything that makes filmmaking more democratic can can be great. You know, people who find tools that can enable them to create it will allow more people, more talented people, to enter the space," Michael Clear says.

He cautions that audiences want things to feel authentic, as though the horror on the screen is genuine.

"When it comes to our movies, I think one of the things that just happens to be a characteristic of our genre is that the things that are scariest are the things that feel the most real. So really, when you get down to the way that AI images or whatever may impact movies, you know, our focus is always on doing things as real as possible. Doing things as practically as possible," Clear says.

The 'Disney of horror'

Abhijay Prakash told The Ankler early this year that his goal for Blumhouse Atomic Monster is to be the Disney of fear.

He breaks down what he means:

"Every place that consumers engage with scary stories is a place that we as a business, as a company obsessed with horror and scary stories will be. And then it's only a question of the business model," Prakash says.

Prakash says the studio is exploring creating an attraction from its Five Nights at Freddy's franchise and he also points to the popularity of the stage version of Paranormal Activity.

"So that really is a guiding principle for our company. We want to be everywhere where horror is relevant and it's taking a bigger and bigger place in the culture," Prakash says.

Michael Clear says the idea isn't just to cater to existing fans of the genre, but to grow the fanbase for all things spooky itself. "We like to think that we can provide a kind of gateway horror," he says.

Next week we get a lesson in horror storytelling from one of the most prolific writers in the genre — Stephen Graham Jones.

Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo  by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar.

If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.

Telenor operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022 with 18 million subscribers. After the February 2021 coup, Telenor faced pressure after the junta demanded compliance with its surveillance and content blocking directives. Telenor decided to leave Myanmar, but civil society groups raised strong objections that its local operations would be sold to a company with links to the junta.

In December 2024, activist group Justice For Myanmar filed a complaint against Telenor in Norway for breach of the Sanctions Act. Norway rejected it, but the complaint was refiled in October 2025 with an additional charge of aiding and abetting crimes against humanity.

The Norwegian state has a 54-percent stake in Telenor. In December 2025, the Norwegian Parliament initiated an investigation into the operations of Telenor in Myanmar. The leader of the disciplinary committee of the Parliament said: “We must uncover how a state-owned company could cooperate with a brutal military regime (by handing over) customer information about the opposition [in Myanmar].”

In April 2026, a civil class action lawsuit was filed against Telenor in Norway by Myanmar citizens for sharing their sensitive personal data with the junta. The complaint alleged that Telenor shared at least 1,253 phone numbers with the regime. The data also included call logs and location data, names, addresses, ID numbers, Facebook, and bank accounts linked to mobile numbers.

Among the complainants is Tha Zin, the widow of rapper and lawmaker Phyo Zeya Thaw, who was arrested based on a trumped-up charge, convicted, and later executed by the junta. Tha Zin said her husband was arrested right after his account information was accessed by the junta.

I lost my husband. It is not just a wife losing her husband. It is also a loss to the movement. It is also a loss to democracy because my husband was committed to democracy and a youth leader. Losing him means a loss to the country.

Lawyer Jan Magne Langseth summed up the content of the complaint.

Telenor ASA in Norway clearly contributed to the practice of handing over user data, despite the inherent risks for its customers in Myanmar. We have evidence of cases where the team at HQ expressly recommended the data to be handed over.

In September 2026, Norway’s National Criminal Investigation Service and the interior security service searched the office of Telenor related to the charges filed against the company.

Justice for Myanmar spokesperson Yadanar Maung welcomed the decision of Norway authorities to investigate Telenor.

Telenor’s transfer of spyware to a military-linked company and sharing of sensitive data with the military junta was extensively documented

We hope this will finally lead to accountability for the harms Telenor has caused Myanmar people through its conduct and its dangerous divestment.

In several statements sent to the media, Telenor said it is cooperating with authorities with regard to the ongoing investigation. It added that it needed to defend its employees in Myanmar.

In Myanmar, refusing requests from the military authorities could, in the worst case, have led to imprisonment, torture or the death penalty.

Telenor Myanmar had no real options. We could not play Russian roulette with the lives of our employees.

Telenor media relations director David Fidjeland reiterated the same point.

Our employees risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty if the military authorities’ orders were not complied with. We found that we had no real choice and that we could not put our employees’ lives at risk.

Telenor acknowledged the brutality of the junta, but it asserted that the welfare of its employees should not be endangered.

Telenor acknowledges that human rights due diligence must consider all rights-holders. However, when faced with the brutal force of the military, Telenor maintains that an employer cannot give instructions that put employees’ lives at direct risk.

Civil society groups said the investigation is a step forward in fighting impunity. Civicus said companies should not enable human rights abuses.

The Telenor case has the potential to challenge impunity. It should refocus the minds of democratic states and companies headquartered in them, offering a warning that they can be exposed for complicity in the junta’s atrocities. It should give fresh impetus to civil society’s efforts to hold states and companies to account.

Faiz Naeem, Asia Pacific policy analyst at Access Now, added that Telenor’s case is a reminder for companies that their obligation to users does not end when leaving a country under an autocratic regime.

The decision to investigate Telenor for crimes against humanity should be a wake-up call for every technology and telecom company operating in a high-risk environment: leaving a market does not mean leaving your human rights responsibilities behind.

The civil class action lawsuit is seeking damages of EUR 9,000 (roughly USD 10,500) per customer.

Forget sharks, bears and other terrifying creatures. One of America’s most threatening animals could be curled up on your couch.

An estimated 4.5 million Americans are bitten by dogs every year, with a dog-bite victim ending up in an emergency room every 80 seconds, the CDC estimates.

Now, a new study has revealed where US residents face the greatest risk of a dog bite-related insurance claim.

The Empire State placed 9th in the ratings with 1,308 claims in 2025, with 1 in 15,189 odds of getting chomped on by Fido, according to research by Gamble Mind.

Across the Big Apple, reported dog bites jumped nearly 25% in a single year, soaring from 4,041 in 2024 to 5,049 in 2025.

Staten Island is the city’s dog-bite hotspot, with residents facing the highest reported bite rate of any borough. The borough recorded 395 reported bites in 2025, equivalent to roughly one bite for every 1,261 residents.

Manhattan and Queens tied for the most reported bites, with 1,192 each. But Manhattan’s smaller residential population meant its rate was considerably higher, at one in 1,393 residents, compared with one in 1,944 in Queens.

Brooklyn emerged as the borough with the lowest bite rate, despite recording 1,126 incidents, with approximately one bite for every 2,325 residents.

In the bigger picture, Michigan takes the crown, with resident facing annual odds of one in 7,073 of being involved in a dog bite insurance claim, according to the study.

The Wolverine state recorded 1,432 claims in 2025, putting its populated-adjusted claim rate a whopping 69% above the national average and more than three times that of Texas.

Just last March, a 5-day-old baby girl was mauled to death when she was left alone with a dog the family had just taken in.

Indiana came in second with 824 claims and odds of one in 8,463, followed by Ohio, which recorded 1,348 claims and odds of one in 8,828, narrowly ahead of Pennsylvania, where odds of getting bit by a dog are one in 9,864, with 1,324 claims filed.

Illinois, which had 1,283 claims and odds of one in 9,914.

Florida placed sixth with 2,347 claims — a relatively high total — but its larger population brought the odds down to one in 9,958.

New Jersey landed seventh with 818 claims and odds of one in 11,673.

California actually recorded the most claims of any state on the list, a staggering 2,830, but its enormous population pushed it down to eighth place, with odds of one in 13,933.

Texas placed in 10th spot with 1,313 insurance claims and a one in 23,832 chance of suffering a teeth-gnashing from a pooch.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton unveiled a plan to clear every homeless encampment in the state by the end of next year at a San Diego news conference today.

The plan calls for a network of Homeless Recovery Centers, using the Sunbreak Ranch project in San Diego County as the prototype, according to the Hilton campaign.

The centers would provide beds, meals, showers, medical care, drug treatment, psychiatric care and job training. Each person would have someone responsible for helping them get into stable housing, with continued care for those who need it, campaign officials said.

“No one is going to get their life back on track on the streets,” Hilton said. “We are going to get people off the streets and into place where they can actually get help.”

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s 2025 count found California has 181,934 homeless people, including 115,583 living without shelter, according to Hilton, who said the state has allocated almost $24 billion to homelessness and housing in recent years, yet the state auditor found it failed to consistently track spending and results.

Hilton says he will meet with mayors and county leaders in his first month as governor to set public deadlines for clearing encampments, with a Labor Day 2027 deadline for local leaders and a final deadline of Dec. 31, 2027, for every encampment to be cleared.

Hilton also plans to declare a homelessness emergency to waive permitting barriers, enforce public camping bans once suitable facilities are available, and audit homelessness spending through Operation Zero Waste to redirect money from failing programs.

If loocal leaders do not act, he said the state would step in. “Leaving people to deteoriate in tents is a disgrace,” Hilton said.

“By the end of 2027, every encampment will be cleared, and Californians will have their sidewalks ad parks back.”

The campaign of Hilton’s opponent, former U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to  “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude  and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

The president of a sorority at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is breaking her silence on an explosive discrimination scandal that rocked Greek life and sparked a revolt among sisters.

Alana Nielsen, president of Alpha Phi, told the California Post that the shocking controversy exposed a troubling power imbalance between local sorority sisters and the national representatives entrusted with overseeing their recruitment process.

And now, the furious sisters are fighting to take back control.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

“Honestly, I felt sick to my stomach,” Nielsen said of the moment she realized something was seriously wrong. “I couldn’t imagine letting the day end without giving our members an opportunity to speak.”

The scandal erupted in late September after an outside recruitment adviser was accused of discriminating against women of color during the chapter’s annual rush process.

Roughly 1,200 prospective members initially participated, but that number reportedly plummeted to approximately 250 after the first round on Sept. 26.

When active sisters returned, they noticed that numerous women they had wanted to advance, including candidates from diverse backgrounds, had mysteriously vanished from the pool.

Nielsen said the troubling pattern only became apparent as the day unfolded.

“It was more of a gradual realization throughout the day,” she told The Post. “As members started talking to one another and comparing their experiences, it became increasingly difficult to ignore how many women we had wanted to return were missing from the candidate pool.”

The apparent purge was especially disturbing because sisters had been told their evaluations would help determine which hopefuls advanced.

Instead, Nielsen said members began questioning whether their input had been disregarded entirely.

“We had been taught to trust the people overseeing recruitment,” she explained. “These were older, more experienced representatives who had been doing this for years, and we had never been in a position where we felt we needed to question the process.”

Meanwhile, existing sisters of color were allegedly being excluded from recruitment activities themselves.

Black sorority member Sky Achola previously told the Santa Barbara News-Press that nearly every woman of color in her sorority family group had been removed from recruitment rounds.

Nielsen said members were told there simply weren’t enough sisters to participate in every round.

But that explanation quickly came under scrutiny as certain groups of women were repeatedly assigned recruitment rounds, while others were consistently left out.

“Members could see that certain groups of women were consistently being scheduled to recruit, while many women of color were being assigned significantly fewer rounds or none at all,” Nielsen said.

As tensions exploded, Nielsen pushed for a chapter-wide meeting, despite an outside representative allegedly suggesting the day end on a “happy note” with music and dancing.

The sorority president wasn’t having it.

“It felt wrong to send everyone home without acknowledging what was happening,” she said.

What followed was an emotional uprising inside the chapter house, with sisters crying, shouting and demanding answers.

Recruitment director Emerson Novosel previously described the extraordinary scene to the Daily Nexus as feeling “like a revolution happening right now.”

Nielsen said she refused to silence the women.

“Once one woman stood up, it empowered others to do the same,” she explained. “That was incredibly powerful to witness.”

The unidentified volunteer adviser, a UCSB Alpha Phi alumna who had previously assisted with recruitment, subsequently left her position.

Nielsen declined to publicly identify her, stressing that the controversy exposed deeper issues within the sorority’s recruitment system.

“For me, the larger issue isn’t just about one individual,” she said. “It’s also about the structure that allowed outside representatives to exercise so much influence over our recruitment process.”

The president said the chapter still has unanswered questions about who made decisions and how candidates were selected.

Alpha Phi International’s Health, Wellness, and Accountability department has since met with members, but Nielsen said emotional support alone isn’t enough.

“Our members aren’t only looking for emotional support,” she said. “We also want to understand how these decisions were made, what factors influenced them, and what accountability will look like moving forward.”

The chapter is now collecting written accounts from sisters and establishing a committee to overhaul its recruitment system.

Nielsen wants future outside advisers relegated to clearly defined support roles, with local members retaining control over decisions.

“We want clear procedures for how scores are used, transparency around how return decisions are made, fair and clearly explained opportunities for active members to participate in recruiting,” she said.

UCSB condemned discrimination in a statement to The Post.

“Discrimination is not tolerated at the university. Reports of discrimination are investigated by the university’s Office of Discrimination and Harassment Prevention and referred to Student Conduct as appropriate,” a university spokesperson said.

The university did not confirm whether a formal investigation into these specific allegations is underway.

Despite the ugly fallout, Nielsen insists the sisters aren’t backing down.

“Moving forward doesn’t mean moving on without accountability,” she said. “It means using this experience to build something better, with our members’ voices at the center of it.”

The California Post reached out to Alpha Phi International for comment.

Fox News host Will Cain discusses singer Kelly Clarkson's social media post about her feud with a toy store in Brooklyn, N.Y. on 'The Will Cain Show.'

Kelly Clarkson’s public dispute with a Brooklyn small business over a $15,000 mechanical bird could damage the relatable image she has built over the past two decades, a crisis PR expert warned.

"There will certainly be some naysayers who think Clarkson was acting like a rich and famous prima donna and using her platform vindictively," Steve Honig, founder of The Honig Company, told Fox News Digital. "But most people will likely think that, for the most part, she acted accordingly and in many ways was a role model for standing up for oneself."

The controversy began after Clarkson claimed she was treated like Julia Roberts’ character in "Pretty Woman" while shopping at Art of Play in Brooklyn.

KELLY CLARKSON'S STORE CALLOUT SHOWS THE 'POWER' OF CELEBRITY STATEMENTS: EXPERT

Kelly Clarkson sparked a public feud with a Brooklyn boutique store over a sales dispute.  (GC Images)

Clarkson said an employee appeared to judge her based on her appearance and suggested she look at "something comparable" instead of the $15,000 mechanical bird she wanted to purchase. She also called the employee an "idiot" and said the store lost a major sale.

Art of Play, which sells puzzles, games, toys, books and other specialty items, responded to Clarkson's original social media post, saying the business had been bombarded with hateful messages from "8 million people" after the singer's accusations.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity. Thanks to all our friends for their support and welcome to all the curious folks who discovered us amidst the drama. We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday. As a talented popular singer once said ‘what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger,’" the store wrote on its Instagram page on Sunday afternoon.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

After Art of Play's Instagram post, Clarkson responded Sunday afternoon on X and Instagram stories to the store's assertion that the mechanical bird wasn't for sale.

"Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," Clarkson wrote, adding a thumbs-up emoji.

The singer continued: "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone "yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can." That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it," adding a checkmark emoji.

Kelly Clarkson likened a recent shopping experience to Julia Roberts' character in "Pretty Woman." (Getty Images)

Clarkson added: "And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things. I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t."

Clarkson’s post also prompted criticism online, with some users accusing her of using her platform to target a small business. The store reportedly received a wave of negative Google reviews after the singer’s comments went viral.

SELMA BLAIR SAYS 'NO ONE RETURNED MY CALLS' AFTER ANTI-ISLAM COMMENT LED TO HOLLYWOOD FALLOUT

Art of Play shared another post on Instagram Sunday to "clarify one additional detail" about Clarkson's visit.

"During the 5 minutes she spent in the store, she inquired about our mechanical bird puppet named Molly. We explained that while Molly is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a de facto mascot for our shop, a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines, a brilliant artist named Bliss Kolb who lives in Seattle. He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000. We explained all of this to Kelly Clarkson."

Kelly Clarkson won the first season of "American Idol" in 2002. (Kevin Winter/ImageDirect)

"We also offered to show her a different singing bird automaton, made by a traditional clockmaking shop in Germany, that she could have taken home with her that day. It costs about $2,000. She did not stick around long enough to see it."

"We’ve reached out to Kelly directly to try and clear the air," the shop concluded. "We really do wish her the best and hope that someday we can all laugh about this misunderstanding."

Adam Rubin, co-owner of Art of Play and a children’s author, spoke with Fox News Digital inside the Brooklyn store Tuesday morning, claiming the singer has put his business in danger after their viral dispute.

Rubin claimed the backlash has extended beyond angry comments online, with people associated with the business allegedly facing threats and having their personal information exposed.

"We've got incredible support from our neighbors and fans over the past few days, and all of them have been attacked, threatened, doxed," he said.

Molly, a mechanical singing bird designed by Bliss Kolb, is displayed at Art of Play in Brooklyn. The price tag now reads $15 million. (Fox News Digital)

Evan Nierman, CEO of crisis PR firm Red Banyan, said Clarkson’s long-established reputation will likely protect her from any lasting damage — but warned that continuing to discuss the dispute could change how some people view her.

"Arguing with a boutique toy store over a $15,000 mechanical bird is not going to make or break the long-term reputation of a literal ‘American Idol,’" Nierman said. "Right or wrong, she initiated this conflict by telling her 9 million followers that the owners of the store are idiots who lost a huge sale and mistreated her."

TAYLOR HICKS CREDITS FAITH AND BLUE-COLLAR BIRMINGHAM ROOTS FOR KEEPING HIM GROUNDED AFTER 'AMERICAN IDOL' WIN

"Prior to this incident, she was perceived as a down-to-earth and relatable celebrity, but this acrimonious back and forth over social media is sullying everyone involved," he added.

The co-owner of Art and Play told Fox News Digital, "I am afraid for the safety of our shop. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger." (Denise Truscello/Getty Images for Live Nation Las Vegas)

Honig argued that the dispute could ultimately strengthen Clarkson’s image because she presented herself as someone standing up to unfair treatment.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The dispute is more likely to strengthen Clarkson’s image than undermine it because she was standing up against being judged based on appearance," Honig said. "This was not really about a $15,000 item, but about how she says she was treated when she tried to buy it."

"Just as in ‘Pretty Woman,’ someone appeared to be judging a book by its cover," he added.

Still, Honig acknowledged that the situation could become more damaging if the dispute continues.

"There will certainly be some naysayers who think Clarkson was acting like a rich and famous prima donna and using her platform vindictively," Steve Honig told Fox News Digital. "But most people will likely think that, for the most part, she acted accordingly and in many ways was a role model for standing up for oneself." (Matthew Stockman/Getty Images)

"The only risk is if the dispute drags on and starts to look like a celebrity using her platform against a small business," he said.

Nierman also urged Clarkson to let the controversy fade rather than risk having the dispute overshadow her career.

"Clarkson has built up over two decades of goodwill since winning ‘American Idol.’ She has built a deep reservoir of trust, and her fans will give her the benefit of the doubt every time in a fight like this," he said.

"Every new round of arguing over Molly the Bird makes it more likely that the general American public will start to make conclusions about Clarkson and her character based on this dispute, which does not serve her," Nierman added.

Kelly Clarkson rose to fame after winning the inaugural season of "American Idol" in 2002 and has since built a successful career as a singer and television host. (Art Streiber/NBC via Getty Image)

"Clarkson should do what she can to move past this, since she wants the first thing people think about her to be her musical accomplishments and not a petty and protracted fight over a singing birdie."

Honig said Clarkson should eventually "declare victory and move on," while Nierman suggested she ask her supporters to stop harassing the store.

"Kelly’s silence has been helpful and the right move," Nierman said. "But if she really wanted to win the day and come out permanently ahead, she could call on her fans to stand down and leave the store and its employees alone."

A representative for Clarkson did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Here is your weekly horoscope…

FREE WILL ASTROLOGY – Week of October 17, 2026
Copyright by Rob Brezsny, FreeWillAstrology.com

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22):
One morning soon, I predict you will open your inner eyes as well as your outer eyes and discover that you feel freer than you have in ages. Old specters that once pestered you will seem strangely powerless. Worn-out customs will have loosened their hold, and an ancient obligation will finally be settled. By some grace that neither you nor I can quite explain, at least some of the chains you fashioned in your own mind will have fallen away. What then? Celebrate! Host a personal “Out of Captivity” party, and give yourself a day or two to revel in your newfound liberty. Once you’re ready to make purposeful use of that delightful independence, ask yourself: “Where in my life do I most need a clean beginning?”

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21):
Not so long ago, you got hints and clues that you were on the verge of getting a taste of tantalizing and off-limits treats. Weren’t you ready to accept when the invitation suddenly dissolved? And by now, haven’t you nearly stopped expecting to enjoy another chance? Then imagine your surprise if that temptation winds its way back to you soon. When you finally take a bite, it may taste and feel nothing like you anticipated. The wisest move will be to let go of your old assumptions and welcome the experience as it is. My prediction: You’ll be delightedly surprised by how deeply and sweetly it alters the way you understand reality—even if at first it feels disorienting.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21):
Your upcoming challenges call to mind a feat once accomplished by conservationist and entertainer Steve Irwin. No, you won’t, as he did, feed a huge crocodile by hand while holding an infant in your other arm. But you may need to bring together qualities that seem at odds: fierceness and tenderness, a wild spirit and a protective instinct, boldness and love. Luckily, I am very sure you will summon the power and flair to do that.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19):
Ecologists have found that transition zones, like where forests meet meadows or where land meets water, can support high biodiversity. They may include species from both neighboring habitats as well as species adapted to the distinctive conditions in the boundary zone. I propose we make these places your power metaphor for the coming weeks, Capricorn. You, too, can flourish in edge habitats. Instead of feeling compelled to choose one identity, community, philosophy, or style, appreciate your role as a translator between worlds. Your greatest gifts may emerge because you refuse to belong exclusively to any single camp. Revel in your fertile in-between-ness.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18):
After pondering what might bring fresh vigor to your love life, I’ve arrived at an audacious suggestion: Offer a smoldering prayer while making love to a saintly soul in a place you regard as sacred. If that combination proves impractical, try just one or two parts of it: Pray wildly during an intimate encounter; flirt with or even seduce a person of uncommon goodness; kiss and hug and cuddle in a setting that feels holy to you; or speak to the divine in a titillating language you wouldn’t use in a formal religious service. The point is to let sensual delight and spiritual longing meet rather than keeping them apart.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20):
You sometimes regard pleasure like a reward you have to earn through suffering, as if joy were a luxury item requiring payment in pain. But I have an alternate theory: Relaxed glee and earthy enjoyments are essential nutrients that are key to your health. So in my view, denying yourself beauty and comfort depletes you. I hope you will heed my guidance in the coming weeks, which is to treat yourself to almost more fun, happiness, bliss, and amusement than is allowed by law. See if you can break all previous records for rejuvenating delectation. New law of your universe, at least for the next four weeks: The quest for jovial gusto and zesty zeal are mandatory aspirations.

ARIES (March 21-April 19):
Before Aries-born Maya Angelou became a celebrated author, she was San Francisco’s first Black female streetcar conductor, a calypso dancer, a cook, a journalist in Ghana, and an actress. She didn’t publish her first memoir until she was 41. She spoke six languages and refused to believe that any single identity could contain her. I offer her as your role model in the coming weeks, Aries. It’s time to celebrate the wondrous truth that you don’t have to be just one thing. In fact, the astrological omens suggest you’ll thrive by rejoicing in the many disparate selves you are and have been and imagining new ones you might like to add. How kaleidoscopic do you dare to be?

TAURUS (April 20-May 20):
Here’s a hypothesis worth entertaining: You don’t fully know everything you want. Not yet. Not at the core, where desire isn’t well-behaved but turns wild and intense. Your fluency with surface desire can sometimes keep you from excavating the mysteries that live below it. The familiar longings override the stranger, stronger ones that haven’t found their bearings. So there are aspects of your primal yearnings that remain unexamined, simply because they require a particular stillness and courage to unearth completely. The good news: Now is an unusually favorable time to go looking.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20):
Is your mental agility a gift or curse? It depends on whether you use it to avoid taking a stand or else deepen your understanding. In the coming weeks, Gemini, I hope you will practice the cagey skill of holding multiple truths simultaneously without letting that multiplicity become an excuse for never choosing or never committing. The goal is to encourage your magnificent mind to serve your heart rather than to override its tender wisdom. I love it when you unleash your clever analysis and it doesn’t devolve into sophisticated evasion.

CANCER (June 21-July 22):
Astronomers searching for planets around distant stars rarely see the planets directly. Instead, they notice tiny wobbles in the stars or faint dips in their brightness as the planets pass in front of them. You can and should practice a similar art now. Dramatic evidence may be unavailable, so watch for subtle shifts in mood, timing, synchronicity, and atmosphere. Small disturbances may reveal important hidden influences. Your most useful discoveries won’t come from looking harder but from noticing more gently.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22):
Glassblowers repeatedly place molten glass into blazing furnaces as they shape it. They don’t heat it once and expect it to stay pliable forever. Again and again, they return it to the fire so new possibilities become available. This reminds me of the current chapter of your life story, Leo. Emotional intensity keeps recurring, repeatedly returning you to the heart of the heat and pressure. This may sometimes feel like a test or ordeal, but I think it’s the best way for you to master the crucial lessons and ensure the healing transformations. Be patient as you forge your masterpiece.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22):
Master storytellers know that memorable heroes are admired because they continue moving despite uncertainty. Courage entails a resilient and affectionate partnership with doubt. I hope you’ll remember this if your confidence temporarily flickers in the coming weeks. There’s no need to waste precious energy trying to eliminate every hesitation before taking your next meaningful step. Let your questions accompany your convictions. They may sharpen your judgment. The coming weeks favor brave, thoughtful action, not flawless self-assurance.

six-flags-georgia-reopening-fatality:
It looked like a typical October evening at Six Flags Over Georgia. The sinking sun cast a golden light over families standing in line for haunted houses and rides. Children shouted, amped up on sugar and adrenaline, while orange leaves crunched under their feet.

Yet behind the amusement park’s ornate entrance gates, it was more than just a fun October evening. Friday marked the park’s reopening after the Monday death of a teacher, who fell from the park’s signature roller coaster, a teal and orange “hypercoaster” called Goliath, a 210-second ride reaching 70 mph and a height of 200 feet, according to the Six Flags website.

His family and the community are still reeling, and many questions remain unanswered after CNN analysis shows Goliath appeared to have passed recent safety inspections despite other alleged maintenance issues and guest injuries at several Six Flags parks.

Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, an Atlanta resident and “cherished member” of Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, died after falling from the coaster, according to police. Several other parkgoers were injured.

He was at the park with his fiancee and the family of her brother, Joshua Nelson, to celebrate the 13th birthday of one of Nelson’s daughters.

She was sitting next to Kariem on the ride, Nelson said, adding she has been “really strong and resilient” since the incident.

Four minors were injured in the incident, police said, but no further details about their condition will be released because of their age.

Parkgoers told CNN on Friday they started lining up outside the gates around 4:30 p.m. ahead of the park’s 6 p.m. opening. They expressed excitement to participate in annual Fright Fest events including haunted mazes and nighttime roller coaster rides.

One mother who said she visits the park about two or three times per week told CNN she and her children had just finished riding Goliath on Monday evening when she noticed people screaming and running.

She said the incident, while tragic, had no effect on their decision to return.

“It’s Fright Night!” She said, adding she teaches her children not to be “scared of anything.”

Other patrons had similar sentiments. “I feel bad for the family. My heart goes out to them, but you know, accidents happen,” a Texas grandmother told CNN while waiting to enter the park.

One Georgia native said his grandchildren were looking forward to an evening of fall break fun. “They’re concerned, they’re compassionate, but they’re not worried.”

An investigative team is conducting a review of the evidence, equipment and documentation, Georgia Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner John King said in a statement Thursday, to determine if state safety requirements were followed.

King is planning to hold a news conference next week with an update, he told CNN.

No investigative findings were released at a Friday news conference held by local authorities, with officials citing the active investigation.

Cobb County Police are assisting park and state officials as they work to determine a possible cause of the incident, according to Cobb County Chairwoman Lisa Cupid, who said verified information would be shared with the community “when it is appropriate.

“Agencies are still active and need space to do the work without speculation,” Cupid said, emphasizing the importance of Six Flags Over Georgia to the community.

“Our community deserves a fact-based review, a thorough review with clear answers when the responsible agencies are able to give them,” she added.

Sitting at the center of the park, Goliath has been closed since the incident, Cupid confirmed.

As the investigation remains underway, CNN analysis has revealed alleged maintenance issues and guest injuries at several Six Flags parks.

Safety records between 2016 and 2026 reviewed by CNN show Goliath appears to have passed annual state safety inspections.

“Goliath’s most recent OCI inspection occurred on March 16, 2026. No violations, deficiencies, citations, or red tags were reported during that inspection,” King said in a statement Thursday obtained by CNN affiliate WSB.

Records show some issues with Goliath, such as a ride inspection report earlier this year, which noted the bushings on the roller coaster needed replacement.   Bushings are components that help reduce vibration, according to WSB.

CNN has reached out to Six Flags to determine where the bushings are located.

Government records reveal mechanical failures, faulty restraint bars and broken bones at Six Flags theme parks

“Safety is at the center of everything we do,” Six Flags said on its website. “Daily inspections are undertaken by park teams, while third parties, including state ride inspectors, insurance inspectors and engineering experts, also regularly evaluate the rides.”

At least 10 roller coasters across six other Six Flags locations in the US and Canada are also closed “out of an abundance of caution” in the wake of Kariem’s death, a Six Flags spokesperson told CNN on Tuesday.

Six Flags Over Georgia remains “focused on supporting those affected and maintaining the safe operation of our park and attractions,” according to a Friday statement from the park’s president. “All other rides and attractions that were scheduled to operate will be available to guests, subject to normal operating conditions and availability.”

Goliath is manufactured by Bolliger & Mabillard, a Swiss company with a “stellar” safety record, according to Brian Avery, a professor at the University of Florida who specializes in ride safety and risk management.

Bolliger & Mabillard issued a statement calling Monday’s deadly accident “tragic” and offering condolences to those affected.

It said it is investigating but would have no further comment, “until we have a better understanding of what transpired.”

Goliath features a waist restraint but has no over-the-shoulder harness like some other roller coasters –– a secondary restraint Avery believes should be considered.

“If you have your primary fail, what are you left with? Yeah, nothing,” he said. “And it’s an impossible feat to stay contained if it did fail because of the forces, the speed.”

At the news conference, Cupid urged patrons to be “mindful” of the tragedy and communications from the park and the state as they plan their visits.

President Trump has famously pushed the bounds of executive power since he returned to the White House. In arguments Friday before a federal appeals court in Washington, administration lawyers will make an especially bold claim: that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump, not to the American people. The move comes amid a series of actions under Trump's second term to test the limits put in place after the Watergate scandal, and could be another case that ends up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Six months ago, the Justice Department moved to invalidate the Presidential Records Act, a federal law in place since 1978. Conservative lawyer Michael Edney cast the move in a long line of other attempts to pare back statutes from that era.

"This is a story about a post-Watergate, overbroad statutory incursion into the prerogatives of the executive branch," Edney said in a recent webinar sponsored by the Federalist Society.

For some 200 years, presidents could decide for themselves what to do with the papers they created in office, until disputes with Richard Nixon prompted Congress to weigh in. Every president since then has complied with the records law, until this year.

"The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and a clear violation of the separation of powers," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The White House's reinterpretation of the act comes after Trump was indicted on obstruction of justice charges for allegedly stockpiling classified documents in a bathroom, ballroom and office at his Mar-a-Lago resort. A federal judge threw out the case for technical reasons, related to the appointment of the prosecutor, and the Justice Department ultimately dropped the case after Trump won reelection.

Nikhel Sus is chief counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group that sued over the Trump move.

"If the courts were to accept it, and we are hopeful that they will not, it would mean the people really have no right of access to the president's papers and that would be a major loss for archivists, historians and to the American people writ large," Sus said.

Senior U.S. District Judge John Bates, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, ruled against the Trump White House this year, in a decision that opened with a passage from George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past," the judge wrote.

Three judges from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit will consider the issue on Friday.

The Trump administration said in court papers that keeping all those records imposes a burden on the White House and that it could chill advisers from having honest conversations with the president.

But former government officials say being able to consult these papers is essential.

"Access to the records on national security issues of former presidents is really vital for the continuity of our government," said John Bellinger, who served as legal adviser to the National Security Council under George W. Bush.

Bellinger said he and other members of Bush's staff sometimes requested the papers of President Bill Clinton, to understand conversations Clinton had with world leaders and members of Congress.

"Often the only record of what a president has said to a foreign leader — or perhaps even more important, what a foreign leader, friend or foe, has said to the president of the United States — is in a written document," Bellinger said.

To not be able to see those papers, he said, will leave future presidents at a "terrible disadvantage."

Edney, who also worked for Bush's National Security Council and Justice Department, said he believed that Congress could probably pass a "thoughtful" records preservation statute. He said parts of the current Presidential Records Act that provide Congress with automatic access and presume the records will be publicly disclosed are "constitutionally problematic."

Edney said he has some doubts about whether the watchdog groups suing to challenge Trump's move actually have legal standing to proceed.

But the Trump administration appears to have breezed past those concerns, because they have a higher goal in mind.

"They want this to go to the Supreme Court," Edney said. "I think they want this resolved at a time of their choosing, with arguments of their choosing, and a court of their choosing, and with the Solicitor General's office that's making their arguments, as opposed to a subsequent administration."

what-sets-japanese-sweet-potatoes-apart:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

If you’ve bought a Japanese sweet potato, cut into it expecting orange, and found creamy white instead, you’ve already spotted the first thing that sets it apart. The skin is reddish-purple, the flesh is ivory, and the flavor is sweeter and earthier than the orange kinds most of us grew up with. The nutrition is different too, so the difference isn’t just skin deep.

They have about 26 grams of carbohydrates per 103-gram serving, nine percent of the daily value for adults. But unlike a plain starch, they come with fiber, potassium, and vitamin C alongside. Registered dietitian Danielle Smiley of NutriDS, LLC notes they’re well-suited for people who are physically active: the carbohydrates fuel effort and help with recovery. Registered dietitian Alyssa Smolen puts the fiber at about four grams per serving, which is enough to keep you full for a while. She suggests building them into a meal with a protein and some healthy fat rather than eating them on their own.

Orange sweet potatoes are high in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A. Japanese ones run higher in vitamins C and E and carry more anthocyanins, the same pigments behind the color in blueberries and red cabbage. Research on different varieties shows considerable variation in carotenoids, flavonoids, and other plant compounds depending on flesh color. If you eat both types across the week, you get more of that range. They’re doing different things, basically.

There’s no target number. “There isn’t an evidence-based recommendation that says someone should eat a certain number of Japanese sweet potatoes per day or week,” Smiley says. Most healthy adults can have them regularly, even daily, as part of a varied diet. A small to medium potato is a reasonable portion, though how much you need shifts with activity level. “An athlete, for example, may need substantially more carbohydrates than someone less active,” she adds.

What matters more is variety overall. Leaning heavily on any one food, even a good one, tends to crowd out the grains, legumes, and other vegetables that supply things Japanese sweet potatoes don’t. They’re a solid addition to what you’re already eating, not a replacement for any of it.

The couple built their audience by sharing their journeys to far-flung, picturesque locations, travelling the country with their four children. Their established presence gives them significant influence within the so-called 'van life' community – a central issue in the court proceedings launched in late 2024 by Masterpiece Caravans.

In May, the photogenic family of nomads were ordered by default judgment to pay $1.2million to Masterpiece Caravans after the company alleged two YouTube videos breached a settlement agreement stemming from a dispute about defects the family had raised in their caravan.

In 2022, the Cartwrights purchased an Optimum CRZR 25' Quad Bunk 2023 for $198,550 from Masterpiece Caravans, before embarking on an Australia-wide road trip.

By August 2023, their idyllic life on the road was tested, with the Cartwrights alleging their van had a number of serious defects, which were disputed by Masterpiece.

A settlement was reached in November, with the Cartwrights returning the caravan for a full refund on the proviso they refrained from making disparaging comments and talking negatively about the company.

At-home health testing has been mired in overblown claims and outright fraud. But German startup TimeTeller, which has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm, is led by CEO Angela Relógio, who is the polar opposite of Theranos’ disgraced founder Elizabeth Holmes.

Relógio is a physicist-engineer and molecular biologist who spent years researching oncology, circadian biology, and systems medicine in Germany before leaving academia to build TimeTeller. She is careful about what the test can and can’t do today.

It would be easy to oversell: Relógio’s last name means “clock” in her native Portuguese, and TimeTeller has the potential to reduce side effects from cancer treatment and improve outcomes by timing treatment to each patient’s internal clock. That’s also why she’s careful to warn that TimeTeller itself operates on two timelines.

The long-term goal is to determine when cancer treatments will be better tolerated and most effective, and doing so much more granularly than just telling whether someone is a morning person or a night owl. But its direct-to-consumer kit won’t help patients figure that out on their own. “That is something that we need to calculate for every single medicine; we do that in the context of clinical studies,” Relógio cautioned.

According to Relógio, TimeTeller started accepting direct orders because of demand from longevity clinics, which focus on healthy aging and understand that individual data on a person’s circadian rhythm can be used to offer personalized advice on sleep, nutrition, light exposure, and physical activity.

TimeTeller could also apply to metabolic diseases (such as diabetes) and neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s), performance, and women’s health, but cancer is its core mission. It was while studying cancer that Relógio made the discovery that led her to leave academia.

She noticed that many cancer patients stopped or started their treatment because of side effects. “As a scientist, that was just impossible to watch, particularly when I was convinced that part of the problem might not only be what treatment we give, but when we give it,” Relógio said. This led her to develop the circadian rhythm test at the core of TimeTeller — which she knew had to become a company.

“I personally funded our first patent because I strongly believed that this discovery should not remain in scientific publications,” she said. The startup spun out of Berlin’s Charité university hospital but has since moved to Medical School Hamburg, which provided access to patients and funding. It also offered a fallback: backup employment for TimeTeller’s team of 10 if the company couldn’t pay them.

That’s a safety net TimeTeller may not need. Having enlisted biochemist and market access specialist Benjamin Dose as a co-founder, the startup secured a partnership with Techniker Krankenkasse, one of Germany’s largest health insurance providers. The partnership started out as a reimbursement deal in which the insurer pays back the cost of the test for a subset of cancer patients, and both sides are now ready to expand it to more of the insurer’s 12 million members, Relógio said.

Despite her caveats about the direct-to-consumer test, TimeTeller has become a solution that cancer patients can actually access. Ahead of her appearance at TechCrunch Disrupt, where Relógio appeared onstage today in San Francisco as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, she made clear that the company has broader ambitions: a future in which asking “when” is central to precision medicine, because “almost every process in our body is timed.”

Calls are pouring in for the U.S. Supreme Court to take up and stop California’s ongoing barfare against constitutional attorney John Eastman.

The Heritage Foundation’s Oversight Project and the America First Policy Institute (AFPI) filed amicus briefs on Tuesday urging the nation’s highest court to hear arguments in Eastman v. State Bar of California during its 2026 term. At least four justices must agree to hear a case before it can be considered by the full court.

At issue is California’s recent decision to strip Eastman of his law license over legal advice he gave President Donald Trump regarding the latter’s 2020 election challenges. The Claremont Institute senior fellow is one of several conservative attorneys targeted by the left’s barfare machine for his 2020 election conduct, with other notable victims including Ken Paxton and Jeff Clark, who signed onto the Oversight Project’s amicus filing as part of his role with the organization.

In their briefs, the Oversight Project and AFPI laid out several arguments on why the Supreme Court should grant Eastman’s petition to take up his case.

The Oversight Project contended that the California Supreme Court’s decision affirming Eastman’s disbarment rules afoul of the Constitution’s supremacy clause because the California Bar’s Review Department “conceded that strict scrutiny governs Eastman’s core political speech” advising the president, “then announced that the standard mattered only ‘[t]o the extent’ it was ‘relevant.'” “State tribunals,” the group reasoned, “cannot demote this Court’s First Amendment holdings to optional reading.”

The Heritage-aligned organization further argued that the California Supreme Court’s decision should be vacated because SCOTUS’s precedents indicate that the issues at play are strictly federal matters. “Put together, California had no authority to disbar Eastman on this record,” the brief reads.

🚨🚨🚨We've just filed our Oversight Project amicus brief in support of John Eastman's petition for certiorari to the U.S. Supreme Court asking the Justices to take up, and hopefully reverse, his disbarment in California.Our position is that Dr. Eastman's advocacy for…

Meanwhile, AFPI described Eastman’s disbarment as “the culmination” of the left’s ongoing barfare campaign targeting conservative lawyers they disagree with. Allowing such a scheme to succeed against Eastman, they noted, “threatens attorney independence, the right to counsel, and public trust in the integrity of the profession.”

“State bar regulated attorney discipline exists to protect the public and ensure that political influences present in everyday politics do not dictate attorney-client relationships or infect the integrity of the profession,” the filing reads. “Hijacking attorney disciplinary processes for political vendettas harms not only attorneys and their clients, but also the public’s trust in the fairness and impartiality of our judicial system.”

“Amici call upon this Court, the Court of last resort for Petitioner and many others, to protect the independence and neutrality of state bar disciplinary proceedings from outside organizations and maligned actors who seek to weaponize those proceedings against their political and ideological opponents,” it added.

The AFPI brief was signed by Conservative Partnership Institute senior legal fellow Cleta Mitchell, Judicial Watch senior attorney Christina Bobb, former Trump Justice Department senior official Ed Martin, and numerous others.

The Supreme Court has not scheduled Eastman’s petition for distribution at any of its upcoming conferences as of this article’s publication, according to the case’s docket file.
