cornells-president-responsibility:
We’re apparently at the part of this “Cornell Seven” saga where the Ivy League university’s president needs to go through a ritualistic struggle session, enshrined by the political left, and he chose the most fitting location: The New York Times.

In an interview published this week, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff, surely having already tortured himself with grubby lawyers and P.R. midwits, said he was sorry for an incident he had no control over, the details of which are unclear (even the people directly involved are in dispute about what happened).

“I think that this is a problem that relates to 20-year-olds, 21-year-olds leaving home for the first time,” he said, “coming into an environment where there’s access to alcohol, where there is unfortunately in some cases access to drugs. And they’re not prepared. And of course they’ve been exposed to social media, pornography, misogyny.” He described the fallout of the “gang rape,” as alleged by a woman known publicly as Jane Doe, as “a challenge for us” at Cornell. “We have to respond by building character, judgment, responsibility, care for each other.”

I’m so sorry something happened that I had no part in and that actually may not have happened at all. Please don’t hurt me!

It’s the part where Kotlikoff mentioned “character, judgment, responsibility” and “care for each other” that’s most important. So he does understand those concepts, though either not in the way he should or not in such a way that he’s willing to demand them of the school’s student body.

Everything we know about Jane Doe’s allegations between the night of the incident in October 2024 and now is that in the days immediately after, she was adamant that what happened was consensual, legal, and of her own volition. About two weeks later, she seems to have changed her mind about what she told those involved, and her sorority sisters who learned about it. Then last month, she filed a lawsuit against seven of her peers at Cornell and others, claiming she was gang-raped and was incapable of controlling anything that happened after she got drunk at her sorority house. That includes her attendance at two bars, where she continued to drink, and her solitary foot commute to a fraternity house, where she snorted ketamine.

All of that, according to Doe’s lawsuit, was someone else’s problem to handle, to ensure she remained the angel she was in her own mind right up until intoxication. It wasn’t up to her, a 20-year-old woman, to take care of herself. Why should it have been?

By the way, things like character, judgment, responsibility, and caring for one another aren’t the purpose of universities, even elite ones. It’s in the purview of parents and loved ones to impart those things to children, into adulthood. A little reinforcement doesn’t hurt, but at the moment of legal maturity, a more passive approach is presumed: mutual respect and courtesy, not overt instruction. Not to put too fine a point on it, but everyone has to eventually accept responsibility for himself (or herself, as the case may be).

If Cornell’s president should be “sorry” for anything, it’s for perpetuating a certain environment at the university. It’s apparently not one of responsibility.

WASHINGTON — Russian diesel is expected to reach the American market before the Nov. 3 midterm election, sources told The Post — as fuel costs hit a record $6.53 per gallon last month.

The fuel “should be here in the next two weeks if we get everything done,” one American source told The Post, noting Russia agreed to send “a pretty substantial” amount.

Trump announced Friday that he was suspending US sanctions on Russian diesel exports — with Russian President Vladimir Putin also lifting a diesel export ban imposed last year.

The sources did not specify the exact plans to ship Russian diesel to the US and Trump had previously framed the deal as easing global price pressure.

“That’s not being released to us,” Trump told reporters Tuesday. “That’s a diesel deal that’s going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices.”

Trump reached the deal with Putin after growing frustrated with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s ambitious campaign to blow up far-away Russian oil refineries, damaging all major hubs and putting upward pressure on prices.

The US repeatedly asked Zelensky not to hit Russian refineries, but Ukraine “ignored” the requests, prompting Trump to make the diesel deal.

“When you hit refineries, that hurts American consumers, and that’s not acceptable,” a US source told The Post.

Zelensky fumed about the fuel arrangement with Russia — calling it a “weak” decision that would fund Russia’s ongoing invasion. Still, he belatedly agreed to the US president’s demand not to strike refineries.

Experts have estimated the diesel deal could generate $4 billion in new revenue for Moscow.

Trump on Sunday announced a limited “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine.

A US official said that Russia — which Zelensky accused of violating the pact by immediately striking natural gas facilities — only agreed not to hit Ukraine’s oil refineries and gas stations if Kyiv stops its drone assault on Russian refineries.

Ukraine has no operating oil refineries, but in theory could rebuild them during the pause.

Putin did not agree to cease attacks on other targets in Ukraine, including its electricity grid.

Trump has taken other actions to address high diesel costs, but they have had little impact, including allowing untaxed “red dye” diesel to be more broadly purchased by drivers.

The national average cost of diesel is currently $6.30 per gallon, nearly double the $3.66 of one year ago and down only slightly from an all-time high of $6.53 in late September, according to AAA data.

Those costs are passed on to consumers, with inflation rising again in September to an annual rate of 3.7%.

Trump’s efforts to tamp down costs come as Republicans face a potentially bleak midterm election with polling showing broad disenchantment, despite the president’s coast-to-coast barnstorming to advertise accomplishments such as new tax breaks and more promising data on job gains and foreign investment.

Fuel costs have risen dramatically over the past year, largely as a result of Trump’s nearly eight-month war with Iran that throttled shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Flock CEO Garrett Langley said the company’s gunshot-detection microphones detect “just gunshots,” but Flock’s website paints a far broader picture of what other ambient audio also gets picked up.

Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, the co-founder of the surveillance company defended Flock’s audio-collection product called Gunshot Detection, which listens for gunshots and other ambient audio across nearby neighborhoods to provide “earlier awareness” to potential public safety events.

Flock’s website says that the company’s audio systems can pinpoint gunfire instantly, while also being able to “detect street takeovers early to stop chaos before it escalates,” and “identify severe crashes in real time so help arrives faster.” It also says they can “expand awareness beyond gunfire with alerts for car crashes, fireworks, and sideshows.”

The company’s Gunshot Detection feature, announced last year, faced immediate pushback. In announcing the feature, Flock said the technology would listen out for sounds of “screaming.” Privacy groups condemned the company for listening for human voices, prompting the company to amend its website to instead say “sounds of human distress.” Flock later said it pulled the ability to detect “distress” altogether from its customers who tried it.

During the interview, Langley pushed back against what he described as misinformation about his product, arguing that many of its critics misunderstand how its products work. The comments come as public opinion continues to shift against Flock and other license plate reading companies amid growing unease about mass surveillance — sentiments that were visible in San Francisco, where protesters gathered to voice their opposition outside the venue as Langley took the stage.

“Most people don’t call 911 when they hear a gunshot, and so that’s why we built the product,” Langley told TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos onstage. “And then some of our customers said, ‘Oh, we have these in parking lots. It would be great if we could get alerted if someone was being abducted, if someone was being harmed.’”

Langley said that the idea seemed logical, so the company prototyped it and rolled it out to a couple of customers, but said that some people then had a lot of concerns. Langley conceded to making mistakes but that he was listening to his customers.

“There’s only a couple customers that were prototyping it with us, and we said, ‘OK, great, it’s just going to do gunshots, plain and simple.’ If a gun goes off, we’ll notify, and if not, that’s all it’s going to listen to,” said Langley.

When asked about the contradiction between his remarks and the company’s marketing materials that say the audio systems can detect more than gunshots, he responded, “It’s just gunshots.”

When reached by TechCrunch, Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said: “Flock’s gunshot detection technology is primarily used to detect gunfire but is also capable of detecting fireworks, sideshows, and potential car crashes. CEO Garrett Langley’s remarks were intended to emphasize that Flock’s Audio Detection technology is not designed to monitor conversations or analyze speech and does not currently detect human screaming or distress.”

An FAQ section of the website notes that “in addition to gunshots, Flock Gunshot and Audio Detection can detect fireworks, sideshows, and other disruptive community events.” It goes on to state that the company’s “detection library is continually expanding to include emerging threats that are relevant” to customers’ specific needs.

Langley stated that the number of Flock’s microphones is comparable to ShotSpotter, which as of 2024 had about 25,000 microphones, per reporting by Wired.

Langley’s comments come amid mounting scrutiny of Flock from privacy advocates, including the ACLU, and members of the public who are concerned about the misuse of its technology, with some going so far as destroying the surveillance cameras. The remarks also come as Texas and Florida have moved to end their relationships with Flock, and Amazon’s Ring has ended its partnership with the company.

Former federal prosecutors are pushing back on Democrats' accusations that the Trump administration violated Justice Department policy by searching the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., just weeks before an election.

"It's difficult to not point out the dirty hands of the people that might complain about election interference," Jim Trusty, a former federal prosecutor, said, pointing to former special counsel Jack Smith's prosecution of President Donald Trump ahead of the 2024 election.

"Democrats definitely can't contend that it's a politicized investigation after everything that happened in the Trump era," Abhishek Kambil, a former federal prosecutor, told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, released a lengthy statement alleging that the Justice Department violated protocol by conducting "overt actions in politically-sensitive matters in the 60 days before an election."

HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)

"Just 22 days before the elections, this is blatant political intimidation and an attempt to interfere with the Congresswoman’s reelection," Raskin wrote in his press release.

But Kambil pointed out that the U.S. Department of Justice Manual, which outlines procedures for federal criminal investigations, does not explicitly impose a 60-day period before elections in which investigative actions can't be conducted.

"The 60-day requirement is not something that's in the justice manual," Kambil told Fox News Digital. "That's basically an unwritten practice of what DOJ typically does, and the justice manual itself does not have the time frame on that."

Kambil said that any actions which could be perceived as influencing an election will require prior approval from either the attorney general or the deputy attorney general.

The Justice Department has long followed an unwritten practice known as the "60-day rule," which discourages politically sensitive investigative actions close to an election. The practice came under scrutiny in a 2018 DOJ inspector general report examining former FBI Director James Comey's decision to notify Congress of new developments in the Hillary Clinton email investigation just 11 days before the 2016 presidential election. The watchdog concluded that Comey had disregarded longstanding department policy and practice, calling his decision a "serious error of judgment."

"It doesn't create a ban; it just creates effectively a consultation requirement to higher level leadership before it can happen, but there is no statute or anything else preventing this," Kambil told Fox News Digital.

The Justice Department also was accused by President Donald Trump of ignoring its "60-day rule" when special counsel Jack Smith filed a revised indictment against Trump just 70 days before the 2024 presidential election. Weeks later, Smith submitted a 165-page brief outlining evidence against Trump in the federal election interference case, which was made public just 34 days before the election. Alex de Minaur has taken a giant stride towards clinching another ATP Finals berth after roaring into the last eight of the Shanghai Masters.

Continuing to defy the hip flexor injury that threatened to end his season less than a week ago, de Minaur downed dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov 6-3, 6-4 to jump to seventh place in the Race to Turin's live standings.

Crucially, Australia's baseline warrior has leapfrogged Novak Djokovic and Frances Tiafoe, who have already been eliminated in China, as he chases more valuable rankings points in the quarter-finals — and potentially beyond.

Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

But Alexander Zvererv, who will be the year-end world number one, stands in his way after the German beat Alexander Bublik 7-6(6), 4-6, 7-6(1).

In his fifth encounter against Khachanov, de Minaur knew efficiency was key.

"It was really important for me to serve well and I think I definitely did that, especially down the stretch," he said.

"I got into a little bit of trouble, a couple of love-30 games, and I was able to find some good serves when I needed it."

De Minaur, who reached the semi-finals at the prestigious season-ending tournament last year, cut a forlorn figure after being forced to retire early in the second set of last week's China Open final against Djokovic, when a set down.

"I know that once I'm fit physically and mentally, I'm the player that I [want to be] and I'm excited to be competing and going to the tail end of these tournaments and feeling great about myself."

“I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe… have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts?” the comedian continued, speaking directly to live audience members.

Gillis went on to make a joke about women dressing in revealing attire while exercising at gyms and then becoming offended if they catch men looking at their bodies, adding, “And don’t look. You’re not allowed to look.”

“For real, don’t look, because they are filming. I’m in the background of, like, ten TikToks right now,” the comedian further quipped.

Viewers took to social media to express their frustration with Gillis’ joke.

“I hate this fucking guy,” another declared. “He wants to be the pied piper of knuckle dragging shitheads so bad.”

“The worst thing they can say about women is that we wear shorts,” another said. “How dare women wear SHORTS while EXERCISING.”

Actor Dan Levy also called out Gillis, describing the comedian as a “misogynist,” and even bizarrely going as far as to suggest the joke equates to “complacency” that leads to “sexual assault.”

“Women wearing short shorts to the gym does not make them whores,” Levy proclaimed puritanically, adding, “It makes the men calling them whores misogynists.”

By ALEXA LARDIERI, US HEALTH EDITOR

Published:  06:34 AEDT, 14 October 2026   |  Updated:  07:57 AEDT, 14 October 2026

Two people have died from a mosquito-borne disease that is surging across the United States.

The deaths occurred in two North Carolina residents who had contracted West Nile virus, according to the state Department of Health and Human Services.

The department did not release details on the deceased or where in the state the deaths occurred.

Local media had reported that three people tested positive for West Nile virus in Mecklenburg County, home to 1.2 million residents in the south-central part of the state around Labor Day.

Two people in Cabarrus County, home to 225,000 people also in the south-central part of the state, got the virus in August.

The first positive West Nile virus case in North Carolina was in Gaston County, home to 227,000 people in the same region, at the beginning of August.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports 15 cases of West Nile virus in North Carolina.

Cases of mosquito-borne diseases and mosquitoes carrying dangerous pathogens, including West Nile virus, are increasingly spreading across the US.

Two people have died from mosquito-borne disease West Nile virus in North Carolina

Your browser does not support iframes.

Warmer temperatures, rapid urban growth and global travel are all helping the mosquitoes – and the disease – expand into places where they have never been a problem before in numbers larger than typical.

While most patients who contract West Nile virus have few or mild symptoms, some may suffer potentially life-threatening brain swelling, along with infections and paralysis.

West Nile virus is transmitted by a bite from Culex mosquitoes and is most common in Great Plains states like North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska and Colorado, though cities like Los Angeles, Chicago and Dallas-Fort Worth also record high levels due to large populations.

Many of these states have also extended mosquito season, which runs from late spring through early fall, due to the increases in mosquito prevalence later in the year.

The disease usually causes no symptoms, but in one in five patients, it can lead to fever, headaches, nausea, diarrhea, joint pain and pain behind the eyes.

About one in 150 cases are neuroinvasive, a severe complication when the virus penetrates the blood-brain barrier and travels to the meninges, causing meningitis and potential paralysis.

CDC data shows there have been 1,328 cases of West Nile virus and 1,004 cases of West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.

Forty-five states are reporting cases.

The above map shows diagnoses of West Nile Virus by state

Last year, there were 2,167 cases of West Nile virus in total.

It's unclear how many of last year's cases were neuroinvasive, but CDC data shows there were 1,342 hospitalizations for neuroinvasive disease.

There were 172 deaths recorded last year.

Older adults, people with weakened immune systems and those with certain chronic conditions face the highest risk of severe illness due to West Nile.

Survivors of severe West Nile illness may experience long-lasting complications, including memory problems, chronic fatigue, muscle tremors or permanent neurological damage.

West Nile virus can be prevented primarily by avoiding mosquito bites.

CDC officials recommend using insect repellents that contain the ingredient DEET, wearing long sleeves and pants outside and staying inside between dusk and dawn during the summer.

63 years ago today, the second, and often considered best film starring James Bond, was released as From Russia With Love. In the film, Bond, played by Sean Connery, is sent to assist in the defection of Soviet consulate clerk Tatiana Romanova in Turkey, where SPECTRE plans to avenge Bond’s killing of Dr. No. by using Romanova as bait in a cleverly laid trap. The film was a critical and commercial success, grossing $78 million worldwide while critics found the film nonsensical, illogical, lurid, mad, and absolutely delightful because of it. READ more… (1963)

The British Film Institute’s screen-online guide called the film “one of the series’ high points” and said it “had advantages not enjoyed by many later Bond films, notably an intelligent script that retained the substance of Ian Fleming’s novel while toning down the overt Cold War politics (the Cuban Missile Crisis had only occurred the previous year).

The casting for the role of Tatiana included English, Italian, Swedish, Danish, and Polish actresses, but none who could actually speak Russian.

The score was written by John Barry traveled with the crew to Turkey at the request of the studio to try to get influences of the local music for the many scenes shot in Istanbul, but ended up using almost nothing apart from finger cymbals to give an exotic feeling, since he thought the Turkish music had a comedic tone that did not fit in the “dramatic feeling” of the James Bond movies.

Recalling his visit to Istanbul, John Barry once said, “It was like no place I’d ever been in my life. [The Trip] was supposedly to seep up the music, so Noel Rogers and I used to go ’round to these nightclubs and listen to all this stuff. We had the strangest week, and really came away with nothing, except a lot of ridiculous stories.”

More Good News on this Date:

19 years ago, Sheikh Muszaphar Shukor Al Masrie became the first-ever Malay to enter outer space when he rode up to the International Space Station aboard a Soyuz TMA-11 with the Expedition 16 crew. An astronaut and orthopedic surgeon, Alma Matter of Manipal University, Shukor Al Masrie performed experiments on live cancer cells to catalogue the effects of things like leukemia in space. He is the only Malaysian, representing the 20th nation, to visit the space station.

Since Sheikh Muszaphar is a Muslim, and as his time in space coincided with the last part of Ramadan, the Islamic National Fatwa Council drew up the first comprehensive guidebook for Muslims in space.

The 18-page guidebook is titled “Guidelines for Performing Islamic Rites (Ibadah) at the International Space Station”, and details issues such as how to pray in a low-gravity environment, how to locate Mecca from the ISS, how to determine prayer times, and issues surrounding fasting. The orbit of the ISS results in one day/night cycle every 90 minutes, so the issues of fasting during Ramadan are also addressed. (2007)

70 years ago today, the epic Western drama film Giant was released. Focusing on the struggle between wealthy oilmen and cattlemen in Texas in the mid-20th century, the film starred Elizabeth Taylor, James Dean, and Rock Hudson.

Giant was the final of Dean’s three films as a leading actor—and earned him his second Academy Award nomination, before he was killed in a car crash prior to the film’s debut. George Stevens won the Oscar for Best Director.

Martin Scorsese said in the 70s, “I’ve seen this film over forty times. There’s more here than people have seen. It has to do with the depiction of a lifestyle through the passage of so many years. You see people grow.”

A huge box-office success, the film’s earnings of $35 million for Warner Brothers were not surpassed until the 1970s with their release of Superman.

In the story, Dean is given a small plot of land, bequeathed by the rancher’s sister after her death. He toils until one day he strikes oil. He becomes wealthy, but rots inside from the unrequited love he maintains for the rancher’s wife through the decades, even after taking her daughter as a lover. The film also explores racism in the South, with Rock Hudson defending Blacks and Hispanics at the local cafe when they are unwelcome and thrown out. Another subplot centered around Taylor, who was raised on the East Coast, refusing to be deferential to men, as was customary in Texas, just because she was a woman. WATCH the scene where ranch hand James Dean strikes oil and express, in vain, his love for the rancher’s wife, Elizabeth Taylor… (1956)

And, on this day in 1902, the Gibson Guitar Company was formed in Kalamazoo, Michigan. It was founded with the intention to make mandolins, by Orville Gibson, a luthier with no formal training. The company ended up building one of the world’s most iconic guitars, the Gibson Les Paul in 1952—a solid-body electric instrument designed by their V.P. Ted McCarty and famed guitarist Les Paul.

Mr. Gibson invented the archtop design for his instruments, which made them louder and more durable, by constructing the same type of carved tops used on violins. The musical innovator never saw the riches that were distributed to the businessmen who took over the company, but only was paid for his hourly labor. By the 1930s, after Orville’s death, the company made one of the first commercially available hollow-body electric guitars, like the ES-150 popularized by Charlie Christian.

46 years ago today, Pac-Man first debuted—and it went on to become the highest-grossing video game of all time. The arcade game was deliberately designed to appeal to women as well as men, eschewing the popular war themes of the day, and instead using characters that were cute and colorful.

Its designer, Toru Iwatani, was 24 at the time and for a year led a small team of nine at his company (Namco, of Japan). With so many instant fans eager to gobble up all the dots in its maze, while avoiding the 4 ghosts, Pac-Man within a year had grossed over $1 billion in quarters.

The character named in Japanese after its shape—a hockey puck—generated more than $14 billion for Namco and is indeed the highest-grossing video game of all time. (1980)

And, on this day in 1868, Carlos Manuel de Céspedes issued the Grito de Yara in Cuba (the Cry of Yara), proclaiming Cuban independence, which began the “War of 10 Years”.

That morning, after sounding the slave bell (indicating it was time for his plantation slaves to work), they stood before him waiting for orders and Sr. Cespedes announced they were all free men—and invited to join him and his fellow conspirators in battle against colonial Spain. For this, he is called Padre de la Patria, Father of the Homeland.

Happy 57th Birthday to Brett Favre, the NFL football legend who became the first quarterback to throw for over 70,000 yards, complete over 6,000 passes, and tally over 500 touchdowns in his career.

At the helm of the Green Bay Packers for 16 years, he became the first player to win the league’s MVP Award three years in a row. A graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, where he grew up, Favre led the Packers to victory in Super Bowl XXXI and he also was the starting quarterback in an astonishing 297 consecutive games—321, including the playoffs, through 18​1⁄2 seasons—an all-time record, and the one for which he says he is most proud.

He joked around constantly and played the game like a kid, but Brett was the only athlete to become a grandfather while an active NFL player. After retirement, he became the offensive coach for a Mississippi high school that soon after won a state championship. (1969)

Editor’s note: This article discusses mature themes.

We’re wasting an awful lot of time talking about “consent” and sexual regret right now, thanks to a young woman suing several men she had group sex with at Cornell University, when we really should be talking about the powerful effect of not consuming hard drugs.

TMZ this week published newly revealed text messages between who we now know as Cornell’s “Jane Doe” and one of the Chi Phi fraternity members she accused of gang raping her two years ago. “[I]f you have any regrets or anything you want to talk about i am always here to talk about it cause that was a lot,” Doe wrote in one of the messages. “i really do love u and matt and i promise i wont get quiet and weird w u like i did last time.” The name Matt appears to be a reference to another one of the men she is accusing, though public evidence shows she justified and defended their sexual engagement in a similar message to him as well.

And here’s the truly relevant message she sent to one of the accused, as reported by TMZ: “ps. i’m not sure if u remember but i did ket off your d–k at some point?” she wrote. “[A]nd i honestly think that was one of the most insane/jaw dropping moments of the night.” Her use of the word “ket” is apparently a reference to the drug ketamine, which her own lawsuit indicates she snorted an alarming amount of on the night in question.

That brings us to where we should have been all along. College students, ladies in particular, don’t do hard drugs. Especially when it involves a group of men.

We don’t know yet what exactly happened in October 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity house with Jane Doe. We probably never will. But all public evidence currently indicates a 20-year-old woman got drunk at a sorority house, went to a couple of bars, then went to a frat house where she met a male friend and initially agreed to a threesome that ultimately included drugs and may have included other men.

No one begrudges a college student, whether male or female, drinking underage. If she’s legally old enough to have died for her country, she can have as many drinks as she wants (so long as she’s not caught). But drinking comes with consequences. Everything does. That includes consuming hard drugs.

Jane Doe reportedly said in other text messages days after the night of partying that she could only “sleep and cry all day.” Without concluding whether she was raped, that testimony isn’t discernibly different from any person who has done hard drugs and is on a come-down. Drugs like ketamine create a hyper sense of euphoria while it’s in the system. And once it’s gone, the user crashes. Depression and anxiety are normal. Those feelings are almost certainly heightened when the user engaged in risky behavior while under the influence. That’s true whether it’s ketamine or alcohol or Adderall.

There’s a lawsuit playing out and now, potential criminal charges. Regardless, there’s a big lesson to be learned. Don’t do drugs and just stay in school.

As the iconic U Street Ethiopian restaurant prepares to close, thousands on social media shared their praise and memories

The outlet is pitching its newly robust metro section with ads and activations around town

The Revada Arts Center will be home to a theater company, film house, and “anti-opera” collective.

The presumptive mayor is pledging a new approach. But can she push past critics?

Ward 4 Councilmember Janeese Lewis George says her young son, Pierce, lights up and points whenever he sees a Metrobus approaching. The District’s presumptive next mayor is similarly enthusiastic when it comes to bus travel.

She chose to mark the annual “Week Without Driving” by riding the D44 from Petworth to her office in the Wilson Building with a small clutch of pro-transit organizers, chatting all the while about the bus-centric projects she hopes to bring to fruition as mayor. That includes one particularly near and dear to Lewis George’s heart: the installation of dedicated bus lanes along Georgia Avenue.

The project, which could speed up buses on one of D.C.’s busiest corridors, has been in the works for years, but it has yet to expand beyond a few blocks. As commuters languished in late-morning rush hour traffic a few feet away, Lewis George said that sort of inaction will end after she takes the reins of the city government.

“We don’t need to study the study,” Lewis George said. “We've been talking about this for a decade. Let's get it done. My goal is to have the infrastructure investment there and the will to actually deliver on these projects.”

Her pledge, much to the delight of the transit enthusiasts on board, is that she’ll “empower” her DDOT director to “unstick stuck projects.” Ironically enough, that’s a catchphrase that’s been deployed many times over the years by Lewis George’s predecessor, Mayor Muriel Bowser—though the current executive generally uses that mantra to refer to major development deals, not bus lanes.

Indeed, Bowser has frequently attracted the ire of the urbanist set by hemming and hawing on such projects or folding in the face of neighborhood opposition and budget concerns. Citing the Connecticut Avenue bike lanes, the D.C. streetcar, the D.C. Circulator, and smaller projects, activists argue the outgoing administration has had a tendency to pitch big transit plans but retreat when the going got tough. Lewis George is promising a different approach.

“The loudest person doesn't get to influence basic safety infrastructure that we know works,” Lewis George said. “It's time that we stop believing that everyone has to love an idea in order for an idea to happen. That's not what governance calls for us to do.”

Those comments will be music to the ears of readers of Greater Greater Washington, the prominent pro-transit group that organized the bus ride, after years of an uneasy relationship with Bowser. She aligned with the organization’s interest in building more housing in the city, but transit was another matter entirely — the group memorably had to go to court to compel the mayor to release a study on congestion pricing.

But Lewis George’s approach will come with its own pitfalls. While she may not worry about pissing off the most dogmatic opponents of such transit projects (such as Nick DelleDonne, the anti-bike crusader who has been busy attending her citywide listening sessions), that doesn’t mean she has nothing to fear by pushing past those “loudest” voices.

Bowser’s decisions may have frustrated advocates, but they generally came because she was listening to constituents, including nervous business owners on Connecticut Avenue and influential church congregations in Shaw who felt they were being pushed out of the neighborhood. (Her critics argue she was too deferential to those voices, overall, but she did still oversee a substantial expansion of the city’s bike infrastructure.) A new mayor, still hoping to win over skeptics and launch an ambitious first-term agenda, may prove similarly sensitive, regardless of what she says on the campaign trail.

And unlike Bowser, who largely governed during D.C.’s boom times, Lewis George will take over as the city’s economy faces serious challenges. She might want to do things like build new bus lanes or find a new dedicated funding stream for Metro, but that would likely require serious tradeoffs elsewhere across the budget.

Perhaps Lewis George’s biggest test will come along H Street, where Metro General Manager Randy Clarke dreams of running a dedicated lane for buses to connect Union Station to the new RFK stadium (a concept generally described as “bus rapid transit”).

If this new “Gold Line” sounds a lot like the original plans for the D.C. streetcar, that’s no mistake. Clarke has been forthright about his interest in righting what he sees as the design choice that doomed that project to failure, pitching it as a solution that will give fans more transit options to reach the stadium beyond the cramped Stadium-Armory train station.

“That's what the streetcar should have been and it wasn't,” Clarke said on WAMU’s The Politics Hour with Kojo Nnamdi in July. “I think everyone acknowledges that system design failure.”

But it’s not as if the gridlock on H Street was unpreventable – planners recognized 20 years ago that the service would only be successful if it ran along dedicated lanes in the middle of the road, avoiding frequent conflicts with traffic and parked cars. A major reason that never happened is the same reason any dedicated lane project faces pushback: complaints from businesses and drivers that they would reduce parking and increase congestion. It was simply less controversial to design the streetcar such that it ran alongside parking lanes.

The city advanced plans several years ago to address some of the issues by creating new priority lanes on H Street, but Bowser scrapped them before they could ever be installed, citing budget pressures. The streetcar’s shuttering followed soon afterward.

If Lewis George hopes to avoid history repeating itself, she’ll have to confront the issue head-on when she assumes office. And she may have an uphill battle to fight in doing so. Ward 6 Councilmember Charles Allen, the chair of the Council’s transportation committee, has already criticized Bowser’s plans for the RFK area for making no more than a “passing reference” to the Gold Line. Council Chair Phil Mendelson also recently sounded a note of skepticism of the wisdom of “spending tens of millions on dedicated transit down H Street,” a notable statement given his decisions to pull funding away from the streetcar.

“The commitment to the [bus rapid transit] line seems uncertain, far less certain than the construction of giant parking garages there,” Cheryl Cort, policy director at the Coalition for Smarter Growth, said at a Council hearing on the subject last week. (Plans for a behemoth parking garage have already drawn indignation from the neighboring community.)

But Lewis George says she’s invested in such transit projects, and she plans to meet dissenters  with “communication and transparency” that “help people understand why we're taking those steps.” The next few years will test her commitment to that approach.

“If we get more people out of cars and onto transit, we can transform our city,” Lewis George said. “I hope more people buy into that.”

Americans should rise up in defense of Somali immigrant Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) after federal officials searched her house, says Bill Kristol, the former neoconservative and current NeverTrump leader.

“Now is the time for all good men to come to the aid of their country.” Kristol posted on X after the search was announced.

Kristol also offered an excuse for possible citizenship fraud by Omar, who is reportedly the daughter of a former general in a Somali warlord army. He wrote:

Trump’s DHS raids Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home because of paperwork filled out by her father in 1995. The Trumpists are desperate. But loyalists at powerful agencies will obey orders. Desperation is dangerous.

The evidence is murky, but Omar may have lied about her birth date to get automatic citizenship as a dependent of her father. But she has also been accused of aiding widespread welfare fraud by Somali-managed businesses in Minnesota.

“I’m ok,” Omar tweeted midday, adding:

Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.

In 2017, Kristol said the federal government should import migrants to replace most Americans, saying:

A MAN WHO made an “idiotic decision” to pick up a visually impaired woman in his car who believed he was a taxi driver has been jailed for false imprisonment.

Dublin Circuit Criminal Court heard that the woman had been socialising with a friend. They went to a taxi rank in the early hours of 8 May 2022, where they tried for some time to hail a taxi to bring the woman home.

Nicolae Zgherea (30) stopped his car at the taxi rank and spoke to the woman’s friend who believed his response confirmed he was a legitimate taxi driver.

The woman got into the car and after realising there was no taxi licence or meter displayed, she asked Zgherea if he was a taxi driver.

When he confirmed he was not a taxi driver, she asked him to pull over but he continued driving. She called 999 and put her phone on loudspeaker, with the emergency operator also asking Zgherea to pull over, which he did. The court was told the call lasted just under two and a half minutes.

Zgherea, of Fox Park, Finnstown Abbey, Lucan, Co Dublin, pleaded guilty to false imprisonment.

David Perry BL, prosecuting, told the court the plea was accepted by the Director of Public Prosecutions on the basis that Zgherea recklessly took actions which amounted to the false imprisonment of the woman.

Today, Judge Orla Crowe imposed a sentence of four years. She suspended the final 12 months of that sentence on strict conditions.

Judge Crowe said she was particularly struck by the woman’s “courage and fortitude” in the face of everything she went through. She noted the significant impact it had on her.

She said given the woman had a white cane with her at the time, it was indicative to anyone that this was someone with a visual impairment.

Judge Crowe also noted that Zgherea had not stopped when the woman realised he was not a taxi driver and asked him to pull over, noting that she had to ultimately call emergency services.

She commended the emergency service operator who eventually convinced Zgherea to pull over and noted that the woman was still in the car when gardaí arrived in a distressed state.

“It was an utterly terrifying experience for a young woman who had the courage and bravery to re-engage in society after Covid,” Judge Crowe commented before she accepted evidence that the woman was unable to work for a period of time afterwards and that Zgherea had “robbed her of her safety and security”.

Judge Crowe also noted from the woman’s victim impact statement that due to her disability she has to take “a significant leap of faith” and put herself in the hands of strangers and rely on their goodness and kindness.

Judge Crowe set a headline sentence of five years before imposing a term of four years. She took into account mitigating features including the fact that Zgherea had written a letter of “unreserved apology”, that he has a strong work history and is the father of two young children.

Defence counsel, Karl Moran BL, said that his client made an “idiotic decision” to stop his car with the intention of picking up the woman and her friend for financial gain and had no right to do this.

Moran said his client apologises unreservedly for his actions and accepts he had no lawful right to do what he did.

Counsel noted this would have been a “terrifying experience” for the woman, who expressed its impact “very eloquently” in her statement.

The court was told the woman is visually impaired and describes herself as almost completely blind when it is dark.

In a victim impact statement read to the court by her brother, the woman outlined that what happened continues to have a significant effect on her.

The woman said she must trust that strangers will not take advantage of her as she cannot always rely on the vision she has left to read a person’s body language and their intentions.

She said what happened that night has affected her trust in others, her independence and her confidence.

She described enjoying a night out with a friend, the relief of getting a taxi, then her disbelief and panic when Zgherea told her he was not a legitimate taxi driver.

She said her first thought was: “I guess this is just my turn. This is what happens to people like me.”

She said she considered opening the door and jumping out of the moving car.

She said what happened felt much longer than it was and “like it would never end”.

The woman said she experiences flashbacks and questions daily why this happened. “Was I targeted because of my gender, disability, or both?”

She said while she never felt completely unsafe before this happened, she did have an underlying fear of being more vulnerable as a woman and as a visually impaired person.

She said the lifelong consequences for her feel inherently unfair, but she is slowly rebuilding her confidence, trust in others and independence.

Garda Ciara Parsons gave evidence that Zgherea was not a taxi driver and not operating a taxi when he stopped at the taxi rank.

The woman and her friend were holding their extendable canes while waiting at the taxi rank, the court heard. After she got into the car, her friend left to catch his bus.

After becoming aware it was not a legitimate taxi, the woman asked to be let out immediately and Zgherea responded that he would drive her home safely. The woman insisted she wanted to get out, with Zgherea continuing to drive even after she rang 999.

The court was told the audio of the emergency call includes Zgherea being asked repeatedly to stop by the woman. After two minutes and 27 seconds, Zgherea confirmed he had pulled over, gave his correct name and said that the car was on Mespil Road.

When gardaí arrived, Zgherea was still in the car along with the woman, who was in a distressed state.

When interviewed, Zgherea admitted he was not a taxi driver. He claimed the woman put out her hand to stop him, sat into his car and then he decided to bring her home.

He said he did it without thinking and denied that the woman had asked if he was a taxi driver before they were already on the road.

He accepted that the woman asked him to pull over, but said they were in a bad location and that he pulled in a short distance later.

He denied the woman was scared and that he kept her in the car.

Zgherea pleaded guilty on a trial date. The court heard that the charge of false imprisonment relates to the period when the woman realised he was not a taxi driver, her requests to leave the car and where he stopped.

He has 11 previous convictions, all for road traffic offences.

Gda Parsons agreed with Moran that his client’s guilty plea was of assistance to the prosecution.

Moran noted that his client said he was not aware that the woman was visually impaired. It was accepted that this differs from the woman’s account that Zgherea was aware of her disability.

Counsel noted that the emergency call transcript states around the one-minute mark that the woman asked his client to pull over in a safe place, and he agreed to do this.

A letter of apology was submitted, which the woman did not wish to receive, the court was told.

He submitted his client was bringing the woman to her address and had no bad intentions towards her.

Counsel noted the parties were not known to each other, that there were no threats or physical violence, though he acknowledged the woman understandably felt threatened by the situation.

Moran asked the court to consider the short time span of his client’s offending and his co-operation.

Zgherea is married with two children and works full-time. Moran said Zgherea’s family are financially dependent on him and will be affected by the decisions he made.

The cold-case murder of an 8-year-old Chicago girl that remained a mystery for over 65 years was finally cracked with the help of new DNA technology — and her killer turned out to be one of the very people who was supposed to protect her, a cop.

New DNA evidence gathered from a genetic ancestry website led Chicago Police Department investigators to suspect former Chicago homicide detective Thomas Francis McInerney was responsible for the death of little Gloria Kowalewicz on Nov. 12, 1960, the Chicago Tribune reported.

Gloria’s murder shocked the Windy City more than six decades ago after her body was found in a ravine miles from her family’s West Englewood home. She had been shot twice in the head.

The little girl was last seen starting off from home on a short walk to a nearby church in order to receive communion.

The shocking murder ignited a massive manhunt for the killer by local and state police, as well as volunteer help from local firefighters, Boy Scouts and veterans, the Tribune reported.

Investigators made some progress – deducing that Gloria hadn’t been killed until she was taken to nearby woods and collecting eyewitness reports of a little girl seen with a young man, but they hadn’t been able to identify a suspect.

The investigation was finally broken open earlier this year, the outlet reported, after the FBI was able to connect McInerney, who was 24 at the time, to the crime scene thanks to DNA submitted to a family tree website.

Further testing of DNA, fingerprints and ballistics led the department to conclude that McInerney, an Army veteran who lived around the corner from Gloria, was responsible for the little girl’s death.

CPD’s Chief of Detectives Kevin Bruno praised the dedication of investigators who’d worked tirelessly on the case for over six decades, telling the Tribune it was proof “we don’t forget.”

“The fact that he was a police officer is deeply troubling to all of us that have made a career out of this most noble profession,” Bruno told the outlet. “But at the same time, it’s not something we’re going to minimize or shy away from.”

Gloria’s brother Adam Kowalewicz said that he was relieved that his sister’s killer had been identified, and had hoped it would allow his parents, who have since passed, to “rest.”

Still, Kowalewicz is frustrated that McInerney, who died in 2006, was able to escape justice for his actions.

“He never paid his dues,” Kowalewicz told the Tribune. “You hope he’s going to pay his dues with the good lord.”

McInerney was on the Chicago police force for 28 years and then worked for the Federal Public Defender’s Office in both Las Vegas and Reno as an investigator until retiring in 2004, according to an online obituary. He was named Outstanding Federal Defender Investigator in 2003.

Family for McInerney, who was a dad of five — including three daughters — and grandfather of many, could not be reached for comment.

The family of a man who died during an NYPD scuffle that started over an open can of beer claims the cops used excessive deadly force, according to a new lawsuit.

Shelton Ennis — a 54-year-old reputed ex-con on parole — died June 26, 2025, after NYPD probationary Officer Karl Yelenic pursued and tackled him during what started as a routine front-up in Upper Manhattan, court documents said.

“[Ennis] lived in the area. He was enjoying a pleasant night,” said the family’s lawyer, Michael Pecorella, to The Post. “There’s no reason why it should have had to end this way.”

Body-worn camera footage showed Yelenic and Officer Marc Leandre exit their vehicle near Riverside Drive and West 136th Street and approach Ennis, who was leaning against a stone wall around Riverside Park holding a black plastic bag.

Ennis — who was once charged with attempted murder and ended up doing nearly 26 years behind bars over vicious drug raps, only to seemingly be on his way to turning his life around, according to the New York Daily News  — had apparently just tossed a beer can.

“Why you throw it away?” Leandre said.

Ennis responded that it was empty, but Leandre continued to ask four more times why he threw it away, video showed.

Leandre then asked Ennis for his identification, and the man said he had it at his apartment nearby, according to the footage.

“I’m not bothering nobody,” Ennis told the cops.

“I just came out the house for a little second to relax before I go to work tomorrow,’’ said the man, who coworkers told the News was a “residents’ assistant’’ at the Skyline Hotel in Hell’s Kitchen.

When officers asked for his name, Ennis falsely told them Cedrick Ennis, according to the attorney general’s report on the man’s death.

The video showed Ennis repeatedly tell the officers that he would show them his identification if they took him to his apartment.

“We don’t do that. … The thing we do, we take people back to the precinct, and you can call someone. … Drinking in public is a violation,” Leandre said in the body-camera footage.

Ennis replied, “Call your sergeant.

“I’m not going nowhere.”

A few moments later, the footage showed Ennis start to run between the two officers.

Yelenic pursued  Ennis and tackled him to the ground from behind, according to the video.

After Yelenic stood back up, footage from his body camera showed Ennis lying unconscious face-down on the ground.

“Rather than render emergency and immediate aid, defendant officer Leandre immediately handcuffed Shelton behind his back,” the lawsuit said.

After handcuffing the unconscious Ennis, the officers called an ambulance to take him to the hospital.

Medical records said Ennis lost his pulse while in the ambulance. He was pronounced dead after arriving at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital.

The medical examiner determined the cause of death to be hemopericardium due to blunt impact to the chest.

The ME ruled the death a homicide, although that does not indicate a crime has occurred. Acts of self-defense and the lawful use of force by police are two examples of homicide, or a death involving another person, that would not necessarily result in criminal liability.

The state attorney general’s office, which must conduct probes into every death involving some kind of police action, interviewed Yelenic, who said his intent was to apprehend and handcuff Ennis, not to tackle him and make him fall.

At the time of the incident, Yelenic was a probationary officer who joined the NYPD less than a year before. The NYPD’s Force Investigation Division, which probes cop-involved incidents, is still looking into the case, officials said.

The Police Department would not say whether the officers are still on the job.The AG’s investigatory unit has already decided not to seek charges against anyone, concluding that there was not significant evidence to prove that Yelenic’s force was unlawful.

“There is no evidence that the officer intended to cause injury, nor evidence of criminal recklessness or criminal negligence under the law,” the report stated.

But in the lawsuit filed by Ennis’s family Sept. 22, the dead man’s brother, Aaron Ennis, who is being repped by the law firm Fredson Statmore Bitterman, alleges numerous civil-rights violations by the city and the two involved officers, including over the use of force, reputed negligence and alleged unlawful stop.

“We’re hoping that you know the city does the right thing for this family,”  Pecorella said.

NEW YORK CITY — Somaliland’s President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known colloquially as “Irro,” told Breitbart News in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) that American President Donald Trump is a “great man” who can “make more history” than he already has by formally recognizing Somaliland as its own country.

Somaliland, a partially recognized nation-state inside of Somalia, has been fighting in recent years to fully break away from Somalia over the corruption, terrorism, and piracy that dominate Somalia. Somaliland has won formal recognition from its first country, the state of Israel, which came late in 2025. While it does not have formal recognition from others yet, the partially recognized country has been building deep ties with the West in a significant way in recent years, positioning itself as pro-American and aiming to align closely with Trump in particular.

“Well, I think President Trump is a great man,” Abdullahi told Breitbart News in an exclusive interview in his hotel suite in midtown Manhattan in late September. “He made history, and he could make more history by recognizing a new country called Somaliland, which will cooperate unconditionally in the fight against terrorism, in the fight against piracy, in the fight for marine security, and safer world trade routes as well, in a strategic, very important location.”

Abdullahi said that the ports in Somaliland, particularly in the coastal city of Berbera, are able to handle major shipping companies’ needs and are already moving large quantities of goods.

“Berbera, as I said, has a very strategic location, and now, because of the certain conditions in the world which now exist regarding the war, even some of the world’s largest shipping companies now use Berbera to bring their goods, and later they ship again to their destinations because of security reasons,” Abdullahi said. “So Berbera’s need and demand is increasing, and Berbera is a viable port that can handle large containers as well.”

He also made clear he supports Trump getting the Nobel Peace Prize for everything he has done worldwide to end major conflicts, including the longest war in the world, which is on his continent of Africa — between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda.

“I may be on the record that I am the first African leader to refer the president for a Nobel Peace Prize, because so far for the short time he has been in office, he has resolved many conflicts in the world,” Abdullahi told Breitbart News.

During his trip to the United States, while he has not yet gotten the U.S. to move towards formal recognition of Somaliland, Abdullahi said it was a productive couple of weeks in Washington and then New York for the UNGA.

“We had a very cordial, friendly reception in the United States,” Abdullahi said. “We had a productive week in Washington, and met with congressmen. We met with senators. We met with the administration, including the State Department, the Department of War, the Department of Energy, and Department of Treasury. We also met prestigious institutions in Washington, and I have a speech here at the CFR in New York. Yes, we also spoke and met with different organizations in the United States and New York. We have met with some friendly countries, some organizations as well.”

While formal recognition has yet to materialize, Abdullahi told Breitbart News that so far the “level of engagement” between the United States and Somaliland has Somalilanders “satisfied” for now.

“Well, we are actually satisfied with the level of engagement we had in the United States now,” Abdullahi said. “We didn’t get the recognition now on the table, but hopefully things will move forward, and we make great progress, and we are satisfied with the level we have so far done.”

He also told Breitbart News he sees ties between the U.S. and Somaliland—which already exist on anti-piracy, counterterrorism, and economic fronts — deepening in the coming years. Part of that, he argued, is the strategic use of Somaliland’s ports.

“No doubt I see a great future cooperation of the United States and Somaliland, and it is not the first time that the United States is using the ports of Somaliland during an administration,” Abdullahi said. “They use it; they prepare a port as a base or as a facility, and before them, the Russians were using it. So we also see that Somaliland has the capacity to be a very large trade corridor to Africa, into landlocked Africa, including Ethiopia, which is about 130 million people, and many other nations beyond to East Africa and Central Africa. We can be a logistic hub for the whole world because now the importance of Somaliland is increasing, so it can be a very great logistical hub in the whole world.”

Africa is increasingly seen by world leaders as a majorly rising region in the world, with hundreds of billions of dollars in outside investment pouring into a continent rich with natural resources — something Abdullahi is quick to highlight as a major opportunity for the world’s leaders.

“Economically, $400 billion are now in Africa,” Abdullahi said. “So Africa is important for the United States, for Europe, and for great economic powers because Africa now has the highest resources in the whole world in minerals, in energy, in agriculture, in industry, so Africa now is the future.”

The geopolitical significance of Somaliland, Abdullahi further argued, is only increasing with the rise of the Houthis in Yemen and with Iran’s intransigence in the Strait of Hormuz.

“For 35 years we have been single-handedly securing our waters, which is very important for the world global trade,” Abdullahi said. “Only 100 kilometers from Yemen, Somaliland was always in a strategic location, but now, because of the problem in Hormuz, the problem in Yemen, Somaliland’s strategic importance is more important now, and the world is paying a lot of attention to our country, to our location, to our geography, to our patriarchy. So, Somaliland is very important for the world in general and for the world security, for water-time security, for the safety of world trade.”

He said the counterterrorism ties between the U.S. and Somaliland are in discussion to deepen — and there is room for more economic ties.

“We are already in discussion with the United States on cooperating with counterterrorism,” he said. “We’re ready to partner with the United States, and also Somaliland historically was fighting alone, single-handedly, as I said, against terrorism and piracy. I see there is a great opportunity for the partnership between the United States and Somaliland in economy, in trade, in security, in counterterrorism, in national security, and more.”

Israel’s recognition of Somaliland as its own country, Abdullahi said, was a game-changer for Somaliland.

“I think I can say that the recognition by Israel of Somaliland was the icebreaker,” Abdullahi said. “Now Somaliland is feasible to the whole world.”

With regard to Gaza, he said Somaliland is ready to commit 2,000 peacekeeping troops to the Board of Peace efforts led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and by White House special envoy Steve Witkoff.

“I think I have been questioned by one reporter about what we can do in Gaza,” Abdullahi told Breitbart News. “I told them we can provide 2,000 peacekeepers in Gaza. Yes, we are ready for that.”

Abdullahi added that he wants Americans to know that despite the issues with Somalia, in Somaliland there is a bright future with endless opportunity.

“For those who read, my message is that there is an existence of a very democratic, peaceful country called Somaliland, very strategically located,” Abdullahi said. “For the president again, my message to the president is that he can make history by recognizing Somaliland as a country, a democratic partner, a security partner who can cooperate unconditionally, fight against terrorism and piracy.”

Abdullahi also wants Americans to know that Somaliland is not looking for handouts or government aid, but for opportunities for partnership in the future.

“My last message is that we — as a Somalilander — we didn’t come here for a list of requests or aid,” Abdullahi said. “We came with partnership. Somaliland is not for aid; it is not for handouts. Somaliland needs partnership in trade, in security, and economic cooperation. I think Somaliland can be part and parcel of making America great.”

analysis

By Russell Jackson

Topic:Cricket

Steve Smith's incredible catching points to an Australian Test win in Durban, with time the greatest concern for the tourists. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

What is it that separates the best cricket teams from the merely good ones? There were hints sprinkled throughout an absorbing day three of the Durban Test, in which Australia's most formidable obstacle on the path to victory is now time.

All the fundamentals Australia had to get right with the ball today, it did: tight lines, safe hands, bowling in partnerships to coherent plans. In the face of this, South Africa simply lost its head.

The Proteas scraped together a first innings total of 284 — a 106-run deficit that Nic Maddinson and Travis Head extended to 139 by the time bad light prematurely stopped play for the third day running.

With his epic 190 in Durban, Matt Renshaw not only changes the game, but shows he is capable of the real Test batting the Australian cricketing public is longing for.

But the moment of brilliance that highlighted Australia's edge in this context came not from a bowler or batter, but in the field: Steve Smith leapt like a salmon for four highlight-reel catches that moved him to the top of the all-time list for Test catches, and one in particular will linger in the memory long after this game is done and dusted.

It was Smith's third catch of the day, aptly reviewed by his most vocal teammate: "Oh my God, Smudge," bellowed a disbelieving Marnus Labuschagne. For that one, Smith seemed to have a better idea of the flight path of Kyle Verreynne's reverse sweep of Nathan Lyon than the batsman did.

Darting to his right from the standard slip position while the batsman was still constructing his shot, Smith then dived at full stretch to reel in the catch, like a security guard nabbing a shoplifter before he'd even fully grasped his loot.

The English cricket writer John Arlott once settled on a similar scenario as an exemplar of what makes Australian cricketers a different breed. It was a catch taken by Sid Barnes in a tour match during the 1948 Invincibles summer.

Like Smith, Barnes was something of an eccentric. On this particular day, he was going to field a bat-length away from Essex batsman Ray Smith at silly mid-on. "You can't drive me away," Barnes warned the batsman, but Smith gave it a go, thumping a drive so crisply it ricocheted off Barnes's boot and out to the boundary.

When a silent Barnes refused to budge, Smith tried it again, crunching an even lustier blow directly into the Australian's chest, whereupon an unflinching Barnes stuck out his hand, caught the deflection and repeated himself to the dismissed batsman: "You can't drive me away."

Arlott dubbed this attitude "Australianism". Steve Smith has it in spades. It was not just the sheer absurdity of the Verreynne catch, nor the skill it required, but the domineering attitude Smith was projecting: you shall not pass.

Otherwise, it was Australia's bowlers and their captain's efficient organisation of them that told the story of the day.

Where Temba Bavuma had let things slide for the home team on day two, Pat Cummins was a model of enterprise, rotating his attack as the circumstances demanded while bowling with tremendous vigour and skill himself to take three wickets.

The disappointment, as far as the hope of a more even contest goes, rests on the shoulders of South Africa's top order, which had teased early in the day. An 84-run second-wicket partnership between World Test Championship final hero Aiden Markram and the stylish number three David Bedingham was hurtling along at four an over and at that point, the game looked like a genuine contest.

Aiden Markram looked set for an important innings for South Africa before Mitchell Starc sent him back to the pavilion on day three. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

As is so often the case, up stepped Mitchell Starc to take the initiative. The left-armer came around the wicket, pulled back his length and roughed up the batsmen with a nasty blow to the hands for both. Soon after, Markram was gone. Later, like clockwork, Starc returned to nip another 50-run partnership in the bud.

And as has usually been the case in Australia's recent run of 13 wins in 16 Tests, each of the frontline bowlers posed his own unique problems for the Proteas. Cummins attacked the off-stump relentlessly. Josh Hazlewood sat in cruise control, slightly back of a length, impossible to get hold of for long.

Unlike the local spinners, who'd been paddled and swept into submission by Matt Renshaw, Nathan Lyon was at his jagged, probing best and deserved more than his two wickets.

"Bavuma — caught Smith bowled Lyon 3 (26)" doesn't read too dramatically, but the Proteas skipper was subjected to a genuine ordeal before finally losing the plot and departing the same way as Verreynne.

There lay another telling difference between these two sides so far: whereas Australia's imposing total was, in the end, built on discipline and patient accumulation, the South Africans constantly lost the micro-battles.

Bedingham, who made a sparkling 49, was denied scoring shots for a frustrating 20-minute period before finally losing his patience. Trying to move things along when there was no need, Travis Stubbs and Wiaan Mulder squandered starts with similarly impetuous shots.

From South Africa's perspective, what was so deflating about the general approach of the top six was that bad light had already truncated this game significantly and was likely to continue to do so. The tail battled gamely, but it's unlikely it'll be enough this time around.

The remaining questions are how quickly Australia can get to a defendable total and how many overs it reasonably expects to be played. Advantage Australia, in other words.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz discusses agency safety efforts amid a reported plague outbreak in Russia at WSJ's "Future of Health" summit Wednesday. (Credit: The Wall Street Journal and WSJ The Future of Health, Oct. 7)

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is coordinating with federal agencies to monitor travelers entering the United States from Siberia amid concerns about a possible pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia, the agency's director revealed Wednesday.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said the Trump administration is working across multiple agencies to identify travelers arriving from the region following the mysterious death of a Russian laboratory worker, while emphasizing that the risk to Americans remains minimal.

"We are very confident that the threat to the United States is extremely low," Schwartz said during a Wall Street Journal health forum Wednesday.

MOTHER OF DEAD RUSSIAN ANTI-PLAGUE INSTITUTE WORKER: 'I KNOW THE TRUTH'

Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died after developing pneumonia of an unknown cause, prompting quarantines and heightened health precautions in the region. Russian authorities say testing has found no evidence her illness was linked to pathogens she worked with. (East2West news)

The concerns stem from the Oct. 2 death of Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, whose death has fueled speculation about a possible pneumonic plague infection.

Russian authorities have maintained that Shipilova died from pneumonia of unknown origin and have not confirmed that she was infected with Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes pneumonic plague.

Schwartz said the CDC is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State and War, among other federal agencies, to track potential arrivals from the region.

"There are about 200 flights that come into the United States from Siberia, that region," Schwartz said, adding that those flights typically arrive at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport.

"We have a port health station set up in JFK so that we can do appropriate surveillance and screening if anyone from that area comes into the United States," she continued.

The CDC director stressed that while pneumonic plague is a serious bacterial infection capable of spreading between people through respiratory droplets, early detection and treatment can prevent deaths.

TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP'

The Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz to be the next director of the Centers for Disease Control. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"The one good thing, if I could say there's a good thing, is that it's a treatable, highly treatable bacterial disease with common antibiotics that most physicians within the United States can utilize," Schwartz said.

The illness is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is considered the most serious form of plague, according to the CDC. Symptoms can include fever, chest pain, coughing and rapidly developing pneumonia. Without prompt antibiotic treatment, the infection can be fatal, the agency warns.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has pressed Moscow for additional information about Shipilova's death.

Russian authorities placed approximately 200 people who had contact with the deceased laboratory worker under quarantine, according to Euronews. On Thursday, Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said preventive measures had been completed and roughly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no pathogens, according to the Associated Press.

RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS

A view of the entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk on Oct. 7, 2026. (TATYANA MAKEYEVA / AFP via Getty Images)

However, Russian officials have not publicly identified the pathogen responsible for Shipilova's pneumonia or definitively ruled out pneumonic plague as the cause of her death, according to The Associated Press.

Asked whether Moscow was being sufficiently transparent with American authorities, Schwartz indicated that the administration was still seeking answers.

"We are still having those conversations about what exactly happened in Siberia," she said, adding that U.S. officials were working with information about an unconfirmed case of pneumonic plague.

There’s no amore lost between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the local Italian-American community.

Mamdani is skipping the Christopher Columbus Day parade up Fifth Avenue on Monday, The Post has learned.

The snub isn’t a huge surprise as the mayor has often railed against the explorer, bashing him as a colonist that abused and displaced Native Americans.

In a June 2020 social media post, Mamdani gave the finger to a statue of Christopher Columbus in Astoria, Queens and said, “Take it down.”

But Italian-American civic leaders said the mayor’s no-show is the latest example of Hizzoner downplaying the community’s contributions to the Big Apple and US.

“He’s disrespectful to the Italian-American community and not coming to the Columbus Day parade confirms it,” said Angelo Vivolo, chairman of the Columbus Heritage Coalition representing more than 50-Italian-American organizations.

“We know he hates Columbus. But the parade celebrates the rich culture and heritage of Italian-Americans.”

Mamdani also riled up local Italian-Americans when he released an ethnic enclave map that listed little-known communities in the five boroughs but omitted Little Italy and Arthur Avenue in the Bronx.

Mamdani did issue a nearly three-minute video statement celebrating Italian Heritage Month.

He paid tribute to Italian immigrants who helped build the city and honored East Harlem Rep. Vito Marcantonio, who fought for Social Security, unemployment benefits and civil rights.

Mamdani, a staunch critic of Israel who has accused the Jewish state of genocide, also boycotted the Israel Day parade in May.
