international-day-of-the-girl-child-2026:
Celebrated every year on 11 October, International Day of the Girl is a global moment to celebrate girls everywhere, amplifying their voices, actions and leadership. It belongs to everyone who cares about girls and their rights. On this day, we come together to recognize and advocate for the full spectrum of girls’ rights.

This year’s theme was developed through consultations with girls, girls’ organizations and girl-led networks as well as civil society organizations and United Nations partners. Together, they called for urgent action to end child marriage and invest in girls’ rights – our 2026 theme.

Every girl deserves a childhood. Every girl deserves the freedom to learn, to grow, to make her own choices and to define her own future. Yet millions of girls are still denied that freedom.

Each year, more than 12 million girls - roughly one every three seconds - are married before reaching adulthood, with the highest prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa (31 per cent). Child marriage remains one of the most widespread violations of girls’ rights, denying millions of girls the chance to stay in school, protect their health, live free from violence and fulfil their potential. It can have severe and lasting consequences for girls' physical and mental health, increasing risks of social isolation, depression and emotional distress at a time when self-harm remains one of the leading causes of death among adolescent girls aged 15-19 globally.

But this is not inevitable. Thanks to investments in girls’ education, legal reform and social protection, an estimated 68 million child marriages have been averted over the past 25 years, proving that progress is possible when girls are supported and their rights are protected. We have the solutions: keeping girls in school; expanding access to health, protection and social services; working with families and communities to challenge harmful norms; investing in girls’ rights and supporting their leadership.

Now we must go further - and faster. It is in our power to ensure that every girl, everywhere, can realize her rights and fulfil her potential. For when girls are safe, educated and empowered, they don’t just transform their own lives, they help build healthier families, stronger communities and more peaceful, prosperous societies.

This International Day of the Girl, stand with girls.

Raise your voice for girls’ rights. Champion the solutions that help girls stay in school, stay safe and shape their own futures, especially in crisis and humanitarian settings. Challenge the harmful norms that continue to drive child marriage in communities around the world.

Advocate for laws, policies and investments that prevent child marriage and uphold girls' rights. Amplify girls' voices and leadership, ensuring girls are part of the decisions that affect their lives and futures.

"I was just a child and suddenly got married. Before I had time to recover from the shock, I got pregnant.” This was Salma's life at 15. Forced into marriage, she suffered gender-based violence. But her story didn't end there. Watch her inspiring journey: She's now back in school, pursuing her dream of becoming a doctor.

In 1995 at the World Conference on Women in Beijing countries unanimously adopted the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action – the most progressive blueprint ever for advancing the rights of not only women but girls. The Beijing Declaration is the first to specifically call out girls’ rights.

On December 19, 2011, United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 66/170 to declare October 11 as the International Day of the Girl Child, to recognize girls’ rights and the unique challenges girls face around the world.

The International Day of the Girl Child focuses attention on the need to address the challenges girls face and to promote girls’ empowerment and the fulfilment of their human rights.

Adolescent girls have the right to a safe, educated, and healthy life, not only during these critical formative years, but also as they mature into women. If effectively supported during the adolescent years, girls have the potential to change the world – both as the empowered girls of today and as tomorrow’s workers, mothers, entrepreneurs, mentors, household heads, and political leaders. An investment in realising the power of adolescent girls upholds their rights today and promises a more equitable and prosperous future, one in which half of humanity is an equal partner in solving the problems of climate change, political conflict, economic growth, disease prevention, and global sustainability.

Girls are breaking boundaries and barriers posed by stereotypes and exclusion, including those directed at children with disabilities and those living in marginalized communities. As entrepreneurs, innovators and initiators of global movements, girls are creating a world that is relevant for them and future generations.

The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by world leaders in 2015, embody a roadmap for progress that is sustainable and leaves no one behind.

Achieving gender equality and women’s empowerment is integral to each of the 17 goals. Only by ensuring the rights of women and girls across all the goals will we get to justice and inclusion, economies that work for all, and sustaining our shared environment now and for future generations.

Women and girls represent half of the world’s population and, therefore, also half of its potential. Gender equality, besides being a fundamental human right, is essential to achieve peaceful societies, with full human potential and sustainable development. Moreover, it has been shown that empowering women spurs productivity and economic growth.

Compelling evidence shows that investing in adolescent girls is not only the right choice for advancing gender equality and the rights of girls and women, but also a smart economic decision. Strategic investment in adolescent girls is essential to building a fairer, more prosperous, and gender-equal world. Learn more

International days and weeks are occasions to educate the public on issues of concern, to mobilize political will and resources to address global problems, and to celebrate and reinforce achievements of humanity. The existence of international days predates the establishment of the United Nations, but the UN has embraced them as a powerful advocacy tool. We also mark other UN observances.

The Texas law enforcement community is in mourning following the death of Texas Special Operations Group (SOG) Staff Sergeant Sterling Matthias Shelton, who passed away on October 8, 2026. The Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) staff sergeant fought a courageous 15-month battle with aggressive brain cancer that was discovered when he suffered a heat stroke in July 2025.

The DPS announced the 29-year-old’s passing on Friday, drawing a massive outpouring of grief, prayers, and tributes from across the Lone Star State.

“The Texas Department of Public Safety mourns the passing of Staff Sergeant Sterling Shelton following his courageous battle with cancer,” the agency said in a statement published on social media. “We honor his service and the lives he touched throughout his career. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, and DPS family during this difficult time. Rest in peace, Sergeant Shelton. Your service will never be forgotten.”

Staff Sergeant Shelton dedicated seven years of his life to DPS — including four with the elite Special Operations Group (SRT-5). He was known for his “extraordinary strength, determination, and willingness to help others,” both on and off duty. In July 2025, what began as symptoms resembling heat stroke led to the discovery of a massive 6-centimeter brain tumor, resulting in a diagnosis of grade 4 astrocytoma—an aggressive form of brain cancer.

Despite enduring multiple brain surgeries, intensive chemotherapy, and radiation treatments, Shelton continued to fight, determined to spend as much time as possible with his wife, Raven, and their two young children, Ember Joy and Tyler Vance, according ot a post by Fox San Antonio reporter Ryan Wolf.

Shelton’s wife, Raven, walked closely alongside him through the final days of his life, which he spent peacefully at home surrounded by family, friends, and his close-knit “Tribe 5” team.

“It is the greatest privilege and honor to be your wife and to be the one to walk you to the other side,” Raven wrote in a heartbreaking post shared after his passing. “I will tell the kids about you, we will keep going, and we will carry your strength with us every day.”

Beyond his service as a decorated Texas Ranger SOG Staff Sergeant, Shelton was an avid runner, ultramarathoner, and dedicated family man who took great pride in being greeted by his wife and kids when he returned home from operations. He was also awarded an honorary black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu during his cancer fight, showcasing the relentless grit and resilience that defined his life.

The Texas Municipal Police Association (TMPA) also joined the state in honoring Shelton’s legacy. “Staff Sgt. Shelton dedicated his career to serving and protecting the people of Texas,” the association stated. “His commitment to duty, his fellow officers, and the communities he served will not be forgotten.”

Shelton is survived by his wife, Raven; daughter, Ember Joy; son, Tyler Vance; his parents, Blain and Stacie; and his siblings, Spencer, Summer, and Ciera, alongside an extended law enforcement family and many loved ones.

Minton-Chatwell Funeral Directors in Borger, Texas, is handling funeral arrangements. Supporters are urging prayers and messages of love for the Shelton family and the entire Texas DPS community as they navigate the loss of a devoted guardian of the Lone Star State.

Die Verhandlungen rund um den Daten-Omnibus im Rat sind in einer heißen Phase. Derzeit sieht es so aus, als würde die von NGOs kritisierte „Pauschalerlaubnis“ für KI-Training beschlossen.  Während die Mitgliedstaaten kurz vor einer Einigung stehen, liegen die Lager im Europäischen Parlament noch weit auseinander.

Die französische Regierung bekämpft die landesweiten Schülerproteste mit Repression und Polizeigewalt. Polizeiexperten und Menschenrechtsorganisationen kritisieren Massenverhaftungen und Übergriffe. Hunderttausende schreckt die Gewalt nicht ab, sie demonstrieren im ganzen Land weiter.

Mit der Deutschland-App will Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger die öffentliche Verwaltung zügig digitalisieren. Umsetzen soll das Projekt die Telekom. Doch die Bundesregierung hat keinen Überblick darüber, was der Konzern genau macht, wie die Antwort der Bundesregierung auf eine Kleine Anfrage zeigt.

Wenige Monate vor ihrem Start fehlten der digitalen Brieftasche entscheidende Funktionen, kritisierten Fachleute bei einer Anhörung im Bundestag. Verbesserte Sicherheit sei nötig, um Vertrauen für d‑you zu schaffen.

Wer Europa als Opfer eines digitalen Kolonialismus inszeniert, negiert historisches Unrecht und übersieht den Ausweg aus Europas selbstverschuldeter Unmündigkeit. In dieser Debatte vergaloppiert sich nicht nur Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer. Ein Widerspruch.

In Sachsen-Anhalt steht die Machtübernahme durch eine als rechtsextrem eingestufte Partei bevor. Das Projekt „Safeguarding Research and Culture“ will nun vorsorglich Daten sichern und ruft zur Mithilfe auf. Vorbild sind ähnliche Aktionen zur Datenrettung aus den USA.

In Kürze soll der gesetzliche Umbau der Geheimdienste durch den Bundestag gebracht werden. Eine bessere Kontrolle der Geheimdienste steht der massiven Ausweitung der Befugnisse allerdings nicht gegenüber. Nicht erst seit dem Skandal um den Ex-BND-Chef Hanning wäre dies jedoch dringend nötig.

Große Unternehmen sollen mehr Steuern zahlen und damit zum EU-Budget beitragen, hat die EU-Kommission im Vorjahr angeregt. Einem Medienbericht zufolge will sie ihren Vorschlag nun anpassen: Herauskommen könnte eine Digitalsteuer, die so nicht heißen darf.

Bundesjustizministerin Hubig hat den Entwurf für ein Gesetz gegen digitale Gewalt erneut nachgeschärft. Hinzugekommen sind Straftatbestände für Fake-Accounts und das Abrufen von Vergewaltigungsvideos sowie der Anspruch, strafbare Inhalte löschen zu lassen. Doch es gibt weiterhin Kritik.

Angriffe auf die IT der öffentlichen Verwaltung häufen sich. Doch statt gezielt in Maßnahmen zu investieren, die IT-Sicherheit stärken, investiert die Bundesregierung in Robotikforschung und eine Vogelstimmen-App. Das sagt ein Bericht des Bundesrechnungshofs, den wir veröffentlichen.

Im Namen des Jugendschutzes plant die EU-Kommission flächendeckende Alterskontrollen im Netz. Zahlreiche Organisationen warnen eindringlich vor den Gefahren: Vom Kinderschutzbund über Elternverbände bis hin zum Chaos Computer Club. Die Übersicht.

Auch bei uns läuft nicht immer alles rund. Denn manchmal tun wir uns mit Recherchen auch richtig schwer: Wir hadern mit Druck von außen, mit der Komplexität von Themen oder mit unseren eigenen Ansprüchen. Darüber plaudern wir in dieser Folge aus dem Nähkästchen.

Die Demokratie wankt. Rechtsradikale greifen nach der Macht und wollen Grundrechte brennen sehen. Die Bundesregierung gießt Öl ins Feuer: Sie rüstet den Überwachungsstaat auf, schränkt die Transparenz ein und schneidet der Zivilgesellschaft die Luft ab.

Wir treten der Faschisierung entgegen. Wir kämpfen für eine freie, offene und solidarische Gesellschaft. Wir verteidigen die Grundrechte für alle. Mit deiner Unterstützung.

Daniel ist Politikwissenschaftler und Co-Chefredakteur bei netzpolitik.org. Zu seinen Schwerpunkten zählen die Gesundheitsdigitalisierung, Digital Public Infrastructure und die sogenannte Künstliche Intelligenz.

Daniel war einst Redakteur bei den "Blättern". 2014 erschien von ihm das Buch "Amazon – Das Buch als Beute"; 2016 erhielt er den Alternativen Medienpreis in der Rubrik "Medienkritik". 

Er gehört dem Board of Trustees von Eurozine  und dem Kuratorium der Stiftung Warentest an.

local-opinion-and-involvement-conservati:
Scientists seeking out why some endangered animals or ecosystems are thriving while others are in decline have made an encouraging determination.

Across a worldwide, cross-section of conservation success stories, they found it wasn’t a question of money, but of the actions of the locals, that determined whether nature flourished or foundered.

Traversing coral reefs in Papua New Guinea, chimpanzees in West Africa, grizzly bears in Canada, and albatross colonies off Tasmania, a University of Sydney study examined the common threads behind these stories with the hopes of developing a framework to replicate their success.

Lead author Dr. Bing Lin from the University’s Thriving Oceans Research Hub said 3 common factors tied these positive conservation stories together.

“Our study examined different species on different continents that are all facing unique conservation challenges. Yet each succeeded against the odds for remarkably similar reasons: local knowledge was valued alongside science, communities played a central role in decision-making, and management adapted to local social and environmental conditions,” Dr. Lin said.

Rather than focus on environmental decline, Dr. Lin and his colleagues reviewed more than 70 studies of environmental and sustainability success, where places, species, and social-ecological systems perform better than expected despite difficult circumstances.

Their review is the first, a statement on the work elaborated, to synthesize seemingly unrelated conservation bright spots and bring them together into a single framework. In doing so, they reveal the common conditions that allow people and nature to thrive against the odds, and offer a way to identify and learn from these unexpected success stories.

“Conservation is often framed as a story of loss and decline, but there are places where ecosystems and the people who depend on them are thriving despite enormous pressures,” Dr. Lin said.

“By bringing together research from around the world, we’ve shown these aren’t simply lucky exceptions. They often share common characteristics that can serve as windows into real-world resilience and help guide conservation elsewhere.”

Although every “bright spot” is unique, common themes included a community with the capacity to implement conservation practices despite challenging conditions, and perhaps  the alure of more immediate, exploitative gain.

Co-author Professor Josh Cinner, Director of the Thriving Oceans Research Hub, has spent more than 25 years working alongside coastal communities in Papua New Guinea, where one of the world’s richest and most resilient coral reef network is located.

“I’ve always known the place was special, but I was blown away when, out of a rigorous quantitative analysis of nearly 1,700 coral reefs around the world, this site came up as one of our global bright spots,” Professor Cinner said, citing the results of his original landmark bright spots study, published in Nature in 2016.

“These villages have maintained a customary practice of periodically closing parts of their reefs to fishing. It’s similar to fallow agriculture, giving ecosystems time to recover before harvesting resumes.”

Professor Cinner’s subsequent research found the marine protection practice has endured because it is woven into community life. Strong relationships between elders and younger generations, shared responsibility for managing the reefs, and cultural traditions that reward participation have helped sustain abundant marine life.

“At a time when the headline story about coral reefs is that they are in trouble, this bright spot provides an alternative narrative as a story of hope and connection,” Professor Cinner said.

“The environmental success these communities have achieved comes from extensive local experience and genuine local ownership of decision-making, management and enforcement.”

A similar pattern emerged in very different places around the world.

In western Africa, researchers found some populations of “Critically-Endangered” Western chimpanzees were surviving despite widespread regional decline. In addition to those in inaccessible and protected areas, the strongest chimpanzee populations were often found where local communities maintained cultural traditions and social norms that discouraged hunting and supported coexistence with wildlife.

MORE COMMUNITY-LED CONSERVATION: A Strategy of Cash-for-Photos Turns Animal Hunters into Animal Protectors in Indonesia

Further south, conservation of Tasmania’s “Vulnerable” shy albatross has shown how close partnerships between scientists, wildlife managers, and policymakers can create more of these bright spots. Collaborative decision-making led to innovative interventions to protect albatross chicks from parasites, expanded conservation programs, and established an enduring process for testing future population management options.

On the other side of the world, in Canada’s Great Bear Rainforest, First Nations communities have led grizzly bear conservation by placing indigenous stewardship and knowledge at the heart of environmental governance.

“Our framework shows that bright spots arise through a positive interplay of process, people, and place,” Dr. Lin said.

GETTING PEOPLE ON BOARD: Leopard Population Has Nearly Tripled in the World’s Largest Conservation Area

“What we hope our study provides is a way for scientists to identify different types of conditions that support conservation success. By developing a ‘common language’ across disparate global ecosystems, we hope that these bright spots can be compared consistently for improved outcomes globally.”

Professor Cinner said the findings offer a hopeful message at a time when environmental news is often dominated by crisis.

“Our review shows that local conservation bright spots are not isolated miracles. They follow patterns that we can recognize, learn from and apply elsewhere. That gives us real reasons for optimism as we work to protect both people and nature.”

from-girlbosses-to-tradwives:
The internet has given women endless ways to look feminine. What women need is a clearer vision of how to become truly feminine.

The internet has spent the last decade inventing new ways for women to be girls. We have had the girlboss, clean girl, soft girl, “girl dinner,” “girl math,” hot girl summer, lazy girl jobs, and the increasingly ubiquitous “I’m just a girl.” Now, after years of telling women that freedom meant climbing the corporate ladder and needing no man, the algorithm has rediscovered traditional femininity. Sourdough, bows, floral dresses, homemaking, “feminine energy,” and tradwife TikTok have arrived as the correction to the exhausted girlboss.

But replacing the pantsuit with a prairie dress does not by itself recover femininity.

Femininity begins with accepting that being female is not an identity a woman constructs but a nature she receives. Men and women share the same human dignity and moral obligations, but they are not interchangeable expressions of the same thing. Sexual difference reaches beyond anatomy. It shapes how men and women relate to one another, to family, and to the generations that come after them.

The female body itself gives us the clearest clue. It is uniquely ordered toward receiving, bearing, and nurturing life. Not every woman will become a biological mother, yet motherhood itself reveals something fundamental about womanhood even beyond the women who experience it biologically: Femininity is maternal and generative. Maternalism is an orientation toward receiving life and helping it flourish.

Healthy femininity notices what others need and tends to it. It creates belonging, preserves relationships, warms a home, passes wisdom between generations, and turns dependence into something dignified rather than shameful. It takes what has been entrusted to it and cultivates it.

This is part of what makes femininity relational. Women often wield enormous influence through relationships, emotional perception, social bonds, and the moral atmosphere they create around them. Mature femininity uses that influence to reconcile rather than divide, to strengthen rather than control, and to make intimacy safer rather than more dangerous.

Healthy femininity is also receptive, a word modern culture often mistakes for passive. Receptivity is the ability to receive love, provision, protection, correction, responsibility, and ultimately other people without experiencing every form of dependence as a threat to autonomy. A woman can be competent without needing to prove she needs no one.

Healthy femininity does not view masculinity as competition. It does not require women to become smaller so men can become larger, but neither does it treat every difference between the sexes as a hierarchy requiring correction. It can admire masculine strength, receive male provision, and respect masculine leadership without concluding that female dignity has somehow been diminished.

Nor is femininity synonymous with fragility. Gentleness requires strength precisely because tenderness without resolve fails under pressure. The feminine woman can endure difficulty without becoming hardened, exercise influence without becoming domineering, and sacrifice without turning that sacrifice into emotional leverage.

These qualities may appear differently across a lifetime. A woman may be a daughter, wife, mother, grandmother, widow, caregiver, worker, mentor, or several of those at once. While her obligations change, her femininity remains across all seasons.

Once femininity is understood positively, toxic femininity becomes easier to recognize. It is not too much femininity. It is feminine capacity turned against its proper ends.

The same emotional sensitivity that allows a woman to understand another person deeply can become emotional manipulation. Relational intelligence can create community or become gossip, exclusion, and reputational destruction. Nurture can mature another person or suffocate them through control. Vulnerability can produce intimacy or become immunity from accountability. A desire for security can build a stable family or become material entitlement. Female solidarity can produce extraordinary loyalty or become a jury that never convicts its own.

Femininity cannot solely be an online aesthetic or trend. Healthy femininity is something much deeper. It receives womanhood rather than inventing it. It embraces the maternal and generative orientation of female nature. It nurtures life, cultivates relationships, creates belonging, receives and gives love, honors sexual complementarity, and directs female influence toward the flourishing of others.

The internet has given women endless ways to look feminine. What women need is a clearer vision of how to become truly feminine.

A St. Petersburg court fined Nikolai Rybakov, chairman of Yabloko, 1,000 rubles on an administrative charge of petty hooliganism.

The court said that on September 20, Rybakov spoiled his ballots at a polling station, “acting deliberately and out of hooligan motives,” and then placed them in the ballot box.

The ballots bore “markings made in green marker,” the press service of the St. Petersburg courts said, without specifying what the markings said. Rybakov voted in front of journalists, checking boxes next to every candidate and writing “Yabloko. For Peace” and “Yabloko. For a Ceasefire Agreement” on the ballots.

“Rybakov’s actions disregarded the interests of society and other voters, ignored the rules of decency and propriety, demonstrated his disrespect for society, and resulted in damage to someone else’s property, thereby showing blatant disrespect for society and violating public order,” the court ruled.

Rybakov confirmed in court that he had invalidated his ballots, saying “more than 900,000 voters did the same.” According to him, doing so “showed no disrespect for society, of which he is a part,” but rather expressed the political position he has held “his whole life.”

Yabloko was the only party that campaigned in the September 18–20 elections with anti-war slogans. Russia’s Supreme Court overturned the party’s registration for the election to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, in August. Afterward, Yabloko urged supporters to go to polling stations and spoil their ballots in protest.

What to Know: Five coal-fired power plants and one running on oil and gas would no longer be online if not for the Trump administration. The Department of Energy used emergency authority to keep the plants going past their scheduled retirement, something that's never been done in the history of the DOE. It was also against the wishes of some of the plants. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said it's about giving people access to more reliable power to help address periods of peak demand. What's odd: several of the plants are running at limited capacity or not at all. That said, utilities are still incurring millions of dollars just to maintain a power plant on standby. Wright told Reuters last year that he expects most of the nation's power plants to hold off on retirement in order to help power artificial intelligence aka data centers.

Why it matters: Electricity costs nationwide are already wildly high as demand increases from AI. Consumers Energy, the company that owns the Michigan J.H. Campbell coal plant, reported to the SEC that the plant has cost them $259 million to continue running since May of last year. The utility has gone to its customers to pay for $138 million of that cost. A recent court decision also found the 'emergency' order was an overstep and threatened the stability of the energy market.

Emergency orders are keeping a generating unit at a coal-fired plant in Colorado going as well. The latest happened Sept. 27. The DOE has to keep issuing them within 90 days. Keeping that plant online would cost taxpayers $80 million annually, according to its Governor. That's without it producing basically any power.

I've been watching a lot of PBS NewsHour lately, which is funny to me, because for the longest time, I wasn't a TV-news person.

I grew up in a Fox News household. Ever since it went on the air in the 90s, there was always a TV in my house turned to O'Reilly, Beck, Hannity or Ingraham. And that shaped my idea of TV news: shouty hosts, flashy sets, woosh-y graphics, and sensational headlines. It wasn't for me, but it certainly wasn't boring. TV that gets your fight-or-flight response going. Because of that, I avoided watching TV news for many years.

Then a few years ago, I started watching PBS NewsHour. At first, I thought, "This is BORING TV." But the more I watched, the more I came to see its boringness as a superpower. It delivers the news in a way that's smart, respectful, non-sensational, calm, and humane. In short, it is boring in the best way.

strangers_tarp_house:
After a storm dumped a silver maple tree down through his roof, Kansas resident Gilbert Kirk told local news that he wasn’t looking for a miracle or an insurance handout.

He just wanted a tarp.

Two days later, last Friday, a stranger arrived at Kirk’s debris-laden front lawn in Wyandotte County, and said he’d be back in 30 minutes with a tarp, some lumber, and a crew to cover up the maple-shaped gash in Kirk’s house.

“OK, whatever, you know,” he remembered thinking, in a follow-up interview with KCTV 5. “And then the next thing I know, he’s back with a load of lumber… and the next thing I know, there were just trucks,” he said, gesticulating to his driveway.

When the storm arrived, 71-year-old Kirk and his dog Beetle were trapped under the collapsed roof for hours. Now, for the first time in weeks, they have a new roof over their heads, and with help from a small arsenal of stand-up fans, the man has the semblance of a home again.

“Oh, it’s unbelievable, the way the community has come together,” Kirk said. “It’s drying out inside now, and I’ve got fans running in there… and it’s just drying it out good.”

norway_glacial_archaeology_arrowheads:
In a mountainous region of southern Norway, scientists are in their 20th year of surveying glaciers for ancient artifacts entombed therein.

The most recent chapter of this long-running saga was the recovery of 48 arrow heads and shafts from different eras and made from different materials, some of which appear like they could have been crafted yesterday.

Organized and conducted in partnership between Innlandet County of Norway and the Oslo Cultural Museum, “Secrets of the Ice” has already yielded 5,000 artifacts, but this season’s fieldwork saw teams recover some of the oldest objects yet.

Arrowheads, crafted from slate, bone, and even a freshwater mussel shell, date from as late as 2,000 years ago to as early as 5,000. The slate arrowhead could be 6,000 years old, while the mussel shell arrowhead was found with an intact wooden shaft, and is believed to be around 3,600 years old.

The work focused around the 3 glaciers of Langfonne, Storfonne and Handklefonne, in the Jotunheimen mountains. Here, the glacier ice formed a longer time ago than any others that remain. The ice is older, therefore the artifacts it contains are older too.

“When we began our work in 2006, most of the artifacts we recovered were less than 2,000 years old, with particularly large numbers dating to the Viking Age,” the Secrets of the Ice researchers wrote in a blog post.

While stuck in the ice, the wood and other carbon-based material rots at a glacial pace—pun intended. The lack of oxygen prevents the formation of bacteria, and can mean that some of the objects can appear almost new.

That can change, however, extremely quickly, so many of the finds are placed in frigid, anoxic display cases at a nearby museum while they wait to be catalogued, studied, and perhaps moved 200 miles southwest to the capital of Oslo.

MORE STORIES LIKE THIS: 1,500 Year-Old Reindeer Trap and Hunting Equipment Uncovered in the Ice of Norway’s Mountains

“Now the picture has changed dramatically. Increasingly, the artifacts melting out of the ice are more than 2,000 years old. Many date to the Stone Age and Bronze Age. The oldest are more than 6,000 years old.”

Since the project began in 2006, it has recorded 73 archeological sites and recovered more than 5,000 artifacts from the ice, notably the world’s oldest ski, and a leather shoe from the time of Ancient Babylon.

biden_doj_targeting_parents:
A Democrat-controlled Congress would give the same party subpoena power, committee leadership roles, and resources to do what it’s done in the past: investigate and harass its opponents.

Sunday marked five years since then-Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a memorandum that instructed his Department of Justice (DOJ) to help investigate and prosecute parents who showed up at school board meetings to complain about far-left initiatives or Covid policies. Five years later we now know that the Biden White House was behind Garland’s effort to target parents, The Federalist’s Matt Kittle reported.

The anniversary and new finding also come on the heels of former Special Counsel Jack Smith’s testimony before Congress last week, in which his lawfare efforts to keep President Donald Trump out of office faced further scrutiny. With the midterms less than a month away, both instances serve to remind Americans of what Democrats will do with power given the chance: wage a lawfare campaign against their political opponents.

Back in September of 2021, the National School Boards Association (NSBA) sent a letter to the Biden administration asking it to take on the “immediate threat” that parents posed to their children’s schools. The “threat” stemmed from parents who were voicing their concerns and criticisms about critical race theory curriculum, mask mandates, and vaccine mandates. The NSBA wanted the Biden administration to treat the parents speaking out as “equivalent to a form of domestic terrorism.” Notably, the NSBA later apologized and acknowledged “there was no justification for some of the language included in the letter.”

Nonetheless, Garland had issued a memo entitled “Partnership Among Federal, State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Law Enforcement to Address Threats Against School Administrators, Board Members, Teachers, and Staff.” The memo instructed the FBI to meet with federal, state, and local law enforcement to focus on the alleged threats and how to respond to them. As a result of this memo, the federal government opened 25 preliminary assessment files regarding alleged “school board threats.”

In other words, a Democrat-led “justice” department decided that questioning or opposing left-wing thought orthodoxy like CRT justified the investigation of ordinary Americans with the intent of prosecution.

Nonetheless, the NSBA claimed that an independent review found that there was no collusion with the Biden administration. But a new report from the DOJ reveals, as Kittle put it, “the Biden White House was squarely behind Garland’s effort to find a federal ‘hook’ to prosecute parents and school policy protesters with federal crimes.”

According to the new report, DOJ senior officials and loyalists Biden put in place there “initially pushed back” on the NSBA’s request to target parents, “questioning the constitutionality of the request.” In fact, one email shows Kevin Chambers, then-associate deputy attorney general, calling the effort to enlist federal law enforcement and the claim that parents were domestic terrorists “ridiculous.” But the DOJ ultimately “moved ahead with issuing the Garland Memorandum based on pressure from Biden Administration officials in the White House and leadership at the Office of the Deputy Attorney General (‘ODAG’) at the Department of Justice.”

The Biden administration also coordinated with the NSBA on “talking points” to counter parents and other opponents of critical race theory and transgender ideology, Kittle reported.

In addition to these further revelations of Biden administration overreach, Special Counsel Jack Smith, an appointee of Garland, and the anti-Trump lawfare he led during the 2024 election cycle again took center stage last week. Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, revealed during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing that Smith obtained communications from more than a dozen media outlets, including those of The Federalist’s Editor-in-Chief Mollie Hemingway. Smith obtained the messages as part of his “Arctic Frost” witch hunt, which was an unconstitutional effort to get Trump that resulted in Smith’s team spying on members of Congress and the media.

Smith’s team also targeted nearly 5,000 Americans who made political donations to President Donald Trump, Grassley announced. One Iowan who donated $10 to the president just months before the 2020 election had his home address, bank information, and other personal information handed over to the Biden administration’s weaponized FBI and DOJ.

Democrats targeted parents who challenged what their children were being taught, journalists who scrutinized the Biden administration, and Americans who gave Trump as little as $10. They used regular acts of political participation as justification for government investigation and overreach. With each abuse of power, Democrats sent the American people a stark message: Speaking up or disagreeing with the narratives of the regime could put them on the government’s target list.

That’s the legacy voters need to remember this November. A Democrat-controlled Congress would give the same party subpoena power, committee leadership roles, and resources to do what it’s done in the past: investigate and harass its opponents. Democrats don’t need to get back into the White House to haul Americans before committees or demand their records. They just need Congress.

zambia-leopard-recovery:
Conservationists say a switch from real leopard skins to synthetic furs in traditional ceremonies has helped reduce poaching and boost leopard numbers in western Zambia

Conservationists say a switch from real leopard skins to synthetic furs in traditional ceremonies has helped reduce poaching and boost leopard numbers in western Zambia

Big cat conservationists in Zambia say leopard numbers are rebounding thanks in part to local communities swapping real furs for synthetic in traditional ceremonies.

Leopards are revered by cultural and religious groups which use their prized pelts as ceremonial regalia.

In western Zambia, during an annual event marking the onset of the flood season, 200 paddlers ferry the king of the Lozi people, the Litunga, on a barge. They wear skirts fashioned largely from leopard skins, and demand for the striking outfits is believed to have been one of the drivers of leopard poaching.

Now the tide appears to be turning following a programme led by the global wild cat conservation organisation, Panthera.

Consulting with communities, the organisation sourced quality synthetic furs, coined Heritage Furs, and secured a royal stamp of approval, with the Litunga decreeing that only Heritage Furs should be worn in official ceremonies.

The shift to Heritage Furs could save between 204 and 1,310 leopards in the region over a decade

Across southern Africa, Panthera has supplied more than 22,000 Heritage Furs, but in-depth evaluation of the initiative’s impact has been limited until now. Fresh research published in the journal Conservation Biology shows that leopard numbers in western Zambia are recovering, poaching incidents are down, and just 10% of the Litunga’s paddlers favour real furs over the alternative.

The collaborative study involving numerous organisations suggests that a shift to Heritage Furs could save between 204 and 1,310 leopards in the region over a decade, while also acknowledging the role of counter-trafficking measures and enforcement in the conservation success.

Lead author and Panthera scientist Aditya Shekhar Malgaonkar wrote: “Our results provide the first empirical link between a demand-reduction initiative based on synthetic substitutes and measurable population recovery of species.”

zelensky-cabinet-crisis:
Protesters in Ukrainian cities have welcomed the change of commander-in-chief but  continue to call for the return of Mykhailo Fedorov

With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?

Not so fast.

The political fallout from President Volodymyr Zelensky's 15 July decision not to re-appoint Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister, as part of a cabinet reshuffle, continues to reverberate about Kyiv and beyond, even as air raid sirens wail and Russian drones and missiles are intercepted overhead.

Fedorov's mostly young supporters are still mounting daily street protests, demanding that Zelensky reinstate the popular young innovator widely credited with driving much of Ukraine's recent technological innovation.

On Thursday, Fedorov said he had rejected Zelensky's offers of alternative posts in government, saying there were only three positions worth having to influence the course of the war: minister of defence, commander-in-chief of the military or president of Ukraine.

"If you don't have a ministry under you, you don't have a budget," ex-deputy defence minister Alina Frolova said, "and you don't actually have the authority to do something."

Mykhailo Fedorov has so far refused any alternative job Zelensky has offered him to come back

Fedorov's reference to the presidency did not go unnoticed. Was this the first public sign that the ousted minister sees himself as a rival to Zelensky?

One former defence official suggested he became a real candidate for the presidency the moment he was dismissed.

But with the country at war and no elections scheduled â Ukraine's constitution still prevents them in wartime â how useful is it to put your head above the political parapet so far in advance?

"He's being childish," one opposition MP told me, on condition that he remained anonymous.

"He's looking to further his political career, which I think is just stupid in the circumstances where we are."

The president's supporters say Zelensky has gone to great lengths to resolve the crisis, especially over the question of who to replace the unpopular commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Eventually he decided on Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, a highly respected former commander of Ukraine's land forces.

Zelensky's change of commander-in-chief has provided only a partial fix to the crisis

"He consulted pretty much every significant figure in the Ukrainian army," former government adviser Yuriy Sak told the BBC earlier this week.

"So the decision that he has taken now is very well informed, and I support it because General Drapatyi is a young, battle-proven, modern general who will take our defences to a new level, hopefully."

But while Drapatyi's appointment has been generally welcomed, it only represents a partial fix by a president scrambling to repair the damage caused by his removal of Fedorov.

Ironically, for a president whose youth and apparent dynamism propelled him to power in 2019, Zelensky seems to have misjudged the mood of young Ukrainians, eager for their leaders â political and military â to represent their values and aspirations.

"It's quite natural that people want to see someone who is a warrior against corruption, who is very modern, who is young," Oleksandr Merezhko, an MP from Zelensky's Servant of the People party, said.

"People want to see something like that in politics, which they consider to be dirty and full of hypocrisy. They need heroes."

Ukraine's ousted defence minister insists on being reinstated

Who is Mykhailo Drapatyi, Ukraine's new commander-in-chief?

Row escalates in Ukraine over army chief's future

But Merezhko agrees that Fedorov's ambitions and almost mythic, popular status may have brought about his downfall, especially for a president with a track record of sidelining those he sees as potential rivals.

"Don't outshine your master," Merezhko says, quoting from Robert Greene's 1998 self-help book, The 48 Laws of Power.

Most analysts agree that last week's reshuffle had one overarching purpose: to cut Fedorov down to size. But Zelensky's strategy appears to have backfired.

"His removal has led to the opposite result," Merezhko says. "His rating soared. Just soared."

Few doubt Fedorov's commitment, imagination and drive, but some question whether his outsized reputation is fully justified.

They point out that he inherited a situation in which Ukraine had already successfully built up its medium- and long-range strike capabilities, something over which the defence minister has little day-to-day influence.

"The energy and clarity he brought to the job was impressive and he showed immense personal courage," a former European defence official said. "But the thing that will carry on regardless is the innovation culture. It's 2,000 companies, not a single individual."

Zelensky (C-R) sought to present a united front this week, standing beside Mykhailo Drapatyi (R), his predecessor and the acting defence minister (L)

One opposition MP, who asked not to be identified, put it more bluntly.

"Ninety-nine per cent of these young people on the street have no clue how the ministry of defence is operating, how the general staff is operating," he said.

"They think Fedorov is good because he wants to fight with drones and Syrskyi was bad because he was looking for people to fight. It's a dramatic simplification which is totally wrong."

But understandable, perhaps, in a country exhausted by 12 years of war with Russia. Who would not want to believe that drones and robots can do the job, rather than a member of your own family, roughly conscripted on the streets of your own hometown?

Everyone agrees that Ukraine needs to put this politically toxic episode behind it before summer gives way to autumn and the country braces itself for another Russian assault on its energy grid.

"We need to prepare for how we will get through the winter," Zelensky said on the Telegram messaging app on Thursday.

Politicians and experts interviewed for this piece mostly agree that while the political damage of this episode continues to undermine President Zelensky's authority and reputation, Ukraine is unlikely to experience significant setbacks on the battlefield.

What Zelensky calls his "long-range sanctions" campaign against Russia is in full swing, causing mounting damage to the Russian economy.

Ukraine's long front lines, meanwhile, remain largely static, thanks to a 15-30km (9-18-mile) wide "kill zone" where anything or anyone who moves is observed and attacked by drones.

As a young, still relatively immature democracy, Ukraine's institutions have been put under colossal strain by Russia's full-scale invasion. But, many argue, the country remains resilient and resourceful.

"The secret of Ukraine's success is that we are much stronger horizontally than vertically," opposition MP Andrii Osadchuk told me.

"I hope the damage will be minimal."

zelensky-sacks-commander:
Oleksandr Syrskyi was praised by President Zelensky for successfully defending Ukraine's capital Kyiv in 2022

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has dismissed the country's army commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

It comes just days after the removal of popular Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov - a move that triggered street protests across the country.

Initial rumours that the end of Fedorov's tenure was related to a conflict between him and Syrskyi were soon confirmed.

Fedorov, 35, has been widely praised for energising the ministry and transforming the armed forces, as well as leading a drive against corruption. Syrskyi, 60, is seen by many in Ukraine as a Soviet-school commander reluctant to implement radical changes in the army.

Syrskyi defended his record in a farewell address, writing on Telegram: "An army that was fighting a difficult defensive campaign two years ago is now on the offensive."

"I am handing over to my successor an army that is not only holding the line but is advancing... I sincerely hope this offensive will continue."

Syrskyi was replaced by Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, who is a popular, battle-hardened general.

"I will work responsibly, with full focus, and with respect for the people who are defending our country today," Drapatyi said on Facebook.

He also thanked Syrskyi "for his consistent work to strengthen the Ukrainian army," adding: "I grew up in it."

In a video post on social media late on Tuesday, Zelensky thanked Syrskyi for his military campaigns, including his role in successfully defending the capital Kyiv during the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Zelensky also revealed that earlier in the day, he met Fedorov and offered him a "worthy position in power", but did not say whether the offer had been accepted.

Fedorov was last week replaced by Yevhenii Khmara, a former top official at Ukraine's Security Service (SBU).

"All decisions will be formalised tomorrow," Zelensky added in his post.

Mykhailo Fedorov has not said whether he accepted a new job offer from President Zelensky

Meanwhile, Fedorov congratulated Drapatyi with his new job, describing his appointment as a "new hope in the fight of free people for freedom and justice".

He said it was "the voice of change that could not be ignored".

Fedorov also revealed that he had called Syrskyi to thank him for the defence of the Kyiv region and other "historic battles".

"But we need to move even faster and write new chapters correcting all previous mistakes," he added.

Fedorov had been appointed defence minister only in January - but has been widely praised for using data to analyse and try to improve performance on the front line.

A former minister of digital transformation, he was active from the early days of the full-scale invasion by setting up a volunteer "IT Army of Ukraine" to launch cyber-attacks against Russia.

Later, he led a successful fundraising campaign called the Army of Drones and brought in elements of "gamification" to the war, designing a system that awarded Ukrainian military units with credits for hitting Russian assets.

Fedorov's ousting prompted six days of widespread protests, with Zelensky coming under mounting pressure to dismiss Syrskyi.

Zelensky appeared to have bowed to that pressure by replacing him with Drapatyi, who is seen as a younger, more innovative commander. Drapatyi is also thought to be a close friend of Federov's.

Federov's clear endorsement of Drapatyi is likely to go some way towards defusing the political crisis of the past week.

For the time being, acting Defence Minister Khmara remains in the position. President Zelensky has asked him and Drapatyi to come up with a new defence strategy, covering key issues like reforming the military corps system, weapons supply and drones.

On Monday, Syrskyi wrote an op-ed for the Militarny website, saying of his relationship with Fedorov: "I perceived our relationship as a working one... If I offended anyone, Mykhailo Albertovych [Fedorov], I'm sorry."

He said the issues of military contracts, procurement and mobilisation were a great deal more complicated than most people realised.

"Decisions on which people's lives depend are not made with slogans," he said. "Real work, not the public drama surrounding it, wins the war."

Protesters will still want to see Fedorov back in a position of real authority, where he can continue to drive forward innovation in Ukraine's battle with Russia.

If he gets such a position, Zelensky will have repaired the immediate damage. But many will not forgive him for making what they saw as the wrong choice in the first place.

Scores of drones ⁠targeted Moscow overnight, hitting the Russian capital’s oil refinery for the second time this week, Reuters reported.

“We don’t ⁠want this war, we never did, and everyone ​knows it, and our partners ‌know it,” Zelenskyy ‌said in a voice message sent to reporters on a ‌WhatsApp group, quoted by Reuters.

double quotation markBut if Ukraine burns, your Moscow will burn.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has just arrived for the EU summit, flanked by the European Council’s António Costa and the European Commission’s Ursula von der Leyen.

Costa says it’s “a historic week for Ukraine,” as the formal accession negotiations are now under way, and the G7 leaders agreed on “clear and strong support” for the wartorn country.

“The EU, the US, and our partners from Canada, Japan, the UK – all of us – are working together to continue to support Ukraine,” he says.

He says there is “a new momentum” in the pursuit of peace in Ukraine.

Von der Leyen hits similar tone, saying Ukraine “deserves it, because you have been working so hard to move forward with the necessary reforms.”

She, too, says “the tide is turning,” as “Ukraine is holding the line, even partially regaining its territory.”

Von der Leyen says that Russia, in contast, is struggling, with its economy “suffering” and growing digital censorship.

In his response, Zelensky says it is “a really great moment for Ukraine.”

He says he hopes to discuss the next steps during the summit tonight, and talk about how they can further support Ukraine and pressure Putin to the negotiating table.

Today’s summit will also see some new faces as Bulgaria’s Rumen Radev and Hungary’s Péter Magyar make their formal debuts in Brussels.

Magyar will also take part in informal talks in the Visegrad Four format, with his counterparts from the Czech Republic, Poland, and Slovakia, which are getting revived after the last few years of tricky relations with his predecessor, Viktor Orbán.

Welcoming Magyar, Poland’s Tusk posted a picture of the four leader, saying: “Make V4 great again.”

Lots of attention during this summit will be on Ukraine and Moldova as they open the first cluster of negotiations in their talks on joining the EU.

Lithuania’s president Gitanas Nausėda says he is supportive of the process and hopes to see them open all clusters in July, and progress at pace toward a full membership.

On Ukraine, he also says there is “more and more evidence that the war in Ukraine is coming closer to the Russian population,” which he calls “a gamechanger.”

“The Russian population will start to realise that this is not about watching the war on the TV screens, but this is about the war on their own soil,” he says.

He says that Russia is still not showing that it is “willing to start the peace negotiations, or at least they are willing to for the ceasefire.”

He says any meaningful discussions – including on who should represent the EU – could only take place if Russia changes its attitude first.

He says the EU still has more instruments it can use to push Russia towards the negotiating table.

Meanwhile, back in Brussels, EU leaders are now arriving for tonight’s European Council summit on Ukraine, competitiveness, and the next EU budget (or “multiannual financial framework” in EU-speak).

Poland’s Donald Tusk is among the first ones to arrive and speak to reporters and he plays up the prospects of Poland seeing permanent deployment of US troops on its territory (15:39).

He says the proposal seems to be progressing faster than he had expected and things are “on the right path”, although no final decision has been made just yet.

Tusk also reacted to the arrest of a man suspected of fatally shooting a Russian activist critical of president Vladimir Putin and Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov.

A 36-year-old man carrying a Georgian passport was arrested this morning.

Tusk said the authorities were taking this “very seriously” given potential links with Russia.

Speaking at the same event, US undersecretary of defence Elbridge A. Colby stressed that the continued support of Nato’s European members for Ukraine will be essential to keeping its fight against Russia alive.

Colby said that the US policy of shifting responsibility for supporting Ukraine onto Europe has worked out well.

“In the past year, European allies have taken the leading role in supporting Ukraine’s defence, assuming the responsibility for the financial support of Ukraine, as well as providing their own arms to Ukraine.

At the same time, we have been prepared to provide weaponry purchased by Europe for Ukraine’s defence through President Trump’s PURL Initiative, which we’ve discussed already today, and allies have contributed significantly to this signature example of practical results-oriented transatlantic cooperation.”

Colby said that “that transition of support to Europe has not only been implemented, it has been correlated with a sustained, effective defence by Ukraine.”

He said “Ukraine’s situation has even improved” as a result.

He said:

“Ukraine has managed to hold the front line and even improve its position in some places, continuing to lay the groundwork for a lasting peace built on Russia’s understanding that perpetuating this war is not only condemnable but also will not pay off for Moscow.”

But Colby stressed that “Ukraine’s defence does hold, but continued and sustained support from allies is essential to maintain it.”

“We in the United States hear time and again how vital Ukraine’s defence is for Europe and for our allies … but our allies must back words with actions.

This is an opportunity for Europe to do precisely that, and in the process help to set and strengthen the conditions for lasting peace in Ukraine.”

Ukraine ⁠and Germany signed an agreement ⁠on anti-ballistic ⁠capabilities, ​president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, calling on other western ⁠allies to join ​the ‌effort and ‌deliver results by ‌winter.

Zelenskyy ​also ​asked to develop ​additional financial ​instruments ‌to finance ​the Ukrainian ​army long-term, Reuters added.

Russia, the world’s third biggest oil producer and ‌a major oil and fuel exporter, is to import fuel by sea this month as it seeks to manage a shortage after extensive Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Russian hardliners called for Moscow to retaliate, with some urging the Kremlin to consider using nuclear weapons against Ukraine.

Andrey Gurulyov, a retired lieutenant general and state duma deputy, called for Russia to “strike the enemy mercilessly” in response to the attack.

zelenskyy_poland_honor:
Ukraine's president has returned a medal to Poland after a decision to strip him of the country's highest honor. Warsaw has been one of Kyiv's key allies since Russia began its war in Ukraine.

Top Ukrainian officials, including President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Saturday that they were returning Polish state honors after Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped the Ukrainian president of Poland's highest award.

Zelenskyy said in a social media post that he had sent back the Order of the White Eagle, which he received in 2023 as a symbol of friendship between Poland and Ukraine.

"Ukraine will remain open to all meaningful formats of interaction with Poland, in order to strive to avoid misinterpretations of the complex and painful pages of the past of our peoples and to ensure due respect for all innocent victims of the 20th century," he wrote.

He called the medal a symbol of Poland's "highest trust," but also suggested it no longer held the same meaning after Nawrocki's decision.

The Polish decision to strip the honor from Zelenskyy could further strain ties between the two close strategic partners as Kyiv seeks to rally international support to pressure Russia to end its war in Ukraine.

"This is a gift to the Moscow aggressor, who will certainly use it against both of our countries," Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, wrote on social media, saying that he was returning the Gold Officer's Cross of the Polish Order of Merit.

On Friday, Nawrocki announced that Zelenskyy would be stripped of the Order of the White Eagle — Poland's highest state honor, which had been awarded by former President Andrzej Duda in 2023.

The decision followed Zelenskyy's move to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA),  a World War II militia that Warsaw accuses of participating in massacres of Poles.

Poland has been one of Ukraine's key allies since Russia's full-scale invasion, hosting hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian refugees.

Nawrocki said the move would not affect Poland's support for Ukraine's defense against Russia.

Ukrainian officials argued that Nawrocki's decision was beneficial to Russia.

Ukraine's ambassador to Warsaw, Vasyl Bodnar, described the move "as a gesture towards all the Ukrainian people" and announced that he was relinquishing his Knight's Cross of the Polish Order of Merit.

Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga also said that he would return a Polish award he received in 2022, calling the decision "a strategic mistake … that benefits only Moscow."

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a political rival of Nawrocki, urged both countries to preserve their solidarity, warning that a dispute between Poland and Ukraine "delights Putin and shocks our allies."

Meanwhile, a Russian airstrike on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv killed at least one person and injured nine others on Saturday, according to Governor Oleh Synyehubov.

Russia's Defense Ministry said on Saturday morning that its air-defense systems had intercepted and destroyed 187 Ukrainian drones across the country overnight.

In recent weeks, Moscow and Kyiv have intensified attacks on each other as US-led efforts to end the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, remain stalled.

zelensky_putin_drones:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin rebuffed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s call for a face-to-face meeting, saying there was “no point.”

Zelensky urged Putin to end the countries’ four-year war in an open letter posted Thursday, as the Russian leader was preparing to address the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum.

But Putin responded with dismissiveness, calling the letter “rude” and voicing skepticism about Zelensky’s true intentions. The Ukrainian president can “come to Moscow” if he wants to talk, a Kremlin spokesperson said.

Zelensky’s timing – in the middle of the event where Russian billionaires schmooze with political leaders and decision makers – is no coincidence. The Russian economy is struggling and Zelensky is hoping he can capitalize on rising disquiet among business elites.

“We can all see that Russians are finally becoming less comfortable with this reality – with the fact that the war is bringing more and more negative consequences to Russia,” Zelensky wrote in the open letter. “They do not like the fact that there is no end in sight to your war.”

The Ukrainian leader said Putin “regularly” postpones deadlines to capture Ukrainian regions, specifically Donetsk.

“And you will not capture it this year either,” he said.

Zelensky struck a personal note in the letter, addressing Putin directly and warning him about his future: “(You) will have to fight much harder for your own existence – not Russia’s, but your own. And this is not a threat from me or from Ukraine. It is a fact of Russian history that you know well: when Russia grows tired, change comes.”

War is coming home to Russia’s biggest cities

“We can work toward that fatigue. You can stop your war,” he added.

Ukraine is nowhere near winning the war, but it does appear to have the upper hand in some areas along the front lines. Kyiv has also greatly increased its ability to strike deep inside Russia, targeting energy facilities and other strategic targets far from the borders.

To hammer home that message, Ukraine struck St. Petersburg just as attendees of the prestigious forum – sometimes dubbed “Russia’s Davos” – were gathering there this week.

Western experts have long pointed out that the way Russia is waging the war is unsustainable – both in terms of the economy and human capital. The International Institute for Strategic Studies has recently noted that the Kremlin will “soon face a fundamental choice over whether to radically escalate its demands on Russia’s economy and society or to scale back its war aims.”

But voices warning about the state of the economy have recently begun to emerge even inside Russia. German ⁠Gref, the boss of Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank, said on Friday that continued economic growth in the ​current circumstances is “already a miracle.”

Still, the Kremlin has so far dismissed the warnings and Putin himself struck a defiant tone during his speech at the forum on Friday. He referred to sanctions imposed on Moscow after he ordered an unprovoked full-scale invasion on Ukraine as “theft” and accused the West of inventing reasons to “fault” Russia.

Putin continues to push his maximalist demands to end the war, including Ukraine giving up even some of the territory that remains under its control. Meanwhile, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday that the country’s economy was “in a state of controlled cooling.”

Zelensky called for a direct meeting with Putin to end the war and stressed that peace shouldn’t wait until the US turned its attention from Iran to the Ukraine-Russia war.

“We see that the United States is fully focused on the issue of Iran, and it would be wrong to simply wait until the war in Europe returns to the center of its attention,” Zelensky said.

“Ukraine proposes ending this war through direct engagement between us – and you. I am proposing a meeting,” he wrote, adding that it should take place in a third country and that a clear date should be set. During those meetings, Zelensky said, a full ceasefire needs to be in place.

“An attempt to establish real silence is the best way to begin talking to one another.”

Zelensky reiterated in the letter that him traveling to the Russian capital is a non-starter – unsurprisingly, given the number of Russian-sponsored assassination attempts that Ukrainian security services say they’ve foiled in the past.

Putin did not mention the letter in his speech, but he was asked about it in the following panel discussion.

Putin said he never refused to meet Zelensky, but, in response to a question from India Today’s Geeta Mohan, he said he saw “no point” in doing that now. “The only point is for the Ukrainian side to stop the advance of our armed forces, that’s it,” he said. “But we need agreements … let the experts do the work, work out some solutions, and after that, we can meet up … sign some documents.”

He called the letter “rude” and said the real intention behind Zelensky’s note is to ensure no meeting takes place.

Putin said his response to the letter would be a message to Russian soldiers fighting on the front lines: “Keep working, brothers.”

Zelensky later decried Putin’s “weak response” to the letter.

﻿“He simply does not want to end the war. I think this response has disappointed many around the world,” Zelensky said.

During the event, Putin allowed several carefully curated audience members to speak.

Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., the US official leading the commission tasked with approving the rebuild of the White House ballroom wing, admired the architecture of St. Petersburg and thanked Putin for the hospitality.

“I appreciate the offer to speak, and we have a lot of ideas to talk about between our two capital cities in the next week,” Cook said.

Putin expressed gratitude to him for the “kind words.”

European Parliament member and Romanian politician Diana Iovanovici Șoșoacă declared to Putin that “Romanian people don’t hate you. Romanian people want peace with Russia.”

Former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl also spoke, asking Putin a question about the rules of engagement around drone warfare. Putin famously attended Kneissl’s wedding in 2018, stopping in for a quick dance with the bride.

Russia is facing a spring of discontent – and Putin is responding the only way he knows how

Meanwhile in St. Petersburg, Putin said proposals made by US President Donald Trump to end the war could “be the basis” for peace agreements but would require compromise from both countries.

“We generally agreed to these compromises. We just need to convince the Ukrainian side of this, and that’s it,” he said. “But overall, I believe they could very well be the basis for agreements between Russia and Ukraine and could put an end to this conflict.”

Trump vowed to quickly end the war when he took office in January 2025, but he’s made no tangible progress and has been criticized for seemingly siding with Russia on more than one occasion.

Putin paid something of a tribute to Trump, calling him a “colleague” and repeating the claim that the US president lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden because of “fraud.” He also said that, had it been Trump who was in power during the run-up to the full-scale invasion in 2022, “it would have turned out differently.”

But the US president suffered a defeat on the issue on Thursday after more than a dozen Republican lawmakers defied their own leadership – Trump himself – by voting with Democrats to approve a major bill to deliver billions of dollars in aid to Ukraine while imposing steep sanctions on Russia.

If passed by the Senate, the bill would be Congress’s first big move on the Ukraine-Russia war since spring 2024, when Biden was still in office. Still, Trump could veto the bill if it were to reach his desk.

CNN’s Zahra Ullah, Kosta Gak and Katharina Krebs contributed to this story.

zoo_crocodile_attack:
A three-year-old boy critically injured in a zoo enclosure was attacked by a crocodile, the BBC understands.

Cambridgeshire Police said a 30-year-old man arrested on suspicion of attempted murder had been bailed and was "unfit for interview". He reportedly has learning disabilities and had been on a trip to Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon, with carers.

It is believed the boy was attacked on Thursday by at least one crocodile after ending up in their enclosure.

He remained in a critical but stable condition. Police said the boy, who was from Cambridgeshire and visiting with his family, sustained serious injuries "while in the enclosure" and was pulled out by zoo staff.

He received medical treatment at the scene before being taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge.

Officers said they were called to the zoo at 13:34 BST on Thursday and were working to establish how long the boy was in the enclosure.

Police said the crocodiles had not been seized or killed.

Det Insp Verity McCann said: "Our inquiries are ongoing as we continue to understand the circumstances surrounding this distressing incident.

"Our thoughts remain with the boy, and his family and specialist officers continue to support them through this difficult time."

The man who was arrested was from Norfolk, police said, and was not at the zoo as part of an organised group visit.

People may be considered not fit to be interviewed because of their physical or mental state.

A witness told the BBC she had seen a man in his late 20s, accompanied by two women wearing lanyards who she believed may have been carers, walking through the zoo about 10 minutes before the incident.

She said they crossed paths as she and her daughter were entering the capybara enclosure and the group was coming out on to the forest walk.

The witness said she overheard one of the carers ask: "Should we go to the crocodile house next?". The man replied: "Yeah."

Cambridgeshire Police confirmed the suspect was white British after misinformation shared on social media.

A spokesperson for Johnsons said on Thursday their thoughts and prayers were with the boy and his family.

They added that the site's Tropical House, which contains the crocodile enclosure, had been closed "out of respect to the family".

Zoo staff were seen arriving at the site earlier on Friday and it opened as normal apart from the Tropical House.

Crocodilians first arrived on the family-run farm in 2006 and species now include broad snouted caiman, Nile crocodiles and American alligator.

They are kept in a converted cattle barn, which has metal-fenced elevated walkways looking down on large pools of water surrounded by tropical vegetation.

To celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first farm shop, a new museum at the site was due to open with a special weekend event starting on Saturday. It is unclear if the opening will go ahead.

One visitor, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC that she "didn't see the incident itself but heard the screams" and added that she later saw staff and an air ambulance responding at the scene.

Another visitor, who left about 10 minutes before the incident, said the crocodiles appeared calm and largely motionless during her visit.

The enclosure included "quite high fences" and they said there was "steel mesh fencing" all around the viewing platform.

A spokesperson from Huntingdonshire District Council, which is responsible for licensing such facilities, said Johnsons was "fully licensed".

"Its licence was renewed in 2024 following the statutory inspection and approval process. Public safety is a fundamental consideration in the licensing regime, including the suitability of animal enclosures and visitor barriers," they said.

The council added it was "not aware of any previous reportable accidents or incidents involving the crocodile enclosure" and that "no other safety-related incidents have been recorded through the zoo licensing process".

It said its environmental health team was in touch with the zoo managers and would "consider whether any further inspection or follow-up action is required".

Chris Newman, director of the National Centre For Reptile Welfare, told the BBC: "It's a reactatory animal. So, if something splashes next to it, surprises it, something jumps, his natural reaction is to turn and bite, and it would just be an investigative bite. They would quite often bite and let go."

He said Tracey Johnson, from the zoo, had shown "remarkable bravery" in entering the enclosure during the incident and pulling the boy out.

He said he had been told Johnson was not injured.

On Thursday, police said they were speaking to people who were at the zoo at the time of the incident.

"We do not believe the man arrested and the child are known to each other," a force spokesperson said.

They added that CCTV from the venue was being reviewed by officers.

Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty urged people to "refrain from speculation online" and said police were treating it as a "critical incident".

A Magpas Air Ambulance spokesperson said a critical care team attended the incident at 13:42 BST on Thursday and "treated one patient at the scene before taking them to hospital".

According to its website, Johnsons of Old Hurst is a farming business that also features a butchers, a farm shop, tea room, steakhouse and zoo.

It says it "houses over 100 fascinating animals" including crocodiles, African lions and a Bengal tiger.

The ex-directors, Newcastle businessmen Rizwan Rana and Satwinder Singh, have strenuously denied any wrongdoing, saying that assets were sold to pay off the company's debts before it went bust, and that temporary company loans used to purchase residential homes were repaid.
