Assistant US Attorney Matthew O'Brien, one of the prosecutors, gives his opening statement. (Illustration via Reuters: Mona Edwards)

Prosecutors have accused Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire in the Los Angeles hills while he was feeling lonely and dejected after a break-up.

Their case centres on proving the blaze allegedly lit by Mr Rinderknecht, who has pleaded not guilty, later grew into the Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people and destroyed up to $73 billion worth of property.

Mr Rinderknecht is facing a sentence of up to 45 years in prison if he is convicted of all three charges levelled against him.

A federal prosecutor has told jurors in the US that 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht was feeling lonely and dejected over a break-up when he allegedly lit a wildfire in January 2025 that grew into one of the deadliest and most destructive in Los Angeles history.

The lawyer representing the former Uber driver countered that the hilltop New Year's Day blaze was triggered by fireworks, not his client, and that the massive Palisades inferno that killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes a week later was a separate fire set by others.

The opposing accounts were presented to a US District Court jury on Wednesday at the start of a high-profile arson trial stemming from one of the worst wildfire calamities on record anywhere in the country.

Mr Rinderknecht was indicted last October on one felony count each of destruction of property by means of fire, arson affecting property used in interstate commerce, and illegal burning of timber on public lands.

Jonathan Rinderknecht is alleged to have started the Palisades fire while angry over a break-up. (US Attorney's Office via AP)

He is accused of starting a brush fire that was suppressed relatively quickly, but continued to smoulder underground in the roots of dense scrub before reigniting a week later due to fierce winds.

From there, it is alleged to have grown into the conflagration that laid waste to the upscale seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.

Mr Rinderknecht, who pleaded not guilty and has remained in custody since his arrest in Florida, faces a sentence of five to 45 years in prison if convicted on all three counts.

Assistant US Attorney Mark Williams said security camera footage and location data from Mr Rinderknecht's mobile phone established that he was the only person in the vicinity of the January 1 fire when it erupted.

He added that investigators had ruled out all non-arson ignition sources, including fireworks.

"The evidence will show that the defendant lit this fire on January 1 and that he did so on purpose, and the evidence will show that the fire that the defendant started on January 1 was the same fire that caused all of that destruction on January 7," Mr Williams told jurors in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom.

The Palisades fire burns through a street in LA's Pacific Palisades neighbourhood. (AP Photo: Ethan Swope)

Defence lawyer Steve Haney, however, said his client had witnessed the January 1 fire erupt from the vantage point of a hill he had climbed to watch a New Year's fireworks display after dropping off his last Uber passenger for the night.

Mr Rinderknecht had in fact tried to alert authorities when he saw it, Mr Haney said.

Mr Haney then played the court a recording of the emergency 911 call that Mr Rinderknecht placed to report the fire, after poor mobile reception thwarted several previous attempts to make the call.

Mr Haney also asserted that prosecutors lacked any physical evidence linking Mr Rinderknecht to arson, or any electronic or digital records showing an intent to start a fire.

The case against Mr Rinderknecht hinges in part on whether the January 1 blaze, originally referred to as the Lachman fire, and the disastrous Palisades fire that occurred six days later were actually the same fire.

Los Angeles firefighters believed they had swiftly extinguished the Lachman fire, which began near a hiking trail in Topanga State Park, part of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.

But after smouldering undetected — a phenomenon experts call a "holding fire" — the blaze erupted again on January 7 near the same spot and grew swiftly into the devastating Palisades fire, federal investigators said.

The Palisades fire is estimated to have destroyed up to $73 billion worth of property. (Reuters: David Ryder)

Fanned by hurricane-force Santa Ana winds, the flames scorched 93 square kilometres and incinerated some 6,000 structures. Property losses have been estimated at anywhere from $US25 billion to $US51 billion ($36 billion to $73 billion).

Days before one of the largest wildfires the area has ever seen broke out in southern California, there were warnings — the region was a tinderbox.

The Palisades fire coincided with another catastrophic wildfire north-east of Los Angeles known as the Eaton Fire, which killed 19 people and ravaged the community of Altadena.

Mr Haney said testimony would show that the Palisades fire was originally treated as an act of arson separate from the Lachman fire, and that investigators only abandoned their two-fire theory in favour of a single-fire explanation eight months into their inquiry.

Ultimately, Mr Haney said, evidence will show that fireworks triggered the Lachman fire, and that the Palisades fire was the work of unidentified arsonists, "not Jonathan".

Moreover, he said, authorities initially failed to secure the Lachman site as a crime scene, thus compromising the integrity of any findings implicating his client.

In seeking to establish a motive for arson, prosecutors have painted Mr Rinderknecht as a malcontent whose life "started to deteriorate" after a romantic break-up in 2024 that left him lonely and withdrawn.

Mr Williams said Mr Rinderknecht became angry towards the rest of society — the wealthy in particular — as he believed it was the cause of all of his troubles.

An examination of the defendant's digital profile showed he turned often to the AI chatbot ChatGPT to express those resentments, the prosecutor said.

Mr Williams said that on one occasion Mr Rinderknecht directed ChatGPT to create an image of thousands of people trying to escape a forest fire while a group of rich people laughed and danced from a safe position behind a gate marked with a dollar sign.

A federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to restore sites changed under an executive order calling for the nation’s museums, parks and landmarks to not display elements that “inappropriately disparage Americans past or living.”

The preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley in Massachusetts also orders a pause on any additional changes, writing that the plaintiffs have shown that these efforts are meant “to rewrite the Nation’s history with a white-out pen.”

“History cannot be faithfully told while excluding the experiences of communities whose contributions, struggles, and achievements form an important part of our Nation’s story,” the judge wrote.

The Trump administration must also provide a status report every week describing the progress they’ve made with these changes, the judge wrote.

“Under the guise of promoting American dignity, this Administration seeks to share a limited history by ordering the removal of all signs, displays, and interpretive exhibits at National Parks that do not align with its preferred narrative, thereby telling half-truths,” Kelley wrote.

The order comes in response to a February lawsuit filed by conservation and historical organizations over National Park Service policies that the groups say have forced park service staff to remove or censor dozens of exhibits that share factually accurate and relevant U.S. history and scientific knowledge, including about slavery and climate change.

Many of the changes were at Philadelphia’s Independence National Historical Park, where the administration removed exhibits on the lives of nine people enslaved at the site in the 1790s under George Washington, the first U.S. president. Other changes included removing a sign at Sunset Crater Volcano National Monument in Arizona describing basalt bubbles because it had an image of a visitor holding a Pride flag while films on labor history were removed from the Lowell National Historical Park in Massachusetts.

President Donald Trump signed the executive order “restoring truth and sanity to American history” at the nation’s museums, parks and landmarks last year. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum later directed removal of “improper partisan ideology” from museums, monuments, landmarks and other public exhibits under federal control.

An email seeking comment from the Interior Department was sent Saturday.

Alan Spears, senior director for cultural resources for the National Parks Conservation Association, one of the organizations that brought the lawsuit, said the ruling will help protect national parks from the administration’s effort “to erase history and science at these one-of-a-kind places.”

“National parks belong to the American people and censorship of any kind goes against the values these places represent,” he said.

Bill Wade, executive director for the Association of National Park Rangers, another organization that brought the lawsuit, said this is especially good news for National Parks employees who “have prided themselves for being able to provide truthful, accurate and unbiased information.”

A member of the radical domestic terrorist group that kidnapped newspaper heiress Patricia Hearst has died at the age of 81.

Bill Harris died of a heart attack at a San Francisco hospital on Sept. 10, his wife, Rebecca Young, told the New York Times on Tuesday.

Harris, who was born in Fort Sill, Okla., served in Vietnam as a Marine before enrolling at Indiana University after returning home.

There, he joined Vietnam Veterans Against the War, moved steadily to the left and met his first wife, Emily Schwartz, a fellow student from an affluent Chicago suburb who was also embracing far-left politics. They married in 1971, the outlet reported.

The couple later moved to the San Francisco Bay Area, where they joined the Symbionese Liberation Army (SLA) — a violent far-left group that had gained notoriety in 1973 for assassinating Oakland schools superintendent Marcus Foster — and helped plan the Hearst kidnapping.

Harris, by then a top lieutenant in the SLA, was thrust into the national spotlight after he and two others broke into Hearst’s Berkeley, Calif., apartment on Feb. 4, 1974, and dragged her away in a violent struggle, stuffing her into the trunk of a Chevrolet Impala, according to the FBI.

Hearst, then a 19-year-old UC Berkeley sophomore, was the granddaughter of newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst, the inspiration for “Citizen Kane.”

At first, the group branded Hearst a “prisoner of war” and made no ransom demand, but later called on her family to bankroll a sweeping food giveaway for the poor across California.

“Patricia Hearst was a symbolic target,” Harris later said of why the group chose her, according to the New York Times.

Pauline Hanson has hit back at Anthony Albanese after he attacked One Nation and accused them of dividing the country following the party's historic win in Western Australia's Secret Harbour by-election.

'Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems,' Albanese said.

'They'll say anything and do anything to win votes. Bend any facts. Peddle misinformation and disinformation. Turn Australian against Australian.

'Across the world, hard right populists are on the march.

'We simply must defeat them. We owe it to history. And we will defeat them.

'We unequivocally support multiculturalism because we know it's part of Australia's strength.

'And because we believe every Australian is equal, whether they are Australian by birth or Australian by choice.'

Pauline Hanson has hit back at Anthony Albanese after he attacked One Nation and accused them of dividing the country following the party's historic win in Western Australia's Secret Harbour by-election

Hanson snapped back at the comments on Monday morning and accused Albanese of crossing the line

The Prime Minister also took aim at some of the offhand comments made by Hanson.

'They think Australians are lazy and overpaid,' he said.

'That people working from home are bludging. That domestic violence is sometimes a woman's fault. That we should somehow become a monoculture.'

Hanson snapped back at the comments on Monday morning and accused Albanese of crossing the line and inciting political violence.

'No matter how worried Jim and Albanese are about losing their jobs, telling Australians that their democratically elected opponents are "dangerous" and a "threat to our country" invites people to treat them as a threat.

'Words have consequences. That is how political violence is incited. The murder of Ann Widdecombe in Britain should be warning enough about the dangers of poisonous political rhetoric.'

Hanson was commenting on the July murder of veteran British politician Widdecombe, who was found dead in her home after suffering severe blunt-force trauma.

'Anthony Albanese says we need to turn down the heat and violent rhetoric in our political discourse,' Hanson said.

Labor lost to One Nation at a WA by-election in Perth's south over the weekend (pictured is winner Luke Herdegen)

Albanese acknowledged the rising popularity of One Nation (pictured is One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce)

'Meanwhile, he and his Treasurer are pouring petrol all over it. Australians are entitled to vote for One Nation without being told by the Treasurer and the Prime Minister that their democratic choice is a danger to the nation.

'The real danger is that Jim and Albanese's incompetent economic management will continue to push your rent, your mortgage and your bills even higher.

'The real danger to Jim and Albanese is that the people of Australia are coming for their government… at the ballot box.'

The comments come a day after One Nation secured its first lower house seat in Western Australia, with candidate Luke Herdegen defeating Labor's Georgia Tree in Secret Harbour.

The result is a major upset, with One Nation taking a seat long considered safe Labor territory, after an 18 per cent swing to the party and a two-candidate-preferred result of roughly 57 per cent to Labor's 43 per cent.

Labor's primary vote crashed by 22 per cent to just 24 per cent, while One Nation recorded a primary of 39 per cent - having managed only nine per cent at the 2025 WA state election in the seat.

The result comes as the latest Newspoll conducted by Pyxis Polling & Insights has revealed that primary support for Hanson's party has risen to 30 per cent, narrowly ahead of Labor on 29 per cent and the Coalition on 19 per cent.

However, Albanese remains the preferred Prime Minister on 46 per cent, well ahead of Hanson on 31 per cent and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor on 23 per cent.

Primary support for Pauline Hanson's party has risen to 30 per cent, narrowly ahead of Labor

Anthony Albanese remains the preferred Prime Minister on 46 per cent

Almost 1,250 voters were surveyed last week for the poll, before One Nation's victory in the the Secret Harbour by-election.

Hanson's personal rating is also on the rise, with 47 per cent of voters satisfied with her performance and 48 per cent dissatisfied.

Albanese remains far less popular, with 38 per cent of voters satisfied with the job he is doing and 59 per cent dissatisfied.

Meanwhile, in a separate Redbridge Group/Accent Research poll, One Nation's primary vote dropped three points to 28 per cent, trailing Labor by one point.

One Nation will now set its sights on the coming Victorian and NSW state elections.

Some Labor sources are becoming increasingly concerned about One Nation.

'The more representation they get, the more they become part of the system,' a senior party source told The Australian.

On Sunrise on Monday morning, Labor MP Tanya Plibersek hit back at claims Western Australia's shock by-election result was driven by federal issues, as she clashed with One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce and host Nat Barr.

Anthony Albanese spent Sunday defending housing taxes at the Queensland ALP conference

On Sunrise on Monday morning, Labor MP Tanya Plibersek hit back at claims Western Australia's shock by-election result was driven by federal issues, as she clashed with Barnaby Joyce over immigration and Labor's record

'To your point that this was run on state issues, the new member ran part of it on federal issues, particularly immigration,' Barr said.

'He said the Albanese government's immigration management had intensified the housing problem and the cost-of-living crisis - so he was running this on federal issues.'

Plibersek insisted the Albanese government was already taking action to reduce immigration.

'We're actually doing it. Barnaby and his mob - you get three of them in a room, they've got three different numbers on what they're trying to do.

'We're actually doing the work to bring immigration down. They're the people who voted against us when we tried to put a cap on student numbers.'

Barr then pointed to polling showing Labor and One Nation neck-and-neck, while One Nation held a significant advantage when voters were asked which party was best placed to handle immigration.

'Tanya, just let me talk to you, because it feels like there's a discrepancy between what you're saying, what you say you're doing and the messaging in the polls today,' Barr said.

'You and One Nation are neck and neck - but when you dive deeper, the party best able to handle the key issue, the rate of immigration, One Nation is at 39 per cent and you guys are at 19 per cent.

'So whatever you're saying, it doesn't sound like it's cutting through. Tanya, what's the problem?'

Plibersek responded by taking aim at One Nation's immigration policy.

'It's kind of comical because they had their party executive admitting that they don't have a clear policy. And yesterday Barnaby, on the TV, wouldn't give a number again.'

Joyce interrupted and accused Plibersek of being a liar.

Plibersek said Labor needed to do a better job of communicating the changes it had made.

'Oh, I think we need to keep making sure that Australians know that we are the ones who are actually delivering real change in this country.

'And, of course, a big part of the job is making the changes. Another part of the job is making sure people understand the changes.'

Joyce interjected again and accused her of being a liar.

'Even what you call your party is a lie. There are no labourers in the Labor Party. There are no labourers in the Labor Party, namely the blue-collar labourers on your frontbench,' he said.

Plibersek hit back: 'We've got plenty of people in the Labor Party with very diverse backgrounds.'

HARRISBURG — Taxes aimed at the tech industry are on the table as Pennsylvania lawmakers negotiate the upcoming budget and look for ways to help balance the commonwealth’s shaky books.

Two options have been floated, including eliminating the state’s sales tax exemption for purchases related to building and maintaining data centers. The commonwealth is projected to miss out on $2 billion in accumulated tax revenue by 2031.

The other proposal would extend the state’s 5% gross receipts tax to firms that sell digital ads. That tax could bring in hundreds of millions of dollars a year in new revenue, although estimates vary.

Such a fiscal shot in the arm would aid policymakers as they tackle Pennsylvania’s longstanding budgetary woes. The commonwealth is on track to spend around $5 billion more than it makes in revenue for this fiscal year. That kind of deficit spending has become routine in recent budgets, and led to cash reserves being halved from $14 billion two years ago to roughly $7 billion today.

Email address

Sign Up

Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has pitched a $53.3 billion budget that would send more money to the state’s poorest schools and bump funding for struggling public transit systems. Although the proposal doesn’t include any major new programs, it would still require the state to dip into its rainy day fund.

Tech taxes are a new direction for lawmakers stymied by partisan and ideological differences when trying to find new revenue — a dynamic exacerbated by special interests. Efforts to regulate and tax recreational marijuana and slot-like skill games have foundered in recent years.

Supporters of creating a digital ad tax and ending the data center exemption argue the revenue would come out of the pockets of giant tech companies rather than small businesses and everyday Pennsylvanians.

“These are people who are making tremendous profit, record-breaking profit, right now. That's who should be paying this tax,” said state Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler (D., Philadelphia), a vocal progressive and prime sponsor of the ad tax.

Tech taxes have also found support from individuals across the ideological spectrum.

Two conservative Republicans — state Rep. Jamie Walsh of Luzerne County and Sen. Jarrett Coleman of Lehigh County — have jointly introduced a bill to repeal the data center tax break and use the money to reduce the cost of gas.

In a memo seeking support, they said the state should not “continue to give a special tax incentive to the thriving data center industry.” Coleman told Spotlight PA, “If [tech companies] are still dead set on showing up, they should have to pay down the gas tax for Pennsylvanians.”

That tech firms are raking in dough isn’t up for dispute. Amazon, Meta, and Google all made tens of billions of dollars in profit in 2025, per Forbes, and policies aimed at reining them in have become increasingly popular in both red and blue states.

It’s unclear if that means Pennsylvania's divided state legislature will actually pass the tech measures on the table, but early signs indicate that both major parties are weighing the option.

A bill to levy the digital ad tax passed the Democratic-controlled state House 139-63 on Wednesday. It was unanimously amended to direct any revenue raised to provide property tax relief for older homeowners.

The bill is now with the state Senate. The upper chamber’s majority leader, Joe Pittman (R., Indiana), didn’t rule out an ad tax or an end to the data center exemption in an interview last week.

“There are concerns about that [data center sales] tax provision, and it’s certainly possible that discussion on what the right approach is will unfold in the weeks ahead,” Pittman said. He floated closing some unspecified sales tax exemptions as a revenue source in 2025.

Both efforts would require defeating the opposition of powerful interests who back the status quo. In- and out-of-state business advocacy groups oppose a digital ad tax, arguing that giant tech firms would pass on costs to businesses through higher advertising costs.

And data centers are not only popular with tech firms but with the trade unions whose members build them. Those unions are key Democratic allies, so an effort to end the data center exemption would likely divide the party.

Shapiro has offered an alternative to totally axing the exemption: He wants to make it contingent on data center developers following stricter transparency, environmental, and energy-use standards.

State House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D., Montgomery) said the chamber would “expeditiously” pass such legislation. The party isn’t unified on that approach, though — almost 30 state House Democrats are backing a bill that would repeal the exemption.

Conversations about these taxes are happening amid growing national backlash against the tech industry and income inequality, and a desire to tackle the ongoing affordability crisis and backfill pending federal cuts by the Trump administration.

“Too many in Pennsylvania are being told to accept scarcity while wealth is concentrated at the top,” Gregory Edwards, a Lehigh Valley pastor and leader of the leftist POWER Interfaith coalition, said at a Capitol rally to support the digital ad tax last week. “We reject that plainly.”

June is also traditionally when lawmakers push new policy ideas ahead of the budget deadline. A handful of top legislative leaders and staff will meet behind closed doors to hammer out a deal in private with little public input.

Democrats who control the state House have advanced a spending plan that matches Shapiro’s budget pitch. Bradford told Spotlight PA that the plan, which would increase state spending by approximately 6%, “reflects House Democrats' priorities.”

Republicans who lead the state Senate have not released a plan publicly, but Pittman said the caucus’ main priority is “very simple and direct — to minimize the growth of spending in our state budget.”

He has an eye on line items he thinks are too costly. For instance, he noted that Shapiro’s budget, even after closing two prisons last year, increased funding for the Department of Corrections.

“That, to me, doesn't compute,” Pittman added.

There have been bumps in the negotiating road in recent years. State House Democrats and Shapiro have criticized Senate Republicans as unable to compromise on issues like a minimum wage increase or legalizing recreational marijuana. Meanwhile, Republicans have called Democrats’ budgets unrealistic and questioned whether Shapiro and his party are on the same page.

The commonwealth’s last four budgets have been late — two by more than 100 days.

Two sources with knowledge of closed-door talks told Spotlight PA that both sides have traded budget proposals. Though the statutory deadline for a deal is June 30, the impact of a late deal often isn’t felt until a few weeks after the deadline.

The senior investigating officer in the PC Andrew Harper case has told BBC Breakfast he is "appalled" that two of the killers will become eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died from catastrophic injuries in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft.

Two of his killers â Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers â will be eligible for early release next year under revised government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

Stuart Blaik, who investigated the killing, said it was "particularly hard to understand" their case for early release and said police officers were shocked at the prospect.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release from prison.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC on Friday that early release is "not okay" - adding that no government should have been put in the position of having to deal with limited prison capacity.

This video can not be played

Stuart Blaik says it 'doesn't make any sense' that two of PC Harper's killers will become eligible for early release

Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case",  Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

PC Harper married Lissie just four weeks before he was killed

PC Harper and Lissie had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.

On Thursday, the police officer's widow said she "will not give up" and hoped people would share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison.

She said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets.

"Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."

Thames Valley Police Federation chair Aileen O'Connor began the petition this week.

"My ask is that the prime minister, the home secretary and everybody else in government gets on the right side of this and does the right thing and makes the changes that keep the two killers behind bars," she said.

"We have been working closely with Chief Constable Jason Hogg and Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber from the outset on this.

"We are all united in our frustration and dismay at the government's ridiculous plans when it comes to releasing from prison early the killers of police officers."

The government said it was trying to avoid running out of prison spaces as soon as October this year.

The justice secretary Alex Norris previously said about 1,000 prisoners would now not be released early following the revision to the scheme.

"If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," said Norris.

Prisoners released on licence, he said, would be subject to "very significant controls on their lives" and victims would be consulted.

TV and Media

Scott Pelley told the New York Times that CBS News leadership instructed him to “inject falsehoods” that aligned with the Trump administration into a piece on immigration enforcement in Minnesota.

By Greta Kaul

Fired “60 Minutes” correspondent Scott Pelley accused new CBS editor-in-chief Bari Weiss of trying to insert “falsehoods and bias” into a report about the Renee Good and Alex Pretti killings in Minneapolis, he said in an interview with the New York Times published Sunday.

Last week, CBS fired Pelley, who worked at the network for nearly 40 years, after he clashed with managers over the direction of the network and the show. Pelley’s firing comes as other former “60 Minutes” journalists have accused managers of seeking to insert political bias into coverage.

Pelley’s firing followed a staff meeting in which he questioned the qualifications of new “60 Minutes” executive producer Nick Bilton and accused Weiss of “murdering” the show, the New York Times reported.

Weiss said Pelley was fired because trust had been broken after his comments at the staff meeting.

In a statement, Pelley accused managers of telling him to “inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story.”

In the interview Sunday, Pelley specified he was referring to a February piece about protests against Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota.

In Pelley’s telling, he and his team had interviewed Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), who was holding hearings on Metro Surge tactics, and built a story around the killings of Good and Pretti and the protests in Minnesota.

“We culled together a lot of video of protesters screaming in the faces of officers because we were going to talk about the killing of Pretti and the killing of Good, and it seemed to me important to tell the audience about the entire context‚" Pelley told the New York Times’ Lulu Garcia-Navarro.

Pelley said the piece went through screenings and rewrites and was approved to run. Four hours after a noon EST deadline — “60 Minutes” airs at 7 p.m. EST — Pelley said his team got a note from Weiss.

“Two of the things in the email include, can we make the protesters look more violent?” he said. “Now, I’m paraphrasing. I don’t have the quote, but that’s what was communicated to me. And the other thing, Renee Good’s car. You need to describe her as driving toward the officer."

Pelley said he felt the team had gone out of its way to show the context of the protests, and they had gone over video of Good’s killing repeatedly to make sure their reporting was accurate.

He said he felt Weiss was asking for revisions to fit the narrative of President Donald Trump and his administration.

“The event was not as the president said and not the way Bari Weiss remembered it,” he said.

Ultimately, Pelley aired the story without those changes. In a statement in response to Pelley’s account, a CBS News spokesperson told the New York Times, “In an email, Bari made four points in the course of editorial back-and-forth. They had no political motivation and were proposed solely to make the piece as strong, fair, and accurate as possible. As is frequently the case in any newsroom that operates with collaboration, not everything she raised made it into the final piece.”

Pelley said the interference remained an issue, as did the chaos he said Weiss caused with the after-deadline email.

Jane Kirtley, professor emerita at the University of Minnesota who was the longtime director of the Silha Center for the Study of Media Ethics and Law, emphasized that Pelley’s account is one side of the story, supplemented by brief statements from CBS, but she said the incident raises questions about CBS’ independence.

“There can be good faith disagreement about what happened during Operation Metro Surge, but as the old saying goes, ‘You’re entitled to your own opinion, but not your own facts,’ " Kirtley said.

Weiss, the founder of the Free Press media company and a New York Times Opinion writer before becoming editor-in-chief at CBS News, was hired to change the prism through which the news organization operates, Kirtley said.

But Pelley’s interview and accounts from other “60 Minutes” journalists who have raised bias concerns and been fired or not had contracts renewed raise questions about the journalistic credibility of the show and the network under Weiss, Kirtley said.

“It’s about truth and accuracy,” she said. Editorial staff exists to keep reporters honest, pushing them to ensure their own accuracy, Kirtley said, but several accounts now raise concerns that Weiss has gone beyond that, asking for stories to be approached from an angle pushed by the Trump administration.

If that’s the case, that’s a problem — regardless of what administration is in power, Kirtley said.

"The whole purpose of the First Amendment, I think most people would say, would be to hold government to account," Kirtley said.

By Nick Campton

Topic:NRL

The Bears are edging ever closer to their first ever season in the NRL.  (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut.  (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France.  (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year.  (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady.  (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997.  (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade.  (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making.  (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting.  (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital.   (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

Motorists are being warned to expect petrol price increases from July 1, as the Federal Government scales back its temporary fuel excise relief.

From midnight, the excise cut introduced following the Middle East conflict will be reduced from 32 cents per litre to 16 cents per litre, before ending on August 2.

The change is expected to deliver about $11 in savings for motorists filling a 65-litre tank, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said in a June 22 statement.

“This extension to the fuel tax cut recognises that economic and fuel stability recovery will take time, and our action provides a graduated return to normal settings for the fuel excise,” he said.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has put fuel retailers on notice ahead of the change, revealing it wrote to companies last week reminding them not to use the partial restoration of the tax to boost profits.

The watchdog said retailers must be transparent with customers and able to justify any claims made about price movements.

ACCC Commissioner Anna Brakey has issued a strong warning:

“We will closely examine fuel price movements and market behaviour, both in the lead-up to and following the increase in fuel excise,” she said.

“We will not hesitate to take action if retailers make false or misleading statements about price movements or if there is evidence of anti-competitive behaviour.”

While prices are expected to rise in line with the higher excise, the ACCC noted the increase may not be immediate, as retailers do not always face higher wholesale costs straight away due to delays in new fuel supplies reaching service stations.

It also stressed that global refined fuel prices continue to play a major role in what motorists ultimately pay at the pump.

“We encourage consumers to use fuel price apps and websites to compare prices at different retail sites before filling up to save money,” Ms Brakey said.

The ACCC’s latest data shows petrol prices in capital cities have already fallen below pre-conflict levels, while diesel prices have dropped to near pre-conflict levels.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the warning from the ACCC was aimed at ensuring motorists continue to benefit from the remaining tax relief.

“It’s been really terrific to see petrol and diesel prices come down very substantially in recent months,” he said.

“In fact, this week we think for the first time both petrol and diesel are cheaper than they were before the war in the Middle East began, but people are still under pressure.

“That’s why we’re extending this fuel price relief for another month at a tapered rate to provide the cost-of-living help that people need and deserve.”

Andrea Hsu

Amber and Neil Petersen serve lunch to two of their children, 11-year-old Eden and 4-year-old Jack, while visiting Amber's parents in Iowa City, Iowa.
                
                    
                    Cliff Jette for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.

Amber Petersen's struggles are likely familiar to any working parent.

Some days at work, she finds herself diverted to family matters. A school nurse calls to tell her that one of her children is sick. She needs to leave work immediately.

Other days, she wishes she could be chaperoning a field trip instead of scheduling meetings and putting together files at the small law firm in Mason City, Iowa, where she works as a legal assistant.

"I feel like that tug of war is constantly on my mind of where I need to be — if I am missing out as a mom, or if I am disappointing somebody at work," she says. "There's just no way to be two things at once and give 100% at both."

A new survey from the Pew Research Center finds that struggle widespread, with two-thirds of working mothers reporting that they can't give 100% at home and just over half saying they can't give their all at work. A smaller but sizable share of fathers agree, with half reporting they can't give 100% at home, and about a third saying they can't give their all at work. The survey focused primarily on families with both a mother and a father who work full time.

Petersen works as a legal assistant at a small firm in Mason City, Iowa. She can leave work on a dime if one of her children falls sick, but she has no paid sick leave so she won't get paid.
                
                    
                    Cliff Jette for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

"We see that parents are facing lots of demands from both work and family, and that the boundary between those is often blurry," says Pew senior researcher Rachel Minkin.

While the findings may not be surprising, they come as the number of parents engaged in the juggling act has grown. The share of families with moms and dads who are both working full time was 31% in 1975. A half-century later, it's 52%, according to Pew's analysis of census data.

Meanwhile, the share of families with dads working full time and moms not working has dropped from 42% in 1975 to 23% in 2025, Pew says.

Peterson says staying home is not an option for her. Even with two incomes, the family is just getting by.

"We don't have an emergency fund because we just can't afford to put anything away," she says. "It's a hard time that we're living in right now."

The survey of 2,242 working parents sought to highlight the kinds of policies and structural support that might help them better navigate work and family.

On that front, Petersen has some ideas. She's grateful that her employer is understanding when it comes to family matters. She's able to leave work on a dime as needed, including to pick up a sick kid. Her husband, who works in a factory painting industrial trucks, would be penalized for such a move, imperiling future raises.

But Petersen pays a price too. She gets paid only for the hours she works. She does have some paid vacation days but no paid sick leave.

"One thing about it being a small firm is they are unable to offer some of those benefits," she says.

Neil Petersen plays with his 4-year-old son, Jack. Neil works in a factory painting boom trucks.
                
                    
                    Cliff Jette for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

The Pew survey found more than half of parents with lower incomes — and single mothers in particular — say they're highly worried about losing pay if they unexpectedly have to leave work to take care of family issues. Black and Hispanic parents worry more about this than white and Asian parents.

Petersen says paid sick leave would help enormously. So, too, would more affordable options for childcare.

A couple years ago, Petersen decided her two daughters, now 11 and 12, could stay home alone — as long as they were together.

"We kind of had to make that decision a little sooner than I would have liked to," she says.

A summer program she was eyeing for them cost a couple thousand dollars, more than the family could afford. It's a familiar problem. The Pew survey found nearly half of working parents needing care for school-aged kids had difficulty finding an arrangement in the summer.

"Luckily, they have each other to kind of keep tabs on one another," says Petersen. "And I only work three minutes from home, which is very nice."

Petersen does pay for childcare for her 4-year-old son. He spends his days at a center that costs $180 a week. It's a strain, she says, while acknowledging the daycare teachers make very little.

Free preschool is gaining ground in some places, but it remains a patchwork across the country. Petersen is looking forward to the fall of 2027, when her son will be old enough to go to kindergarten.

"I find myself wishing away these years — which is awful — because I'm like, it'll be cheaper with him being in school," she says.

Jack, 4, Eden, 11, and Piper, 12, sit with their parents Amber and Neil Petersen.
                
                    
                    Cliff Jette for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Like many parents, Petersen would love more flexibility at work. She wishes she could take part in more activities at school and experience more of her kids' childhood.

"It's kind of disappointing," she says. "You feel like these years are so short."

She does not have the option to work from home. Her law firm doesn't allow it. Roughly three-quarters of parents surveyed by Pew are in the same boat.

But researchers found even those with can work remotely are struggling.

"Working from home doesn't ease all the challenges of balancing work and family," says Minkin.

The Pew survey found those parents experience the most overlap between their family and work responsibilities. Close to 40% of parents who work from home all or nearly all of the time describe frequently taking care of parenting-related tasks while working, the survey found. About a third of these parents say they frequently deal with work matters while spending time with their children.

Amber Petersen and Piper, 12, play together on a patio. Amber wishes she could spend more time with her children, but the family needs two incomes.
                
                    
                    Cliff Jette for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

The Pew findings come as President Trump has called for a baby boom. At a women's history month event last year, he joked that he would be known as "the fertilization president."

"We want more babies, to put it very nicely," Trump was later quoted as saying in a White House handout about IVF.

Vice President JD Vance and his wife Usha are expecting their fourth child this summer. Petersen says she and her husband would also love a fourth child.

Second lady Usha Vance and Vice President Vance arrive for a military mothers celebration at the White House on May 6. She is pregnant with their fourth child.
                
                    
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

"But I cannot imagine what that would look like," she says.

On top of balancing work and family, she and her husband are also now buckling under the high price of health insurance, groceries and gas.

"There would be no way," she says.

California’s Democratic leaders are facing a fresh standoff with the state’s biggest utility after PG&E announced it would pull back billions of dollars in planned spending.

The move now has put renewed pressure on Sacramento to resolve a bitter fight over who should pay when utility equipment sparks catastrophic wildfires.

PG&E said it plans to reduce its 2027 investments by about $2 billion, citing the growing financial burden of California’s wildfire-liability rules.

The announcement comes just after lawmakers ended their legislative session without reaching a deal that would have changed how the state’s major investor-owned utilities shoulder wildfire costs.

The move has put Democratic lawmakers in the position of weighing the utilities’ concerns about financing against demands for accountability when their equipment is responsible for devastating fires.

Assemblywoman Cottie Petrie-Norris, the Democratic chair of the Assembly Utilities and Energy Committee, told KCRA 3 that utilities depend on borrowing to finance major construction projects — and that higher borrowing costs can ultimately affect customers.

“With utilities, like any company, in order to build stuff, they’ve got to borrow money,” Petrie-Norris said. “Much like you and I, when we’ve got a mortgage, if our credit rating isn’t good, it costs us more money.

“And when it costs PG&E or any of the utilities more money to build and construct utility projects, that’s a bill that gets passed on to all of us, and that’s not OK,” she added.

Petrie-Norris said the reduction in spending could affect projects involving infrastructure such as poles, wires and sensors, as well as housing-related work, according to the outlet.

“That’s also not OK. So that’s why I’m concerned, and that’s why it matters for all of us,” she said.

The confrontation follows a dramatic collapse of a proposed wildfire-liability overhaul in Sacramento. PG&E, Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric had pushed lawmakers to shift some wildfire-related costs toward insurance companies. But the legislature ultimately abandoned the proposal after negotiations broke down during the final days of the session.

The failed effort came after the utilities suffered a sharp market reaction with their stock tumbling just the day after.

The broader dispute centers on subrogation, under which insurers that pay homeowners after a wildfire can seek reimbursement from utilities they believe are responsible for the blaze. Gov. Gavin Newsom and the utilities had backed restrictions on that practice as part of a broader liability overhaul, while opponents argued the changes could leave wildfire victims and insurers carrying more of the financial burden.

Petrie-Norris said she hopes PG&E’s spending decision was not intended to pressure lawmakers.

“I certainly hope not. But that is definitely a question you would have to ask their CEO, not me,” she told KCRA 3.

The lawmaker also warned that the fight has drawn an array of powerful interests, including utilities, insurers, hedge funds and attorneys.

“When two elephants are fighting, it’s the grass that suffers,” Petrie-Norris said. “We don’t care about your companies. We don’t care about your industry. We care about what you are doing for Californians.”

PG&E has maintained that its spending reduction is driven by the difficulty and expense of financing its operations under California’s current liability structure.

The company is still planning billions of dollars in investment next year and has said its pullback will focus on projects that can be delayed rather than critical wildfire-safety obligations.

The utility’s CEO has also rejected the suggestion that the announcement was intended as a political pressure tactic, arguing that customers ultimately bear the consequences of the state’s financing and liability framework.

philp-french-navy-incident:
A French patrol officer at the back of the boat was seen pointing a pistol towards the sea

Chris Philp has told the BBC he plans to contact the French ambassador to seek an explanation after a French naval vessel carried out a live firing exercise close to a boat he was conducting interviews on in the English Channel.

Speaking in Dover after the incident, the shadow home secretary said: "I am planning on contacting the French ambassador by next Monday to ask why 17 rounds were fired so close to our boat."

The incident was captured on camera while the BBC was interviewing Philp about the Conservative's proposals to tackle small boat crossings in the Channel.

The French Coastguard said the vessel was conducting a "routine training exercise" and that "all procedures were followed".

Footage showed 17 shots being fired in quick succession from the French naval vessel

In footage, the sound of what appeared to be 17 shots being fired in quick succession from the French vessel could be heard, and an image taken on board Philp's boat showed a naval officer firing a gun out to sea.

Matt Coker, the captain of the boat Philp and media were on, told the BBC he had never experienced a similar incident.

"In 28 years at sea I've never seen anything like this," he said.

"It's very unusual. I had no warnings on the VHF radio or saw any flags indicating what was about to happen."

Chris Philp says he has rejected France's explanation for the incident

Philp rejected the French authorities' explanation, saying: "I don't buy the line from the French that this was routine training. It felt intimidatory and like it was done to stop us following what was happening in the Channel. It felt like a warning."

The French Coastguard said the exercise was intended to "maintain high levels of operability" and that "safety measures were respected".

In a statement, it added the firing exercise "had nothing to do with a British ship in the area".

The UK government said it was in contact with the French authorities to establish the facts surrounding the incident.

phippen_a1_crash_sentencing:
Urwah Tanveer, 20, died after being hit by a car at a service station on the A1(Image: Google Maps)

A driver who careered off the A1 into a service station forecourt and killed a "much-loved" student has been jailed for four years and three months.

Fiona Phippen, 45, was driving at up to 51mph when she hit Urwah Tanveer, 20, a psychology student, as she stood next to her family’s stationary Mercedes at Foston Services near Grantham, Lincolnshire, in June 2024.

Phippen, of Church Close in Great Wilbraham, Cambridgeshire, pleaded guilty in April to causing both death and serious injury by dangerous driving.

At Lincoln Crown Court on Monday, the mum of two sobbed in the dock as the court heard how her victim had been planning her graduation ceremony before she was killed.

Fiona Phippen was jailed at Lincoln Crown Court(Image: PA)

Jurors were shown "graphic and shocking" CCTV footage of Phippen’s Nissan Qashqai striking Urwah, who died in hospital a day after the crash.

Judge Simon Hirst heard that Phippen had missed Urwah’s brother by inches and caused injuries to the chest, ribs and hand of Urwah’s 83-year-old grandmother, who was sitting inside the Mercedes.

Phippen claimed she had been distracted by another vehicle on the northbound A1 immediately before the collision, which took place in "perfect road conditions" on the afternoon of June 29, 2024.

Urwah, from London, had achieved a 2:1 at Queen Mary University of London and hoped to work in the NHS, the court heard.

Evidence presented to the court suggested Phippen was using cruise control and failed to brake in the six seconds after she left the A1, travelling at an "effectively constant" speed of between 41mph and 51mph.

Sentencing Phippen, Judge Hirst said it was accepted that a six-minute WhatsApp video call, using a mobile in a holder on the dashboard, had ended 38 seconds before the crash.

The judge told Phippen: "Exactly why this collision occurred is still unclear. I have heard from Urwah’s parents and sister. It is clear from everything I have heard and have read about her that she was much loved and will be missed for a very long time to come."

He added: "For over six minutes before the collision you were on the phone in a video call. That ended 38 seconds before the collision. It ended 32 seconds before you left the carriageway [off the A1 onto the slip road]. It is plain to me that you had insufficient awareness of what was going on around you on the A1."

Phippen was banned from driving for seven years and six weeks.

Urwah's parents and sister read victim impact statements describing their grief. Her mother, Nahail Idris, an NHS worker who was in a nearby shop at the time of the crash, held up a photograph of her "always smiling" daughter as she addressed the court.

She said: "My daughter was killed in front of my eyes. Having subsequently seen the video footage, I realise how close Phippen came to killing two of my children.

"I now exist with a constant scream within me. I will live with this trauma and the loss of my daughter for the rest of my life. My life will now always be about what Urwah never got to do."

Looking towards Phippen, the mother said: "This is my life sentence and my family’s life sentence."

Saige Miller

Graham Platner built a grassroots movement in Maine. As Maine Democrats weigh what's next now that he's exited the race, winning that support will be key.

MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:  Maine Democrats are scrambling for a new U.S. Senate nominee to take on longtime incumbent Republican Susan Collins. That is, of course, because the Democratic nominee, Graham Platner announced he was suspending his bid after he was accused of rape by a former romantic partner. Planter (ph) denies that allegation. This all leaves Maine Democrats in a race against the clock to find Platner's replacement. NPR politics reporter Saige Miller is here with the latest. Hey, Saige.SAIGE MILLER, BYLINE: Hey.KELLY: So we know Platner dropped out of the race because powerful Democrats mobilized and urged him to get out. How is he explaining his decision?MILLER: Yeah, so Platner posted an 11-minute video on social media where he was obviously emotional and even angry at the situation he found himself in. Platner said he essentially had no choice. His campaign just wasn't viable anymore.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GRAHAM PLATNER: We are going to lose our ability to fundraise. We are going to lose our ability to access voter data. We are going to lose all of the things that any campaign needs on the basic level simply to function.MILLER: Platner has survived a waterfall of scandals since he announced he was running for Senate, but the rape allegation seems to be the nail in the coffin. He added he thinks this was the political establishment's goal all along - to get him and the progressive movement Mainers want off the ballot.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PLATNER: We built a campaign. We engaged in electoral politics. We motivated people. We banded together. We did it the way that we were told we are supposed to make change, and we won. And now they are not going to let us have it, not if it's me.MILLER: Platner said suspending the campaign is not an admission of guilt. He is doing it to keep the momentum alive, to beat Collins in the general election. Platner has not officially filed the paperwork to withdraw from the race yet, though. He has until 5 p.m. on Monday to do so.KELLY: Why? What happens Monday at 5 p.m.?MILLER: Well, if he withdraws by that date, the Maine Democratic Party can get a new nominee and name on the ballot ahead of the November general election. And this is a really important race for Democrats if they want to take control of the Senate. Maine is critical to that goal. And it's undeniable that Platner generated a lot of enthusiasm in Maine. He was running on a very progressive platform of affordability, universal healthcare, getting corporate money out of politics, and he was even endorsed by Bernie Sanders. Though this week, Sanders did call on Platner to drop out. Polls showed that he had a solid chance of defeating Collins, and now the party is faced with a pretty big obstacle - who replaces Platner and can maintain that level of excitement?KELLY: Well, go to that process question. What is Maine - the Maine Democratic Party's plan to replace Graham Platner?MILLER: I mean, they're working on it. The party released a statement right before Platner announced he was withdrawing from the race that they planned to hold a nominating convention to replace him. The statement specifically mentioned working closely with Platner's supporters to select a new nominee. And I think the party knows that they have to involve those who stood behind Platner if they have a shot at taking down Collins.Of course, people have already been lining up and have strong opinions on who should replace him. At least one former state lawmaker, Troy Jackson, has launched an exploratory committee, and he's also already clenched the endorsement of Bernie Sanders' political organization Our Revolution. Still, it's going to be a very tight turnaround. A new nominee has to be selected and registered with the Maine secretary of state by July 27. That's less than three weeks away. And keep in mind, more than 150,000 voters picked Platner as the Democratic nominee, and around 600 people will pick his replacement.KELLY: NPR politics reporter Saige Miller, thank you.MILLER: Thank you.
