PLC Resources has uncorked a whole new exploration frontier at its Abbotts North gold project near Meekatharra, after a high-resolution airborne survey lit up a massive, previously unmapped structure.

The target extends from ASX-listed New Murchison Gold’s high-grade deposits straight into the heart of its own untested ground.

The company says a recent magnetic and radiometric survey has revealed a large antiform, or fold structure, running along the eastern margin of the Abbotts Greenstone Belt.

PLC says the fold was entirely absent from existing regional geological maps and represents a crustal-level feature running north-south through its tenure. The feature extends for more than 14 kilometres of strike and continues south towards New Murchison Gold’s producing ground, home to several high-grade gold discoveries.

Crucially, the survey shows the hinge of this massive fold intersects a deep-seated, east-west crustal formation – a structural geometry widely recognised as a first-order control on major gold deposits right across Western Australia’s prolific Yilgarn Craton.

PLC says the entire eastern margin of the Abbotts Greenstone Belt, where the new target sits, is completely untested by any form of systematic mineral exploration. Management believes it to be one of the most compelling undrilled greenstone targets in the Murchison region.

PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “The results of this survey genuinely open a new chapter for PLC’s Abbotts North project. We came in looking to build a target pipeline, and what the interpretation has revealed is a large, previously unmapped fold structure along the entire eastern margin of the belt - a part of the project that has never seen a single drill hole or soil sample.”

The company’s ground lies within the Abbotts Greenstone Belt, a region with a history of high-grade gold production, both past and recent.

Just to the south, New Murchison Gold has been racking up high-grade hits at its Lydia prospect and the nearby Crown Prince deposit. Crown Prince is now producing high-quality ounces from its expanding 2.2-million-tonne resource grading 3.9 grams per tonne (g/t) gold.

Earlier this year, New Murchison continued its discovery success at the Lydia prospect, returning multiple promising high-grade intercepts, including 3m at a bonanza grade of 32.9g/t gold.

PLC says the structural and geological similarities between Lydia and its own Rochefort prospect are promising.

The company recently completed a maiden five-hole, 1018m reverse circulation drilling program at Rochefort, with assay results expected in the next two weeks.

While the market waits for those results, the new survey has independently delivered what could be a company-making target on the eastern side of the belt, possibly one of the most compelling targets ever identified at Abbotts North.

The company is now planning on-ground reconnaissance, mapping and sampling to refine drill targets along the newly identified go-zone.

Although PLC set out to build a steady pipeline of targets at Abbotts North, it may have just unearthed an embarrassment of riches. Having a large-scale, untested structural corridor that already features proven gold discoveries is a rare opportunity in WA.

With assays from its first drill campaign at Rochefort just around the corner, there could be plenty of news to come from this unloved patch of the Murchison.

Security researchers have confirmed that a European politician had his phone hacked with the Pegasus spyware while serving on an investigatory committee probing abuses of the notorious surveillance tool. This has reignited fresh controversy over governments abusing spyware to collect information about their critics.

The researchers at the University of Toronto’s digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say the confirmed phone hacking of Greek journalist and former politician Stelios Kouloglou during 2022 and 2023 marks the first time that a member of the European Parliament’s PEGA committee, tasked with investigating phone spyware attacks by European governments, has been publicly identified as a victim of spyware.

Kouloglou told TechCrunch in a phone call that the deliberate compromise of his phone was “reckless.” One serving European lawmaker described the hacking of Kouloglou’s phone as a “direct attack on the rule of law,” and called on the European Commission to take concrete action by imposing strict limits on the use of spyware across the 27 member-state bloc.

While spyware attacks on lawmakers are rare, the timing and targeting of a committee investigator by way of the very spyware under his investigation suggests an intense focus on the committee’s inner workings ahead of a widely anticipated report detailing its findings. The hacks open fresh questions about how governments use spyware ostensibly needed for identifying serious crime, but then caught spying on the communications of journalists, lawmakers, and critics.

Citizen Lab’s researchers did not attribute the phone hacking to a specific country but said that the government customer used the same Pegasus-loaded email address that was used in a previous campaign that hacked into the phones of journalists across Europe. The customer’s identity is not known, but the reuse of the same attacking email address implies that the customer had NSO Group’s authorization to use its Pegasus spyware to snoop on phones across multiple countries in Europe.

A spokesperson for the European Commission did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. NSO Group also did not respond to a request for comment about the Citizen Lab report prior to publication.

In its report out Friday, Citizen Lab said Kouloglou was hacked in October 2022 and at least twice during March 2023 using an exploit that compromised a security vulnerability in Apple’s iPhone software. This vulnerability had been patched but the fix was not yet installed on Kouloglou’s phone. The exploit was a “zero-click” bug, meaning the spyware broke in and stole his data without needing any interaction on his part.

The bug abused a previously discovered flaw in Apple’s smart home software used in iPhones. It allowed the spyware to grab private data from Kouloglou’s phone without his knowledge, such as his text messages and other correspondence, location data, and photos.

The timing of the October 2022 hack coincides with intense discussions over email and text message throughout October and November 2022, ahead of the delivery of a first draft describing spyware abuses focused in Cyprus, Greece, Hungary, Poland, and Spain.

The hack also lines up at the exact time that Kouloglou was in the hospital for a pre-scheduled surgery, which may have allowed the spyware operators to listen in to ambient audio discussing his healthcare or other conversations he had with visitors at the time.

Months later on March 6 and 7, Citizen Lab said Kouloglou’s phone was hacked again by the same Pegasus operator while Kouloglou traveled from Athens to Brussels, during a period of committee hearings and months prior to the committee finalizing and adopting their written draft report.

In a call, Kouloglou told TechCrunch that he didn’t know why he was specifically targeted but that he believes it was due to his work on the European Parliament’s committee investigating Pegasus abuses.

He described anger when he learned that his phone had been hacked.

“You realize that all of your personal data [was taken] — not all the professional exchanges or messages with ministers — but also the very private things, like the happy moments and the sad moments,” he told TechCrunch.

Kouloglou said he plans to sue NSO Group, the Israeli-headquartered spyware maker. NSO remains largely banned from use in the United States following a Biden-era executive order that outlawed the government’s use of spyware that could violate people’s human rights.

Last year, the spyware maker confirmed an unnamed American investment group funneled tens of millions of dollars into the company, likely as part of an effort to rehabilitate NSO’s beleaguered brand associated with enabling human rights abuses.

Kouloglou said he was going public with his story “for democracy, human rights, and the fight against corruption.”

“Corruption concerns everybody,” he said.

Andrea Michaels called the situation "awful". (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Zoom appears to be the latest dolphin found dead on the Adelaide metropolitan coastline.

All carcasses will undergo necropsies to determine the cause of death.

Environmental authorities are investigating what caused the death of a popular Port River dolphin, the carcass of which was the latest among several to have been found on the Adelaide metropolitan coastline.

Warning: This story contains images that may be distressing to some readers.

A Department for Environment and Water spokesperson said park rangers were notified of a carcass, believed to be that of Zoom, found at Snowden Beach in the Adelaide Dolphin Sanctuary on Wednesday.

"Rangers did not detect any external injuries but the carcass was in a state of decomposition," they said in a statement.

Whale and Dolphin Conservation volunteer Barb Saberton said they have been monitoring Zoom, aged 30 to 35 years old, for a sunburn injury.

Zoom frequented various parts of Port River.  (Supplied: Barb Saberton)

"I think the greater community is going to be grieving him for sure," she said.

The latest dolphin found dead is believed to be the "stud muffin" Zoom. (Supplied: Barb Saberton)

Ms Saberton said the dolphin, identifiable from a white mark on his left side, was frequently spotted swimming near a carrier ship in the sanctuary.

"It was nice to watch him come in on that and surfing his little heart out, because we don't get the natural waves in the Port River that you do out in the ocean," she said.

The department spokesperson said two dead dolphins had been reported to have washed up at Hallett Cove on June 5 and 6 and the remains of a third found at Henley Beach on June 10.

All four carcasses have been taken to a pathology laboratory to undergo necropsies.

A dead female common dolphin washed up at Hallet Cove beach on June 6. (Supplied: Susan Belperio)

Citizen scientists Susan Belperio and Johanna Williams came across one of the dead dolphins, which they have named Naia, and showed photos to dolphin researcher and conservationist Mike Bossley.

"He looked at the photos that we took and decided, in view of his experience, she appeared emaciated," Ms Belperio said.

"It feels very confronting and extremely tragic."

Johanna Williams (left) and Susan Belperio have been documenting marine deaths since the start of the algal bloom. (ABC News)

Lisien Loan, director of conservation at the Department for Environment and Water, said the algal bloom may not have caused the dolphins' deaths.

"We think it's not directly related to the algal bloom at this time because there hasn't been any sign of the algal bloom off the metropolitan coast over the last three months," she said.

"There may well be an indirect impact from lack of food resources but that's one of the things we're investigating."

Ms Loan said the necropsy results could take months to be delivered.

The department spokesperson said marine mammal death was not an uncommon occurrence.

"The number of reported dolphin deaths in South Australia has fluctuated over the past decade, with around 40 reported on average every year," the spokesperson said.

"Causes of death include, but are not limited to, age, entanglement, boat strike and disease."

In 2021, six dolphins — Doc, Twinkle, Tallula, Hunter, Squeak and another in nearby Semaphore — died within a few months of each other after becoming emaciated.

Inside one of the world's only city-based dolphin sanctuary, the pod population has halved since becoming protected and experts fear some of their biggest challenges are ahead.

A further three dolphins — Hope, Ripple and Namor — died or disappeared in 2022 and 2023.

Last year, three-year-old dolphin calf Rocket died after a suspected boat strike.

Port River and its adjoining inlets are home to the world's only city-based dolphin sanctuary, established in 2005 to protect a pod considered rare for living in an Adelaide estuary.

positive_news_reclaiming_game:
Editor Tom Pattinson introduces the new issue of Positive News magazine, which is out now

Editor Tom Pattinson introduces the new issue of Positive News magazine, which is out now

Going to the football has been one of the rites of passage in my life. As a boy, I went with my dad and my brother to watch my beloved Luton Town. It was where we shouted, laughed, cheered and, more often than not, came home mildly disappointed.

As I got older, football became something I did with friends, a Saturday built around the game, but never just about the game. A place to talk, to share and to celebrate. Now, as a parent, I find myself doing what my father did before me, taking my own boys along and watching them learn the strange, hopeful, occasionally punishing rhythm of supporting a team.

I’ve never been someone who watches much football on TV. For me, the pull has always been the people I’m with and the chance to be together, away from work, school runs, phones, stress and all the small pressures that build over a week. Sport gives people permission to shout, sing, jump up and down, talk nonsense for a couple of hours and, on a good day, believe everything might still turn out well.

That feeling is not unique to football, or to the UK. Across the world, sport has long given people somewhere to belong and be part of something larger than themselves. But in many places, elite sport has drifted further from the people and communities that built it. Tickets have become too expensive for many families, clubs and competitions have been drawn deeper into the machinery of money, and too many stadiums still echo with the racism, sexism and homophobia that should have been left far behind.

So it is no surprise that many people are looking to grassroots clubs, community teams and local sporting groups instead, not just because they are more affordable, but because they often feel closer to what they were looking for in the first place. They are places where volunteers hold everything together, children can get near the action, newcomers can find a way in, and people can truly belong to a club.

Elite sport has drifted from the communities that built it. So it is no surprise that many are looking to grassroots clubs

In the new issue of Positive News magazine, we look at that shift through football, community and the people rebuilding sport from the ground up. We meet those using the game to support physical health, mental wellbeing and social connection, and we see how minority communities are not simply being invited in at the edges, but helping shape what sport can become.

As the World Cup continues amid some controversy in North America, it is worth remembering that football is not only about rivalries and tribalism. Like so many of the stories – from Syria to Italy to Brazil – that you will read in this issue, it is also about what happens when communities come together and build something of their own.

Again and again, the most meaningful change begins close to home – on a pitch, in a street, around a table – among people who know that community is something made together.

Cover photograph: Sam Bush

Website: Atomic Smash

How grassroots football clubs are welcoming communities once pushed to the edges of the game, Matt Haig on acceptance, and why Brazilians live so long – the Jul-Sep issue of Positive News magazine is full of uplifting stories of hope and change.
premiers_ottawa_rcmp_negotiations:
Canada's premiers are calling for more clarity from the federal government around the future of the RCMP and to start negotiations as soon as possible with those who plan on keeping the Mounties as their boots-on-the-ground police force.

According to a joint communiqué, the provincial and territorial leaders discussed what's next in their relationships with the RCMP when they gathered last week in Charlottetown.

"They highlighted policing challenges, such as staffing shortages, vacancies, rising costs and governance concerns," said the communiqué.

"The federal government must provide a clear decision on the future of RCMP contract policing and to urgently begin negotiations regarding new police service agreements for those who want them."

Ottawa commits to keeping Mounties on front lines, says fixing federal policing is priority

In one of his final moves as prime minister, Trudeau argues for bold RCMP reform

It alludes to years of uncertainty and debate about whether Ottawa should keep the RCMP in front-line policing across the country, or shift to solely focus on what's known as federal policing — which includes espionage, violent extremism and terrorism, money laundering, cybercrime and organized crime.

Earlier this year, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told CBC News the government is committed to keeping Mounties in the business of day-to-day policing, while signalling that improving the federal crimes wing is his government's priority.

Eight of the provinces, the three territories and some 150 municipalities across Canada have contracts with Ottawa to use the RCMP as their local police. The current agreements — which see the provinces and territories pay for 70 per cent of the contract and the federal government cover the rest — are set to expire in 2032.

While still six years away, multiple provinces are pushing for those talks to start soon. They say they need more details to plan ahead.

Regional support for the RCMP has wavered in parts of the country. After a heated fight, Surrey, B.C., transitioned away from the Red Serge in 2024 and stood up its own police force.

Late last year the Alberta Next Panel, aimed at finding ways the province can strengthen its autonomy, suggested Premier Danielle Smith's government continue its work in establishing an Alberta Police Service "and transition community policing services from the RCMP to the APS and municipal policing services."

In a statement this week, a spokesperson for Alberta's Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services said the province is "continuing to explore options to strengthen public safety."

"While the federal government has signalled a willingness to negotiate police service agreements beyond 2032, provinces and territories continue to seek formal certainty and an accelerated negotiation process given the long lead times required for policing, recruitment, infrastructure, budgeting and governance decisions," said the spokesperson, Sheena Campbell.

RCMP application process being shortened to 6 months after report finds dire shortage: minister

British Columbia, the largest RCMP contract policing jurisdiction in Canada, said "given the complexity of contract policing, all parties require the necessary time to plan, engage and fully participate in meaningful negotiations.

"It is critical that contract negotiations be initiated to ensure the long-term strategic response to public safety," said a spokesperson for the province's Ministry of Public Safety and Solicitor General.

Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson said he's looking for a renewed agreement "that reflects the unique realities of policing in the North."

"We support greater transparency and engagement with provinces and territories throughout the negotiations, continued federal investment to maintain strong RCMP services and measures that strengthen recruitment, retention and staffing stability in remote communities," he said in a statement to CBC News.

He said he's also looking for sustained support for complementary community safety initiatives like programs looking at prevention and wellness alongside policing.

"Ultimately, improving public safety in the North requires both effective policing and continued collaboration to address the underlying social factors that drive crime," he said.

Both the governments in Newfoundland and Labrador and New Brunswick said they are looking for negotiations to start "as soon as possible."

Staff shortages have been flagged by premiers in the past as an area of concern in their contracts. Multiple reports have concluded the RCMP's multiple mandates are straining the institution.

Earlier this year the federal auditor general found the RCMP didn't recruit enough new officers or effectively assign its members to meet its operational needs.

RCMP failed to recruit enough officers to meet operational needs: auditor general

"As a result of chronic shortages of front-line police officers, the RCMP faces a higher risk of police officer absences and burnout, which could make it more challenging for the force to prevent and investigate crime, maintain peace and order and contribute to national security," said the report.

The Mass Casualty Commission, which investigated the April 2020 massacre in Nova Scotia that killed 22 people, put out a report in 2023 calling on government to review and restructure the RCMP.

As part of its response to the tragedy, the Nova Scotia government announced this week that it's making changes to how it funds and bills for RCMP services.

The federal Public Safety Department didn't answer when negotiations will begin, but said it's been "actively engaging with jurisdictions to identify their policing needs beyond 2032."

The RCMP deferred to Public Safety when reached for comment.

pride-london-2026:
About one million people were expected to attend, organisers said

Attendees at Pride in London have told the BBC that supporting the event is "more important than ever", with thousands turning out for the annual parade.

The festival is the UK's largest Pride and one of the capital's biggest public events and this year the organisation running the event said it was expecting crowds of more than one million people.

This year's festivities come after a difficult year for the organisation which became involved in a long-running legal dispute with its former chief executive.

Pride in London said it was "overwhelmed by the support, love and commitment our community, partners, volunteers and wider stakeholders have given Pride in London this year".

Magda Szewczak says Pride is "more important than ever"

Magda Szewczak, visiting from Poland, said attending felt "more important than ever".

The 25-year-old told the BBC: "I love to see people being free to be themselves and being whoever they want to be."

Many of those attending shared the same sentiment  - that it was particularly important to show their support for Pride in London after a turbulent year for the organisation.

It has been involved in a protracted legal dispute with its former chief executive, Christopher Joell-Deshields, who was sacked following an investigation into alleged misuse of vouchers donated by a sponsor.

The 55-year-old is due to be sentenced later this month after admitting contempt of court for failing to follow a legal order to hand back company property, including access to bank accounts and internal systems.

Nicole Edmondson says she attended to "be with the community"

Nicole Edmondson, 46, who visited from Surrey with a group of friends, told BBC News: "We had concerns, but we felt it was important to come together and be with the community.

"It's a brilliant turn out and it makes you feel good."

Besa Nolan (centre) says the London Pride event makes him less worried about the wider movement

Besa Nolan, 25, travelled from Liverpool and said the size of Pride in London made him less worried about the future of the Pride movement.

"Other cities have downgraded their Prides," he said.

"Everything feels under threat, but today I haven't thought about that because look at the size of the turnout."

Final attendance figures have not been released but organisers said ahead of the event that more than a million people were expected to head into London for the celebrations.

Tens of thousands lined the parade route that made its way through central London

A spokesperson for Pride in London added: "Our priority is to always ensure the safe delivery of Pride for our LGBTQIA+ community and allies.

"Today's attendance, proves the significance and importance of Pride in the capital and we hope that everyone has a safe and happy Pride in London."

As well as the parade, Pride in London also attracts thousands of visitors to its stages around the city, including Trafalgar Square and Soho Square.

This year's main stage is headlined by singer MNEK, with performances from Beth Ditto and Meek.

The London mayor was among 35,000 people taking part in the parade

The event started shortly after midday on Saturday.

Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan - joined by singer Beverley Knight - officially opened the 35,000-strong parade, which featured 600 groups.

The parade made its way from Hyde Park Corner via Piccadilly. It is due to finish at Whitehall Place at around 18:00 BST.

Performers, including Leo Kalyan, have performed at Trafalgar Square

Although there were rumours Madonna would appear on stage at Trafalgar Square, organisers confirmed on social media this was not the case.

Pride in London posted on social media: "In response to the rumours, we can confirm that Madonna will not be appearing or performing at Pride in London.

"We have two fantastic headliners at Trafalgar Square to conclude a brilliant day of protest and celebration."

It is understood that there had been communication between organisers and Madonna but that she was never a confirmed attendee.

Andrew Depass, 60, who is visiting from Miami with his children, was one of her many fans hoping to see her.

"Madonna is the only one that spoke up for us in the 90s when people were dying from Aids. She talked about them," he said.

"That's why she's the most important music icon in my mind."

Other acts that appeared on stage at Trafalgar Square were Leo Kalyan and Bombaymami.

More than one million people were expected to attend the event on Saturday

Pride in London is one of more than 200 Pride events expected to take place in the UK this year - from smaller local events with less than 100 visitors, to city-wide celebrations with big name performers in Manchester and Brighton.

Organisers for such events have told the BBC that rising costs, coupled with a fall in corporate sponsorships, have made it a challenging few years, with some Prides postponed, cancelled or scaled-back.

prison-lawsuits-grievance-denial-investi:
By

Christie Thompson

,

Joseph Shapiro

For any problem in an incarcerated person's life — from not getting enough toilet paper to extreme physical abuse — the grievance system is the primary way to speak out. But in the vast majority of cases, those efforts go nowhere, according to an analysis of federal data by The Marshall Project and NPR.
                
                    
                    Michelle Mildenberg Lara for The Marshall Project
                    
                
                hide caption

A federal prison doctor first found the mass on Terri McGuire Mollica's uterus in 2016. According to a lawsuit, the fibroid was small, and could be removed with a simple, noninvasive surgery.

But officials at FCI Aliceville, a low-security prison for women in west Alabama, never scheduled the procedure, court and medical records show.

Mollica, then 50, started fainting during heavy periods that lasted nearly two weeks. She used five menstrual pads at a time, she said, with blood often soaking through her prison khakis. The pain was an "8 out of 10," she wrote on multiple sick call forms. In 2018, the same doctor determined the fibroid had grown to the size of a grapefruit. Her uterus swelled as though she were nearly five months pregnant.

Prison officials still did nothing.

Mollica had just one path for recourse: the prison's antiquated administrative remedy system. She would have to fill out a stack of carbon copy forms, following a list of specific rules, and submit them to the warden, then the Bureau of Prisons' regional office and, eventually, Washington, D.C. While she had just weeks to file her complaints and appeals asking for treatment, officials would likely take months to respond.

She would do all that knowing the answer was almost always no.

It has always been difficult to get help inside federal prison. But in recent years, it has become nearly impossible, according to an analysis of federal data by The Marshall Project and NPR. The rate at which the bureau granted grievances has fallen from just under 7% in 2000 to less than 2% in 2023, the last full year of data available.

Loading...

For any problem in an incarcerated person's life — from not getting enough toilet paper to being subject to extreme physical abuse — the grievance system is the primary way to speak out. But in the vast majority of cases, those efforts go nowhere. Many are rejected without consideration for the content of their complaint, for arcane reasons such as including too many pages or not filing enough copies.

What should be a gateway to help for people in federal prison, experts say, is instead a brick wall. A 1996 federal law requires prisoners to complete the internal grievance process before filing a lawsuit. If they fail to follow every requirement of that process, their case will likely be thrown out. As a result, the system blocks most people from ever taking their case to court, where a judge could order prison officials to provide relief.

The agency is aware of this drop in grant rates, a spokesperson said, and is working on "updates and additional guidance" related to filing grievances. "The program is intended to solve problems and be responsive to issues raised by inmates," Randilee Giamusso, a Bureau of Prisons spokesperson, wrote in an email, "and does not prevent inmates from pursuing litigation."

She noted that if prison officials don't reply within the established time frame, the filer can appeal to the next level without receiving a formal response, as Mollica did. Giamusso declined to comment on Mollica's experience or any individual cases.

When Mollica first tried to sue officials for neglect, a federal judge dismissed her case, ruling that she hadn't completed the grievance process. But according to court records, she tried to mail her final appeal to the bureau's office in D.C.; officials had never recorded it in the system. A decade after doctors found the fibroid, she is still waiting for surgery. Given the delays, doctors recommend a full hysterectomy, according to her medical records.

After Terri McGuire Mollica didn't get medical treatment for a fibroid while incarcerated at FCI Aliceville in Alabama, she tried to file a grievance with prison officials, but it was never granted.
                
                    
                    Rita Harper for The Marshall Project
                    
                
                hide caption

"They don't even try to fix the problem, they just look for a reason to deny it," said Mollica, who was sentenced to 17 years for defrauding two nonprofit health clinics and sending narcotics through the mail. She was released to a halfway house in Alabama in January. "I've never seen [the grievance system] help anybody."

Across 24 years of prison filings, healthcare-related requests like Mollica's were the third most common reason for someone to lodge a complaint, behind housing problems and staff-related issues. Of all medical grievances decided in 2023, fewer than 1% were granted.

The bureau's approval rate appears to be far below that of many state corrections departments, the news organizations found, though departments track such data in different ways. In California, officials granted roughly 15% of grievances and appeals in 2023, according to an analysis by The Marshall Project and NPR. In Georgia, nearly 13% of cases were "granted, partially granted or resolved," that year, according to the department. In Texas state prisons, over 4% of complaints and appeals processed that year were "resolved in inmate favor" — a very small portion, but about twice the bureau's rate.

This article was published in partnership with The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on  Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.

Federal grievances may be thrown out for being trivial, illegible or not pertaining to an issue that can be addressed through the bureau's system. And in some cases, an incarcerated person might get the help they need without having their grievance officially granted. But the data shows the current system obstructs even valid complaints.

According to bureau policy, prison staff "should be flexible" when deciding whether to reject a complaint, "keeping in mind that major purposes of this Program are to solve problems and be responsive to issues inmates raise." But in 2023, almost half of the complaints decided were rejected due to procedural issues.

Attorneys and people in prison recounted the most frustrating reasons for rejections they've seen, like writing with a pencil instead of a pen, or a woman reporting sexual abuse who was rejected for misspelling her abuser's last name. One advocate recalled a case where a Spanish-speaking prisoner filed a grievance asking for translation services, but was rejected for writing it in Spanish.

Giamusso, the bureau spokesperson, denied that these are reasons a person in prison would have their remedies rejected. "The BOP does not reject remedies solely because a submission contains too many pages, is written in pencil rather than pen, or includes a misspelled staff member's name," she wrote. "However…the Administrative Remedy form instructs inmates to write with a ballpoint pen to ensure the carbon‑copy pages remain legible throughout the review process."

Jack Donson, a former bureau official and executive director of the Federal Prison Education and Reform Alliance, said the system is getting even harder to navigate. "I've seen people rejected for too many copies, not enough copies, the rejections are all over the map," he said. "I've never seen it so dysfunctional." As understaffing across federal prisons continues, there are even fewer employees available to review complaints.

The data analyzed by The Marshall Project and NPR was published in July 2024 by the Data Liberation Project, an initiative committed to making large government databases public. The dataset contained information on nearly a million prison grievance cases filed between January 2000 and late May 2024.

The news organizations filed a records request with the Bureau of Prisons for more recent data in February 2025. The bureau has yet to provide those records.

Only a quarter of complaints in 2023 were actually denied, meaning prison officials evaluated the content of the requests and refused them based on their merits. A growing portion, 29%, were "closed" that year for other reasons. That often meant officials responded with a vague answer to prisoners' pleas that is "for informational purposes only," and not registered as a rejection or denial. According to Giamusso, that designation is used for cases that "do not require any corrective action."

Loading...

In 2024, Robert Ruff filed a grievance from a federal prison in Pennsylvania, asking for access to the recreation yard. The yard was at the top of a steep set of stairs, which were impossible for him to navigate with a walker. He wanted "to be able to get some sunshine" and watch the softball and football games. In a response to his request, the warden wrote "for informational purposes only" that Ruff still had access to indoor recreation like the chapel or arts and crafts.

Ruff worked with The Remedy Project, a nonprofit that helps people in federal prison file grievances, to appeal his case, but he was never given access to the yard. He has since been transferred to a different facility.

"If you were trying to find a case where they sided with a prisoner, it would be like finding a flea on an elephant's back," said Ruff, who has spent over 40 years in federal prison. "In the last 10 years, it feels like the remedy process transferred over so the prisoner is never right. Now, you don't get no type of justice at all."

It wasn't meant to be that way. The bureau established the grievance system in 1974, in part to stem the number of prison lawsuits ending up in federal court. There was also a growing belief among prison officials, around the time of the Attica prison uprising, that being more responsive to prisoners' concerns would reduce the likelihood of violence or rioting. In its initial version, the system had just two levels of review — the warden in each prison and the agency overall. In a four-month trial at three different federal prisons, more than a third of the complaints were granted.

Since then, the process has stretched to require four different levels of review, each with a list of procedural requirements that pose stumbling blocks for prisoners seeking help.

Corrections departments previously had to prove their grievance systems were fair and accessible if they were to serve as a gateway to the courts. But that basic requirement was scrapped under the 1996 law that required filers to complete the in-prison complaint process before filing suit. Now there is an incentive for prisons to complicate their remedy system, said Professor Margo Schlanger of the University of Michigan Law School.

"You have to cross every 't' and dot every 'i' before it counts as exhausted," she said of federal prison grievances. "It's in the interest of prison officials to come up with as many reasons as possible why the grievances are no good."

Recently passed legislation is supposed to provide another outlet for incarcerated people to pursue accountability. The Federal Prison Oversight Act, signed into law in 2024, would create an independent ombudsman to whom prisoners and their families could file complaints. Congress recently instructed the Justice Department to start planning the new office, but has yet to provide the funding needed.

Mollica filed a grievance in December 2019 over her severe pain and bleeding. "As of this date, I have not received any treatment or additional consults for this problem," she wrote, asking for an appointment with an outside specialist or surgeon within a month.

Mollica filed a grievance in December 2019, complaining of severe pain in her lower abdomen, uterus and ovaries. The highlighting and redactions were done by The Marshall Project.
                
                    
                    PACER
                    
                
                hide caption

It took the warden six months to respond, writing in June 2020 that Mollica did have an appointment scheduled with a gynecologist. But "due to security considerations, you will not be told in advance of the date, time, or location of these appointments," she wrote.

Others incarcerated at Aliceville were facing life-threatening health conditions, and made to navigate the same dead-end bureaucracy. The year Mollica was filing complaints asking for surgery, medical requests were the most common grievance filed at FCI Aliceville. None were granted. A 2020 investigation by Reason found three women who had died from alleged medical neglect at the facility, based on interviews and lawsuits.

Hazel McGary died of a blood clot in her heart in 2019, after months of asking to see a cardiologist. "The warden and the region are useless," she wrote in a letter, obtained by Reason, nine days before she died. "They send us through all of these long, drawn-out procedures. By the time [they're done] we will be home or dead."

Officials at FCI Aliceville declined to comment for this story.

Mollica appealed her filing to the regional office; officials took another six months to respond. They replied claiming surgery had not been recommended.

Mollica appealed again, this time writing to the bureau's central office in Washington D.C., via certified mail. She never received a response.

After a judge dismissed Mollica's case, attorneys for the MacArthur Justice Center were able to prove that Mollica had tried to follow every step, and that officials had failed to record her final appeal.

Without attorneys or a certified mail tracking number, Mollica may have been out of luck. In a 2021 court decision, an incarcerated man had tried to sue Bureau of Prisons officials after his cellmate stabbed him and left him blind in one eye. The court threw out his lawsuit because the bureau claimed officials never received his final appeal — which the man said he had delivered in a stamped envelope to the prison mail room. An appeals court upheld the dismissal.

In Mollica's case, the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in August 2025 that her lawsuit should not have been dismissed, almost nine years after a doctor first found the fibroid on her uterus. But she still faces long odds in court, due to a legal precedent that makes it extremely difficult to sue federal agents for abuse or neglect.

When Mollica returned to Alabama in January, "I told a friend of mine, 'I hope when I get off the plane there's an ambulance waiting to take me to the hospital,'" she said. But she remains under the control of the Bureau of Prisons until 2029. Her surgery has yet to be scheduled.

Data reporting and visuals by Ilica Mahajan and Anna Flagg of The Marshall Project, with additional graphics work by NPR's Connie Hanzhang Jin. Art direction and photo editing by NPR's Emily Bogle and Celina Fang at The Marshall Project.

Nate Koppikar wasn’t much older than me: We both came of age after the financial crisis. He often used the word consequences to describe this period, like he was contemplating a scale of justice that existed only in his head. After 2008, the scales had tipped too far. “People on the bottom end of the spectrum faced extreme consequences, where they were thrown out of their homes that they should not have bought,” he said. “And on the high end, they also made terrible decisions, but they were given get-out-of-jail-free cards, and they have gotten phenomenally richer.” When Koppikar told this story, or any of the others involving the scales, an incredulous smile would break across his face, as if to say: This is absurd and we both know it.

After graduating from the Wharton School of Business and a stint on Wall Street, Koppikar found himself working at a long-short fund on the West Coast, where he was tasked with picking undervalued stocks and shorting overvalued shares. The Bay Area was home to a small community of short sellers who spent most of their time finding holes in the stories that Wall Street wanted everyone else to believe. This meant identifying a company whose share price was due a fall, then betting that this would happen. You’d borrow shares from a broker and sell them to someone else, with a promise to return the same number of shares in the same company to the original broker by a certain date. Once their price started to fall, you would buy back the shares you owed at the lower price, return them to the broker, and pocket the difference. They were, unsurprisingly, very unpopular with their targets, and often got accused of representing capitalism’s most sordid side. Viewed from another perspective, however, they were an example of markets working to correct pricing errors.

In 2019, Koppikar founded his own short fund, Orso—the Italian word for bear—with Scott Matagrano. Koppikar and Matagrano told me more than once that they identified with the underdog. This might have surprised the average underdog, given that they were paid handsomely for investing millions of dollars. Perhaps to resolve that dissonance, they had converged upon a sort of homegrown political theory, dividing the world into “bad guys” and everyone else. The bad guys were the ones who inflated share prices and deceived their investors. Yet as the number of investigative journalists had shrunk and white-collar prosecutions had reached record lows, rooting out bad guys had become a dying art. Short sellers therefore occupied a curious position: Pretty much the only people willing to make trouble and ask awkward questions about company valuations were self-interested anti-heroes like this.

Koppikar and Matagrano soon turned their attention to the realm of private equity, which they viewed as a cancer that had metastasized in the years after the financial crisis. Koppikar called it a “Ponzi scheme.” Matagrano was similarly caustic. “You know, I’m a dyed-in-the-wool conservative,” he told me. “But at the same time, I see how much the United States has devolved into this cronyist economy. And private equity really is one of the [biggest] examples of how your average person has seen the American dream get pulled further and further away from them.” For both of them, the sheer proliferation of private equity funds rang alarm bells. Since 2008, the number had nearly doubled in the United States alone. Koppikar and Matagrano weren’t alone in thinking that these were the morbid symptoms of a market where too many people were chasing too few opportunities.

Wall Street was a place where you were more likely to be rewarded for unfounded optimism than rational pessimism. Naturally, Koppikar and Matagrano planned to capitalize on that.

They were up against a formidable adversary, and an increasingly well-connected one.

“In life you have to have a dream,” Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman told analysts on a call within days of Donald Trump’s first inauguration. Schwarzman’s dream, apparently, was to open up private equity to ordinary Americans. That was . . . odd. Private equity had never taken money from ordinary people. That was pretty much the point of it. The crash of 1929 had shown that most people needed honest, publicly available information in order to invest their money prudently, and private funds weren’t willing to hand over this information. That was why the SEC prevented them from raising capital from the general public.

Growth had become more important, it seemed, than making companies work better and selling them at a profit.

In any case, they had never seemed short of cash. Schwarzman’s industry had focused exclusively on smart money, targeting billionaires, family offices, university endowments, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and the like. These were known as “sophisticated” investors, since they hired teams of professionals to advise them on what to do with their wealth, and had experience navigating risks on their own. This very sophistication was part of what gave private equity its allure. It was a private members’ club only open to the world’s richest people, managed by Wall Street’s elite, who made that money grow like nobody else could.

And now this exclusive club wanted to expand its membership to ordinary Americans. There were two reasons that opening the gates to normal people seemed like a bad idea. First, “retail” investors, as they were known, often had no idea what they were doing. Second, they sometimes needed their money back in a hurry. This combination of naivety and necessary liquidity made them uniquely ill-suited to private equity funds, whose managers locked up money for years at a time and were notoriously selective in how they presented their returns. “You have to foresee that there will be people who have no idea of what they’re investing in, and will put a large percentage of their 401(k) into something like private equity, if it’s offered to them,” said Paul Secunda, an attorney who specializes in employee benefits law. “The PE guys get rich, but it’s not clear that middle-class participants benefit at all.”

That criticism was sharpened by the fact that private equity made a lot of money for its fund managers and much less for everyone else. A 2011 report produced by the World Economic Forum observed that the industry had been organized so that “most of the rents from these skills go to the fund managers themselves, rather than to the [investors].” Some of the industry’s most powerful investors—the Saudi royal family, say—had enough clout that they could negotiate better terms, or even come on board as “co-investors,” which meant they didn’t have to pay the fees that made the fund managers rich. Ordinary people would never have this clout. Instead, the risk was that they would become the mark that the fund managers could swindle for fees.

The Trump administration didn’t appear to see any problem with this, and in June 2020, Labor Secretary Eugene Scalia published an advisory letter announcing that Americans would soon be allowed to invest in private equity via their 401(k) accounts. It was supported by Jay Clayton, then the chair of the SEC (Clayton joined the board of Apollo, one of the world’s largest private equity funds, a few months after leaving office). This new encounter between private equity and middle-class Americans would, Scalia explained, help Americans saving for retirement gain access to investments “that often provide strong returns.” It would “level the playing field for ordinary investors.” It would also quite possibly allow fund managers to use these retirement savings as a means by which to transfer even more wealth from middle-class Americans to themselves.

This was alarming, but Koppikar was more concerned by a different question. Why did one of the richest industries on Earth need more money? The early cheerleaders for leveraged buyouts imagined they were creating value by undertaking surgery on bloated conglomerates. But many private equity firms now looked increasingly like those old conglomerates. Specialized funds had morphed into huge asset managers that did a bit of just about everything. They charged a 2 percent fee on the value of the assets they managed, which meant there was an incentive to keep growing bigger and bigger. Growth had become more important, it seemed, than making companies work better and selling them at a profit.

And to grow bigger required a constant inflow of new capital. The industry had already tapped just about every large pool of money in the world. Now it seemed to be running out of fuel. Meanwhile, many funds were having difficulty selling their assets. Managers had developed new tricks to paper over this fact: Some had started buying assets from themselves, while others were taking out loans against their portfolios in order to release cash to their investors without having to sell the actual assets at a discount. These techniques only served to disguise the troubling reality that fund managers were sitting on a bunch of wildly over-valued stuff that nobody wanted to buy. “They were just flipping [stuff] back and forth between one another,” Koppikar recalled.

Taken together, these two developments made the industry look increasingly like, well, a pyramid scheme. The focus was less about actually selling the overpriced hand lotions or herbal supplements, more on finding new housewives to recruit. Economists call this dynamic “Ponzi finance”: A rise in asset prices buoys the confidence of investors, breathless media coverage reinforces their conviction, and money flows into a market. That money is needed to support both the rise in prices and the loans that were made on the premise that the market would keep growing. But all this debt and risk-taking is very unstable. It therefore seemed quite revealing that, given the ear of government, private equity’s visionary elite could formulate no greater ambition than to get into the savings accounts of middle-class America.

At that point, most people didn’t want to imagine that a decades-long boom might be coming to an end. Certainly, the public pension funds that had invested more than one of every ten of their dollars in private equity didn’t want to think about this. But to Koppikar, witnessing these scenes was like seeing all of his doubts coalesce into a single thesis. His letter to Orso’s investors in the autumn of 2022 singled out a company that he euphemistically called “Bad Mark Co.” “The parent for BMC trades as if it is one of the greatest businesses in the history of the markets,” he wrote. “Our view is variant. We think the stock will see a significant correction in the coming months.”

The company he had singled out for his next short was Blackstone.

Koppikar rarely talked about his shorts at dinner parties or weddings. Telling somebody you were shorting their stock was a little like telling them their child was ugly. And this was Blackstone, for crying out loud. It was only possible to short the company because it was one of a handful of private equity firms that had taken the decision, in the aughts, to float themselves on the stock market. Most investment funds loved the firm. It was the most successful company in the world of alternative assets. “To many investors, advisers and finance columnists, Blackstone has the legendary Midas touch,” wrote one consultant. Going after it, Koppikar said, would be like “shorting God.”

If it goes well, the short seller might wind up looking like a genius. If it goes badly, they might end up losing their money and their credibility.

When a company’s management team discovers a short, they will often set about finding the flaws in the short seller’s thesis. If they can produce a convincing enough counternarrative, the company’s share price might go up, attracting new investors, who will push it up again. It’s a painful life lesson that a short seller can be right about a stock but wrong about how the markets will then behave; as John Maynard Keynes is once (perhaps apocryphally) supposed to have said: “Markets can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent.” A short seller may end up pushing the stock price upwards despite all of the evidence marshalled against it, and can end up suffering huge losses: There is no limit on how high a stock price can climb. This makes shorting a duel of public arguments in which the short seller is always the most exposed. If it goes well, they might wind up looking like a genius. If it goes badly, they might end up losing their money and their credibility.

Koppikar and Matagrano knew two things: They knew that Blackstone wanted to go after retail investors, and they knew that this strategy was flawed, because retail investors didn’t behave the same way as their usual customers. The question of how these two flaws would play out in practice was more difficult to answer.

In the weeks after his letter, Koppikar received a call from a contact who worked in the allocations business. “He said, ‘Listen, I got a bunch of clients that are in this BREIT. You’ve got to take a harder look at it.’” Blackstone Real Estate Investment Trust (BREIT) was a company that packaged real estate into bite-sized chunks, which Blackstone had created in 2017. Almost nobody in finance thought private REITs were a good idea (“about as appealing as a condemned apartment house beside a railroad track,” as one Forbes contributor had described them back in 2016). Shares in private REITs weren’t publicly traded, and were typically more expensive than their public equivalents, their price determined by insiders who were prone to inflating the value of properties. BREIT charged its investors an annual 1.25 percent fee on assets under management, and a 12.5 percent incentive fee if its returns exceeded 5 percent. By contrast, you could buy shares in a public REIT that would give you a broad sample of real estate, and you could sell those shares any time you wanted, all while paying a lower fee.

Even so, Blackstone seemed to think that it had something more special to offer, and by 2022, BREIT was one of the firm’s biggest success stories, at least on paper. According to Goldman Sachs, it accounted for about a fifth of the company’s annual fee revenues. It had swallowed up apartments, suburban houses, student dorms, data centers, and shopping malls. It bought the Bellagio in Las Vegas, and a seventy-six-story skyscraper designed by Frank Gehry. It bought a Florida complex for interns working at Walt Disney World. And all you needed to put money into BREIT was a net worth of at least $250,000, or a gross annual income of at least $70,000 and a net worth of at least the same. All you needed, in other words, was a decent job, a savings account, or a modest inheritance. To be clear, this wasn’t private equity, and had nothing to do with leveraged buyouts. Yet BREIT seemed like a trial run for a much bigger goal: to open the gates of giant firms like Blackstone to the middle classes.

The marrow of Koppikar and Matagrano’s thesis was this: Blackstone had created a shiny new product for people who should never have been investing with Blackstone. Now, the company was sitting on billions of dollars of their money, and at some point, it was going to get burned. Retail investors behaved more like mice than giants, scuttling between investments and playing the markets like a game. For most of them, investing was a hobby, not a full-time profession. And they sometimes needed their money back, to pay down the mortgage or cover their kid’s school fees. What would happen if they suddenly wanted to take it out of BREIT? Leafing through the prospectus for Blackstone’s mass-market product, Koppikar noticed a detail buried in its small print. BREIT only allowed its clients to redeem a certain percentage of their total assets each month. If withdrawals breached a monthly limit, and people began clamoring to take too much money out of the product, Blackstone could bring the shutters down and “gate” the trust. This wasn’t unusual: When pension funds invest in private equity, they expect to tie up their money for a number of years. But Blackstone was now dealing with a bunch of people who were used to withdrawing their money as easily as if they were at their bank.

It was during the summer of 2022 that Orso began to build up its position in Blackstone’s stock. By then, the real-estate market had slowed and people were warning of “zombie” tower blocks that were left empty after the pandemic. In San Francisco, as the pandemic receded, nearly a quarter of offices were vacant, and people openly wondered, now that the nation was working from home, whether commercial real estate had a future.

Yet Blackstone seemed impervious to these trends. On an investor call, Schwarzman suggested that was because rents for real estate across the United States had risen two to three times faster than inflation. Since most of the leases in Blackstone’s real estate portfolio were “shorter duration,” the firm could “reprice” these easily. “It’s because we own all this wonderful stuff in the right places,” he told an audience at Davos in early 2023. But this didn’t stand to reason. How could one company be insulated from the downturn in the rest of the market? Finally, in November that year, a news story confirmed what Koppikar and Matagrano had predicted. Bloomberg reported that investors in BREIT were taking their money out. The narrative was contagious: as soon as one group decided to pull their money, others would follow, and the effect would be similar to a bank run.

At a hotel in New York that December, Schwarzman took to the stage to address a conference organized by Goldman Sachs. He told the audience that recent concerns about BREIT were “baffling.” His firm had already announced that it would be limiting the money investors could withdraw, and was being hammered by redemptions. That week, Blackstone’s stock dropped by nearly 10 percent. The whole episode was already being described in the press as a cautionary tale about the perils of opening private equity to the public.

Meanwhile, Koppikar’s Wall Street peers had started to take a new interest in his ideas. The emails he was getting tended to follow one of two formats: Either people would urge him to recant, or they would say that they had been harboring similar suspicions. Institutional Investor, a prominent magazine in the private capital industry, ran a profile that presented Koppikar as an audacious gadfly who had dared to bite a racehorse. In 2022, the piece noted, Blackstone’s shares fell by more than 40 percent, more than double the decline of the S&P 500.

Koppikar and Matagrano couldn’t celebrate yet, though. Blackstone still had another card to play.

On a crisp January morning in 2024, a group of suited trustees took their seats inside a wood-paneled office in Oakland. Jagdeep Singh Bachher sat at the head of the table, wearing a silk pocket square in the same sky-blue shade as his turban. Bachher, the chief investment officer for the University of California’s pension fund, was responsible for $23.4 billion of workers’ retirement money. He spoke in a voice so smooth it almost smothered disagreement. On December 8, seven days after Blackstone prevented investors from taking their money out of BREIT, Bachher got on a call with Nadeem Meghji, the head of Blackstone’s American real estate division. “If we can be helpful,” Bachher said, “we’re here.” The call turned into a conversation that turned into an offer. Bachher pledged to invest $4 billion of workers’ savings into the floundering product. At the office in Oakland that afternoon, a hearing had been scheduled to discuss what seemed like a colossal bailout.

The atmosphere in the room was less like an investment meeting than a courtroom show on daytime TV. A group of campaigners had gathered in the visitors’ chamber. They wore yellow T-shirts printed with the logo of a plucky NGO that had spent the last six years trying to block Blackstone’s purchase of homes across California. One by one, each campaigner took a spot on the microphone to address Bachher and the board of trustees. Their speeches became angrier as the hour wore on. “Blackstone: You are a monster. Really, you are a monster,” said one campaigner. “You treat people like they’re trash,” said another, a diminutive woman whose frail appearance bore no relation to the vigor of her accusations.

To the campaigners, Bachher’s decision was close to sacrilege. He had taken the money saved by thousands of university workers, teaching staff and janitors, and invested it in a company that they regarded as one of the main causes of their hardship. California had one of the highest rates of homelessness across America, and rising rents in the state’s major cities meant 95 percent of the university’s service workers couldn’t afford a one-bed apartment near campus. “Through this partnership . . . the university is literally investing [workers’] hard-earned dollars in their own housing insecurity,” declared one union representative at the meeting.

Bachher had invited two of Blackstone’s most senior executives to speak. After the campaigners had settled down, they took to the floor. “We’re so pleased to be here, to create an opportunity for all of us to get to know one another better . . . and also to have an opportunity to clear up some of the misinformation,” said Kathleen McCarthy, the firm’s global head of real estate, addressing the investment committee. “And . . . one thing I reflect on . . . is just how I think we are such natural partners. Because similar to you, we focus intently on how we can generate high-quality results for the people and the institutions that depend on us, but do that in a way that is highly responsible and high integrity.”

It was a variation on a familiar argument, often repeated by lobbyists: The industry served hardworking teachers and firefighters by providing them with long-term retirement security. Whenever this argument was made, it tended to overlook a less palatable reality. While pension funds accounted for the majority of private equity dollars, they weren’t necessarily the most powerful or important investors, measured by the size of their individual investments. Sovereign wealth funds and family offices often had the power to extract better terms, since their single investments could be far larger. Admittedly, being the natural partner to billionaires and oil sheikhs had less of a comradely ring to it.

The stability of the institution depended less on whether it was doing a good job than on whether it had manufactured enough consent.

“It’s hard to escape the feeling that something has gone horribly wrong when giant sums of money are made by the asset management billionaires at the top of the heap, while the union members of the pension plans they are managing, and profiting from, can’t afford homes,” wrote Imogen Rose-Smith, a journalist who previously worked alongside Bachher, as a fellow in the Office of the Chief Investment Officer at the University of California. “If your pension is secure but you can’t afford a place to live because Blackstone et al. have bought up all the housing stock, are your best financial interests being served?” As the search for returns intensified, funds that invested workers’ money had started playing what Rose-Smith called the “poverty trade”: buying up essential services and wringing value from them to the detriment of middle- and working-class communities, even though members of those communities probably had money wrapped up in these same investments. Meanwhile, a few of the richest people on the planet were creaming off enormous fees from their retirement savings. Workers were getting squeezed in more than one direction.

So why did Bachher go ahead and hand over $4 billion of their money? He declined to give me an interview, so I can only speculate about his personal motivations. Still, a look at the small print suggests an agreement that worked out pretty well for his employers. In return for a $4 billion investment over six years, Blackstone offered the University of California a backstop of $1 billion of its own shares in BREIT as collateral. If Blackstone didn’t achieve its return targets, those shares would go to the university.

There were facts, and then there was narrative. Private equity enjoyed the support of countless politicians in Washington, who had been won over by a vast and well-connected infantry of lobbyists. In the words of David Swensen, an early evangelist, it was “a superior form of capitalism.” With a narrative like this, the facts didn’t stand a chance.

Blackstone bounced back. By October 2024, its stock was trading at a five-year high. The firm’s share price would rally so long as investors kept on pouring money into private equity, and so long as the wider industry’s connections allowed fund managers to shape their own destiny. The second Trump administration was a further vote of confidence. In July 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was signing an executive order allowing private equity into 401(k) plans, giving the industry precisely what it wanted.

By now, shorting private equity was a little like shorting the government. The stability of the institution depended less on whether it was doing a good job than on whether it had manufactured enough consent. So long as its supporters remained happy, the industry, much like the government, could stay powerful far longer than individuals could stay solvent. Koppikar and Matagrano had predicted that people would want their money back, and although that prediction came true, it still had no bearing on reality. Financially, the short hadn’t been a disaster, but nor had it been one of their more profitable theses (they were still shorting Blackstone’s stock in 2025). “If I had to be intellectually honest about this, I’d say that no matter how bad the news is, for private equity, nothing ever matters,” Koppikar told me.

There were, however, warning signs that the industry’s investors were getting tetchy. Between 2022 and 2024, the number of private equity deals dropped by 35 percent, and funds were sitting on a pool of unsold assets that amounted to $3.2 trillion. In early 2024, the management consultancy firm Bain issued a report that assessed the situation using panic-stricken metaphors. “The threat to returns is real,” it declared. “The word for this market is stalled.” Another phrase it used was “gasping for air.” The language was reminiscent of the crisis communications that Koppikar had witnessed in the months before the crash. In May that year, a journalist at the Financial Times discovered that private equity funds had actually taken in $1.5 trillion more from their investors in the preceding six years than they had paid back to them in returns.

Even pension fund managers seemed to be having second thoughts. In early 2024, Bachher told his fellow trustees that unless interest rates came down, the University of California’s pension fund would look to lower its exposure to private markets, at least for a period. Other pension funds and endowments were asking for their money back from previous investments before they committed to allocating more capital. Still others had decided to start shedding their stakes in private equity funds altogether, perhaps concluding that it was better to cut their losses than continue to hope. In 2024, fundraising plunged by 23 percent on the previous year, and the industry’s assets dropped in value for the first time in decades. As Koppikar wrote in a letter to his investors in the summer of 2025, “While nothing ever matters for now, empires are also lost to complacency.”

norway_royal_rape_case:
Oslo court sentences Marius Borg Hoiby, 29, after convicting him of rape, domestic violence and drug offences.

Save

Share

An Oslo district court has sentenced Marius Borg Hoiby, the stepson of Norway’s Crown Prince Haakon, to four years in prison for rape and other crimes after a seven-week trial that further tarnished the image of the royal family.

Hoiby, 29, became part of the royal family when his mother, Mette-Marit, married Haakon in 2001.

The court convicted Hoiby of two counts of rape as well as domestic violence against his former partner Nora Haukland and narcotics offences. He was acquitted on two other rape counts, with judges finding insufficient proof that the encounters were nonconsensual. One of the rapes he was convicted of took place in the basement of the crown prince’s official Skaugum residence.

While denying the rape charges, Hoiby had pleaded guilty to domestic abuse and transporting 3.5kg (7.7lb) of marijuana in 2020.

Hoiby will appeal the verdict, his lawyer Petar Sekulic told dailies VG and Aftenposten. The prosecution said it would consider appealing after digesting the full 127-page verdict.

“This is a victory for our justice system,” said prosecutor Sturla Henriksboe. “No one can get away with serious criminal acts based on who they are or who they are related to.”

The trial captivated Norway, laying bare Hoiby’s struggles with drug addiction, self-recorded footage of intimate encounters and a trove of more than 800 electronic messages submitted as evidence.

Hoiby, who has been in custody since February 1, did not attend the reading of the verdict in person, citing undisclosed medical reasons. Local media reported he followed proceedings via a secure videolink from Oslo Prison, where he remains held.

During the trial, Hoiby spoke about growing up adjacent to the throne without an official title. “I’m mostly known as my mother’s son, not anything else,” he told the court. “So I’ve had an extreme need for recognition my whole life, and that manifested itself in a lot of sex, a lot of drugs and a lot of alcohol.”

Haakon distanced the monarchy from the case, telling reporters that Hoiby is not a member of the Royal House and faces the same legal accountability as any Norwegian citizen. “He is a citizen of Norway and, as such, has the same responsibilities as everyone else,” Haakon said.

The royal household declined to comment on Monday. “The matter has been considered by the courts, and we have no comment on the outcome,” a spokesperson said.

Like other low-key Scandinavian monarchies, the Norwegian royals have had an image of ⁠a loving and relatively low-profile family, sending their children to state schools and enjoying skiing and surfing alongside members ⁠of the public.

But Hoiby’s trial, coinciding with Crown Princess Mette-Marit’s apology for contacts with late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, has hurt their popularity.

nothings-new-headphone-1-pro:
The Headphone (1) Pro is Nothing's newest pair of cans, the company announced on Monday at an evening event in New York City. The headphones resemble Nothing’s first-ever over-ear headphones that debuted last summer, though the design and fit have been refined. The key change, though, is audio quality.

Instead of a single dynamic driver producing the sound in each earcup, Nothing has outfitted the Headphone (1) Pro with three drivers for each ear. Most headphones use a single 40-mm dynamic driver, so a single speaker ends up handling the bass, mids, and treble of your tracks. That can cause some muddiness and distortion. Adding more drivers—one for each specific frequency spectrum—gives the sound more room to stretch out and sparkle.

There’s a 40-mm bass dynamic driver to handle the low end. Then there’s a precision dynamic driver to tackle the midrange sounds like vocals, pianos, and guitars. The company says this driver will render those “S” and “T” sounds with more detail. Finally, there's the treble driver for the highs. Nothing’s driver uses xMEMS technology, which relies on a silicon diaphragm that should make transients—sharp bursts like a cymbal hit or a spiky synth stab—sound clearer.

All of these drivers working together should produce richer sound that’s more detailed overall. Every headphone maker claims their gadget produces the best sound on the market, but at least Nothing has attempted some technical feats here to try to convince you.

What's neat is you can see elements of the triple-driver architecture on the sides of the headphones—Nothing has added a couple of 9H Panda glass panels so you can peep the tech inside. The rest of the headphones are largely aluminum with titanium accents.

You'll no doubt worry about cracking that glass; Nothing claims that it is “shatter- and scratch-resistant," but Philipp Von Lintel, associate principal industrial designer at Nothing, says the glass had to survive durability tests 18 times from a drop of more than 1 meter. Also, the glass construction shouldn't affect repairability much—repair technicians can heat the glass from the outside to remove it and access the internal chamber for fixes. “Even if you crack it, there's a plastic film that keeps the chamber still working,” Von Lintel tells WIRED.

The Headphone (1) Pro is slightly lighter (by 2 grams) than the Headphone (1), with a wider headband and thicker padding, though battery life isn't as long, down to 68 hours with active noise canceling turned off versus 80. It has an IP52 dust- and water-resistance rating, so keep the hood of your rain jacket raised on rainy days.

Almost every gadget maker tosses the “Pro” moniker in the product name to justify a few extra features and a price bump. Yes, the Headphone (1) Pro cost $399, a $100 bump over the standard Headphone (1), but Nothing claims it is specifically catering to not just the average consumer who wants better sound, but also recording artists and audio professionals who work in the studio.

The company is including a feature that activates a flat equalization (EQ) mode—something mix engineers and audio producers prefer when they’re working—that’s triggered by a physical button on the headphones. Nothing collaborated with Metropolis Studio, a pro recording studio, to make the EQ features. There's even a “Studio B” Dynamic Spatial Audio mode that simulates Metropolis' mixing room, and four other Custom EQ profiles, like Concert Hall or Club. And yes, there’s a 3.5-mm jack so you can plug in (or stick with hi-res wireless or USB-C).

Charlie Smith, Nothing’s chief brand officer, says people will want these headphones for their commute to work. “That's fine, but people are making music on the go and need studio-level sound wherever they are," he says.

Nothing also claims the headphones have the best active noise cancellation it’s ever shipped, thanks to the use of 10 microphones to filter out ambient sounds. (Apple's AirPods Max, for comparison, use eight.)
