As the NSW government prepares to approve an energy-from-waste facility on Wiradjuri Country, local Indigenous groups have not been properly consulted and fear its impacts on health and sacred sites.

Later this year, the New South Wales government is expected to approve a plant near Parkes that will generate energy by burning garbage trucked in from Sydney.

Consultation has been under way for seven years, but Indigenous groups have been excluded from recent rounds, adding to fears the project will affect human health, impact the environment and damage sacred sites. An earlier proposal in Western Sydney was rejected on health grounds, which precipitated the plan in the Parkes Special Activation Precinct (SAP) in the state’s Central West.

“This monstrosity they want to put there, it’s got to go,” says Frances Robinson, chair of the Peak Hill Local Aboriginal Land Council.

“My concern is health, contamination of Country that will also affect the farmers and their economy, and our bush tucker. Now they’re talking about the yellow box gum tree. That’s a medicinal tree to us. And there is supposedly a scar tree and some artefacts right there on the site.”

At a public hearing of an inquiry by the Select Committee on Proposed Energy from Waste Facilities, held in Parkes in April, Karryn Schaefer, chair of the Peak Hill Bogan River Aboriginal Advisory Committee, expressed concerns over the impact of emissions from the plant on nearby sacred sites. “Snake Rock is a culturally significant and protected site. We also have Bulgandramine Mission … where there are traditional graves and burial trees,” she said. “This site, like others, sits within the impact pathway of this proposal.”

Development of the Parkes SAP began in July 2018, and planning to include an energy-from-waste facility (EfW) began in May 2019. An international consortium called Parkes Energy Recovery (PER) was awarded a contract to develop and operate the facility in March 2025, under a land lease arrangement with Regional Growth NSW Development Corporation (RGDC).

In its submission to the parliamentary inquiry, Parkes Shire Council expressed doubts over the NSW government’s response to a 2020 report, released by NSW chief scientist and engineer Professor Hugh Durrant-Whyte, that recommended stricter safety controls and monitoring procedures for EfW proposals across the state.

“Council’s position is clear and uncompromising: if EfW facilities can operate safely, then the NSW Government must provide the evidence to prove it,” the council submitted. “If they cannot, then such facilities must not proceed, anywhere in the State.”

Shortly afterwards, the council passed a formal resolution rejecting the development of the EfW.

Asked what consultation there had been by the NSW government with her land council over the EfW, Robinson’s response was simple: “None. Not a blessed thing.”

Both Schaefer and Michael James, chair of the Parkes Aboriginal Community Working Party, echoed Robinson’s sentiments at the April public hearing.

Asked about consultation, James said: “None at all.”

Schaefer concurred: “We were not properly consulted by the proponents of this project. Free, prior and informed consent was not achieved. We are not opposed to progress, but it must not come at the cost of our existence.”

The NSW Departments of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure and of Primary Industries and Regional Development have been instrumental in the development of the precinct and the EfW.

Between 2018 and 2022, the two departments reached out to Wiradjuri community members five times. Consultation centred on determining the potential harm the precinct could have on Aboriginal objects and places through the creation of an Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Management Plan.

Since June 2022, however, there has been no consultation between the two departments and Wiradjuri community members regarding the facility or the development of the EfW within it.

“This monstrosity they want to put there, it’s got to go. My concern is health, contamination of Country that will also affect the farmers and their economy, and our bush tucker.”

This is despite promises from RGDC that the NSW government would “continue to work closely with Parkes Shire Council, stakeholders, and the community” while PER applied for its relevant planning and environmental approvals for the EfW.

As part of these approvals, the PER consortium is relying on the Aboriginal cultural heritage plan developed by the government for the site.

Ed Nicholas, the development chief executive of Tribe Infrastructure Group, the leading company in the PER consortium, says the NSW government “undertook an extensive Aboriginal heritage assessment report back in 2019, and subsequently a cultural heritage management plan. We as a tenant in their precinct are entitled to take advantage of the primary work they’ve done, and they’ve done extensive primary work.”

However, a freedom of information request revealed Heritage NSW, the government agency responsible for protecting cultural and environmental heritage, has repeatedly questioned the thoroughness of the Aboriginal cultural heritage plan and the broader consultative efforts of both the departments of planning and of regional development.

Between July 2022 and August 2023, Heritage NSW raised concerns with both departments about areas within the precinct not surveyed under the cultural heritage plan and warned that Aboriginal consultation remained inadequate, recommending further dialogue “with the identified Registered Aboriginal Parties (RAPs) for the Parkes SAP to identify, document and manage cultural heritage values”.

FOI documents showed the departments took no apparent steps to remedy these issues.

The department of planning also failed to include any Registered Aboriginal Parties in an email sent to stakeholders on January 6 this year, requesting input into the secretary’s environmental assessment requirements, a criterion intended to ensure proposals address all necessary environmental, social and economic impacts throughout approval processes for major projects.

Two weeks later, Heritage NSW again raised concerns with the department regarding a scoping report lodged by the consortium to begin the EfW’s approvals process. It stated the PER consortium’s environmental impact statement should be informed by an addendum to the cultural heritage plan, which “must include evidence of adequate and continuous consultation with Aboriginal parties”.

When questioned on the matter, Nicholas said the Aboriginal cultural heritage plan was being updated by the NSW government. However, he was unaware what changes were being made and how these responded to concerns raised by NSW Heritage.

“It’s really a matter for them to manage that. I think that’s a matter for you to discuss with heritage and planning.”

Both the departments of planning and of regional development declined to answer questions regarding their consultative efforts and Heritage NSW’s recommendations.

The department of planning also failed to respond to questions regarding a potential conflict of interest, given it has held consultative responsibilities with community members and is now the department responsible for assessing PER’s developmental and environmental applications.

PER has conducted its own consultation process including, according to Nicholas, three meetings with the Peak Hill Local Aboriginal Land Council, and one meeting with the Parkes Aboriginal Community Working Party in October 2025.

The land council was given less than a week’s notice to consult with their community for their second and final meeting with PER, in June 2025, after opposing the facility in an initial meeting.

“If they had given us 14 days’ notice, we could have got the word out to all the members of the land council to come and listen and have their say,” says Robinson.

At the April public hearing, Michael James from the Parkes Aboriginal Community Working Party raised concerns about PER’s request to meet just one day before submissions to the parliamentary inquiry closed. Consequently, he declined the meeting.

“I just thought the timing wasn’t very great to present whatever they were going to present. We were one day out from a chance to put a submission for or against the project.”

Wiradjuri people are also disappointed with the level of consultation conducted by the council regarding the EfW.

“For more than 11 years, Parkes Shire Council and Northparkes Mines employed a Parkes Shire Aboriginal Project Officer to represent and work with the Aboriginal community of Parkes and Peak Hill,” Jada Read, a Wiradjuri woman from Upper Bogan River Country, wrote in her submission to the parliamentary inquiry. “She was involved in the SAP consultations, yet she was never informed that an incinerator project was being proposed meaning she could not take this information back to our people for discussion or consent.”

Parkes Shire Council first learnt of the potential inclusion of an EfW within the Parkes SAP in May 2019, under former mayor Ken Keith. Keith declined to comment on consultation conducted with Wiradjuri community members throughout his mayorship.

Current mayor Neil Westcott said the council’s capacity to consult with the community regarding the EfW had been limited by its having been left in the dark by the NSW government.

“This is where the disappointment comes with the state government,” he says. “It’s the state government that should have been out here sitting down with our First Nations people. We simply don’t have information. I’ve had very little to share. The ministers would say otherwise.”

The EfW is in the final stages of its developmental and environmental assessments.

The Parkes Energy Recovery consortium is expected to exhibit findings from the assessment to the public in August or October.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s controversial housing board nominee — who has dismissed local opposition to development as “wealthy homeowner cartels” — was easily confirmed by the City Council Thursday.

John Mangin, the city Planning Department’s housing director and a key architect of recent citywide zoning changes, was tapped to chair the Board of Standards and Appeals by the City Council in an overwhelming 40-6-4 vote.

The five-member independent BSA has the authority to grant zoning exceptions and can also override council objections to some affordable-housing projects — after recent changes to the city charter that voters OK’d.

Mangin was instrumental in writing those controversial charter changes that created the shortcut to bypass council review.

The council had viciously fought Mangin’s revisions in 2025, urging the Board of Elections to keep the charter changes off the ballot. After that effort failed, they rallied publicly against the plan and called on city residents to vote it down.

“I don’t see how we go from a campaign against those proposals to put one of the principal architects in charge of the BSA,” said Council Member Frank Morano (R-Staten Island), one of the few who voted against Mangin’s confirmation.

“We told New Yorkers that local input matters,” he added at the council’s stated meeting.

The other “no” votes came from council members Joann Ariola (R-Queens), David Carr (R-Staten Island/Brooklyn), Vickie Paladino (R-Queens), Inna Vernikov (R-Brooklyn) and Phil Wong (D-Queens), while Chris Banks (D-Brooklyn), Eric Dinowitz (D-Bronx), Linda Lee (D-Queens) and Christopher Marte (D-Manhattan) abstained from the vote.

The change of heart from the council came after Mangin convinced members to back him during one-on-one meetings, according to Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan).

“We had concerns from a good number of members in the beginning,” Menin said Thursday after announcing she would vote in favor of his confirmation.

“He really assured me that he definitely valued community input.”

Mangin has also criticized the community benefit agreements that council members often negotiate with developers for local givebacks such as parks, school seats and jobs, arguing they are too cumbersome and make housing more expensive.

Council members at his Sept. 1 confirmation hearing questioned Mangin about his past positions they said favored steamrolling neighborhood concerns and stripping the council of its say.

Council Member Nantasha Williams specifically accused him of helping to “build a system that lets certain affordable housing projects move faster with less Council control” — and portraying homeowners as “part of an exclusionary problem.”

Still, Williams voted to confirm Mangin Thursday.

“One of the things that he was very clear about is the context in which he wrote those previous writings,” Williams explained. “He was talking about a completely different community, not New York City.”

At the hearing, Mangin said he had been referring to opposition to housing development in suburban communities.

Banks, chair of the council’s Public Housing Committee, pressed Mangin over his past “homeowner cartels” comment.

In a 2014 academic paper, Mangin slammed municipal zoning dominated by affluent homeowners as “homeowner cartels” — keeping housing scarce and reinforcing racial segregation.

“Normal folks would take that offensively, especially when they advocate for their community,” Banks told Mangin at the hearing.

More than a dozen members had expressed reservations about Mangin in a closed Democratic conference last month, according to a report in The Post Millennial.

Mangin still has to be sworn in before he takes over as chair of BSA.

The incident occurred Monday morning out front of lower Manhattan's 26 Federal Plaza, where a federal immigration court and several government agencies, including the FBI's New York field office and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are located.

Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

NYC school kids will be pried from their screens this school year.

A new sweeping policy — said to be the strictest in the nation — will prevent local public school kids in elementary and middle school from using AI or spending excessive time on screens during the school day.

“We’re putting guardrails in place to protect the critical human connection, curiosity, and creativity that helps children grow,” Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said in a statement.

The new rules, which will go into effect this month, prevent kids in preschool through 8th grade from using any sort of generative AI, while high schoolers will only be able to use AI in limited supervised contexts. The policy also firms up guardrails for teachers: no AI for grading, monitoring behavior, or writing special education plans.

Parents, teachers, and students themselves should be cheering. This policy is an encouraging (albeit overdue) step towards freeing childhood from the grips of Big Tech.

Districts across the country have for years embraced laptops, tablets, and gadgets to help “prepare kids for a digital age.”

However, little did they know, what they were really doing is introducing distractions into the classroom that made kids even less prepared for the real world.

At my own elementary and middle school in the early 2000s, educators thought they were doing the best thing by digitizing our black board with “Smart Boards” that upload notes online and arming every 5th grader with a MacBook.

But all that did was unleash cyberbullying, teach us to pretend to pay attention in class while we were scrolling the internet, and condition us for a life lived behind screens — precisely during the school hours when kids are supposed to be learning, socializing, and living in the real world with one another.

In 2026 it has become clear, children need to learn to think for themselves before they get in the habit of outsourcing to a computer.

School districts who were sold over the past several decades on the idea of being “tech-forward” are realizing that was a massive mistake.

Massive pluralities of students with device access from across the world report being frequently distracted during lessons. Reading comprehension is measurably better when text is encountered on a paper. Plus, the weakest students improve the most when devices are removed from the classroom, according to researchers.

The fact that companies were eager to give devices to schools for free should have been a warning of their ulterior motive: hardwiring them to become lifelong customers.

Already, AI companies are courting schools making promises about how their technology will augment education. Google is pushing to integrate Gemini AI into platforms schools already use, and OpenAI has been partnering with schools across the country.

But it seems like New York City has already learned its lesson, and it won’t be falling for the techno-utopianism again.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “We do not see it that way.”

His approach is correct. Yes, AI seems destined to become a larger and larger part of our lives, both personally and professionally. But we don’t need to surrender our children to that inevitability.

What kids deserve — and need — is a childhood protected from the influence of Big Tech, where they can learn to formulate their own ideas, solve their own problems, and interact with the world without a virtual intermediary.

A speeding hit-and-run driver killed a 28-year-old nurse walking home from working the overnight shift at a  nearby Brooklyn hospital on Saturday, according to officials and video of the crash.

Jiayi Zheng — still wearing her forest green scrubs — was walking along the crosswalk at 55th Street and Third Avenue when the operator of a black Cadillac sedan drove through a red light and barreled into her around 7:30 a.m. in Sunset Park, disturbing footage shows.

Zheng was sent flying in the air before landing on the median, just a block away from where she worked at NYU Langone-Brooklyn Hospital as a medical- surgical unit nurse.

Medics rushed her to the same hospital, but she succumbed to her head and neck injuries.

The heartless driver — who police sources said had Pennsylvania plates — never stopped.

“I heard the bang. Her bag was over here, and they left her there,” witness Antonio Perez told News 12 Brooklyn.

“The car just kept on, it never stopped for nothing at all.”

The deadly crash unfolded on a perilous roadway, according to Sen. Andrew Gounardes, who represents the neighborhood.

A Department of Transportation redesign plan for the dangerous stretch of roadway was presented in 2023 but never went into effect.

“While the investigation proceeds, I am once again calling on @NYC_DOT to work with the community to make 3rd Ave safer,” Gounardes wrote on X. “Just over a year age we lost two elderly neighbors to a similar crash, and 3rd Ave remains one of the most dangerous corridors in Brooklyn. Enough is enough.”

The tragedy unfolded just one block away from where nurse Clara Kang, 31, was killed by a motorcyclist when she was heading home on a bike from working at the same hospital in 2020.

Zheng is the ninth person killed by a hit-and-run driver in the last two weeks across the Big Apple — and 11th killed while walking or biking the two-mile stretch of Third Avenue that runs under the Brooklyn Queens Expressway since 2014, according to advocacy group Transportation Alternatives.

“New York City streets should be the envy of the world, but we are the envy of no one today,” Ben Furnas, their executive director, said in a statement.

Zheng’s colleagues remembered her as a “loving nurse and hard worker” in the medical-surgical unit, News 12 reported.

“We are deeply saddened by the passing of Jiayi Zheng, a nurse at NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn,” a spokesperson for the hospital said in a statement to The Post.

“Our nurses play an essential role in caring for others with compassion and dedication, and this loss is being felt across our entire community.”

The driver has yet to be caught as of Sunday afternoon.

Harrowing NYPD body camera footage released Friday evening revealed the final moments before cops fatally shot a crazed knife-wielding woman in Times Square last month.

The footage captures police pleading with Pamela Cisneros — a mentally disturbed mom of three — to drop two knives at 42nd Street and 7th Avenue shortly after her unhinged stabbing rampage where she randomly attacked two people on Aug. 31.

Cisneros, of Queens, had pulled two knives out of a red Target bag and first stabbed Tak Kam, 68, in the abdomen as he exited the subway on West 41st Street and was waiting to cross the street, police said.

She then continued up to 42nd Street and plunged a knife into Bank of America exec Erin Piacenti, 32, killing her just after she returned from maternity leave.

Officers Ryan Brito and Francis Gagliano first encountered Cisneros, 49, and begged her to put the knife down and breathe, the footage showed.

“Put the knife down,” Brito told Cisneros as she held two kitchen knives in front of her chest.

“Come and get me,” Cisneros said, to which Gagliano replied, “I don’t want to get you.”

“I’m tired of this world already,” Cisneros said. “Tired of this s–t.”

“I get it, I understand … I understand, but why? What’s going on?” Brito said. The two cops kept telling Cisneros to calm down and breathe, with Brito trying to appeal to Cisneros’ emotions.

“I get it. The world is hard. Especially New York City. I know New York City is hard. Trust me, we all suffer,” Brito told her.

“You believe in God?” he asked, to which Cisneros replied: “No. Not anymore.”

“You’re going to have to kill me. Yes, you are,” she told the cops. “Either that, or I’m going to kill all of you.”

“Listen, I know you’re going through a lot, but it’s not worth it,” Brito pleaded with her. “It’s not worth it. I promise you.”

More officers rushed to the scene and repeatedly asked Cisneros to drop the knives.

“I’m not dropping anything,” Cisneros vowed.

Cisneros began waving the two knives in a circle to her side — sparking cops to deploy a host of tasers at her.

Seemingly unfazed by the tasers, she began to charge toward the cops while screaming.

Officers Joseph O’Connor and Steven Darcy then fired off three rounds at Cisneros, causing her to collapse forward onto the sidewalk.

The knife-wielding maniac was rushed to a local hospital, where was pronounced dead.

Cisneros had a documented mental health history with police, including a suicide attempt.

One of New York’s Finest was promoted to sergeant Monday — nearly 25 years after his NYPD detective father and FDNY firefighter uncle lost their lives on Sept. 11, 2001.

Joseph Vigiano, Jr., 33, followed in the footsteps of his father, highly decorated Emergency Service Unit Det. Joseph Vigiano, Sr., who was among the first to rush into the World Trade Center complex when terror struck — but never made it out.

“[My dad] was brave. There’s countless stories of his heroism,” Vigiano Jr. said, as his 4-year-old son, Joey — who hopes to be a police helicopter pilot one day — clung to his side.

“My dad loved this job, and I’ve never heard anyone say that he didn’t like the work and doing the type of work that he did,” he said. “And I found that I also enjoy the career as well. It’s a great, fulfilling, rewarding career, and I work with great people.”

Vigiano Jr., most recently assigned to ESU Truck 7, wore his dad’s shield number 4511 ever since he became a detective himself.

“After an unthinkable loss, the Vigiano family chose service again and again,” Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at the 1 Police Plaza ceremony, where Vigiano was among 100 members who rose to the rank of sergeant.

“They knew its cost more intimately than almost any family could, and still they continued to answer the call.”

The elder Vigiano survived two on-duty shootings during his time on the job — earning the American Legion Police Post No. 460 Medal for Valor, according to the Detectives’ Endowment Association.

The newly minted sergeant also remembered his dad as a family man with a sense of humor.

“I remember going to the Boy Scouts with him, sporting events, camping trips,” Vigiano said. “He liked to play jokes, and he was a member of our community. He was a volunteer firefighter.”

Vigiano is also following in the footsteps of his uncle, John T. Vigiano II, of FDNY Ladder 132, who lost his life in the South Tower.

“I remember going over to their house for picnics with my family and having a good childhood,” he said.

He said both men, who gave their lives to save others, would be “proud” of his achievement.

Vigiano also has blue blood on the other side of his family — his mother worked in Brooklyn’s 75th Precinct.

“Holidays, barbecues, birthdays, we spent with them, and I wanted to be part of that camaraderie,” he said.

Vigiano will now attend sergeant school at the NYPD academy before being assigned to a command. He said it’s “bittersweet” to leave his Truck 7 family.

His wife Jenny, who also stood by his side, said it’s “such an honor” to see her husband recognized for “doing what he loves the most.”

“He’s like the hardest worker I know, and just puts everything he has into this job,” Jenny said.
nz_poll_budget_2025:
Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins both dipped in the poll's preferred PM ratings while Winston Peters and Chlöe Swarbrick jumped. Photo / Mark Mitchell

The Government’s Budget had little impact on voter sentiment, according to a poll which has returned a similar result compared with its previous survey.

However, the latest Taxpayers’ Union Curia poll does point to dips in popularity for Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins.

Minor party leaders saw better returns,
         including Winston Peters who is six percentage points shy of Luxon.

The poll, which surveyed 1000 people between June 4-8, found Labour had the highest level of support with 32.2%, a slight increase of 0.3 points from the pollster’s last survey in May.

The poll has a margin of error of 3.1%.

National had registered a 0.1 point increase to 30.1%. The Green Party had edged New Zealand First as the party with the third-highest support at 11.5%, an increase of 1.8 points on the last poll.

NZ First had dipped 0.3 points to register at 11.4%. Act had jumped 1.3 points to 7.8% and Te Pāti Māori dropped 1 point to 3.1%, lower than Opportunity which was on 3.2%, up 0.4 points.

The polling was done days after the Government’s Budget, released on May 28.

Regarding seats in the House, the poll results would only cause changes of  one to two seats.

It would deliver the same configuration as the May poll; 62 for National, Act and NZ First while Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori had 58.

Both Luxon and Hipkins took a hit to their preferred Prime Minister ratings. The National leader dropped 2.7 points to 18.8% while the Labour leader dropped 1.9 points to 17.1%.

That has seemed to be hoovered up by the minor party leaders. Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick had taken the lion’s share, increasing 2.7 points to 8.1%. Act leader David Seymour jumped 2.4 points to 6.3%.

Both trailed Peters on 12.8%, an increase of 1.2 points on the last poll.

That put Peters just 6 points shy of Luxon, the closest the two have been in this poll since June last year.

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

The Obama Presidential Center’s unrelenting marketing campaign and weekslong soft opening have inspired an avalanche of opinions and emotions. For me, one feature rises above all: the new Obama Presidential Center branch of the Chicago Public Library. The 5,000-square-foot space in the center’s plaza is free and accessible to all.

Unlike its peers, the Obama Presidential Center will not house the thousands of artifacts and documents that recorded his saga.

A National Archives and Records Administration-run research facility is not part of the Obama center’s campus, WBEZ Chicago reports. “So technically, it’s not a library. All the material will instead be stored remotely but available to researchers online.”

Instead, the public library will be the first to be installed in a presidential center, with a general collection of 16,000 books.

Books fed Obama’s life.

“When I was young, I used to love libraries, love reading,” Obama told a group of students during a 2015 visit to the Anacostia Library in Washington, D.C.

In his 30s, as he launched his political career, Obama published a well-received memoir. “Dreams From My Father” told the story of his search for meaning as a biracial Black man in America.

Obama touted his favorite reads throughout his presidency. It is said that a stack of books was a mainstay on his bedside table in the White House.

At the Obama public library, I was greeted by gleaming wood shelves and stacks of colorful tomes, and shimmering light streaming through its floor-to-ceiling windows. On one wall is a 70-foot-long mural depicting storytelling and community life on Chicago’s South Side — “Reading Circles/Weaving Dreams/Seeding Futures” by artist Aliza Nisenbaum.

The President’s Reading Room offers up to another 3,000 books personally selected by Obama and his wife, Michelle. There are plans to eventually scale up to 12,000 books.

On one shelf sits an old-fashioned, working record player. On another are LPs by musical artists Prince and Stevie Wonder, Obama favorites.

In a reading garden adjacent to the library is “Book Bird,” one of the final works of the late Richard Hunt, the internationally acclaimed, Chicago-born sculptor.

It “will depict a bird taking flight from a book to illuminate how reading and learning allows readers to enter new places and fly free,” according to the center’s website.

Hunt’s mother, Etoria Inez Henderson Hunt, was one of Chicago’s first Black public librarians.

The reading room is “probably the most serene space in the entire OPC complex,” Tribune architecture critic Edward Keegan writes. “It’s programmatically reminiscent of the Toni Morrison Reading Room in Lorain, Ohio — a space conceived by the writer shortly after she became the first Black woman to win the Nobel Prize in 1993.”

Serenity is a priceless gift. On my visit, I paused to breathe in the learning, history and the healing power of words. I didn’t want to leave the place.

I harked back to my childhood, when every Saturday morning, my mother would march me to the Hall library branch in Bronzeville on Chicago’s South Side.

Walk in with a high stack of books, then walk out with a new set of fresh, exciting choices. Go home and read. And read.

In high school, I worked part time as a page at the South Shore branch, where the nerdy but wise librarians taught me to catalogue and cherish their beloved books.

Like me, the children and families in the neighborhood surrounding the Obama center face social and economic inequities.

At this warm library, “they can” — as Obama would exhort. They can drink in the literature selected by America’s first Black president. Here, they can learn that a Black child can grow to a president — and will again. They can turn pages full of dreamy tales, intellect and growth. Pages that teach us all to imagine, learn, teach and build. Books are an essential ladder to the future.

Books represent truth, facts, analysis, all values that should be treasured and embraced but are now under assault in some quarters. We are in a time when libraries, museum exhibits, public media and more have been banned, censored and defunded.

This library will be a gift to the community, where we can seek credibility and substance. A literary sanctuary.

After the Obamas and the Bidens and the Bushes and the Clintons and the Trumps have faded away, books will remain.

That little library at the Obama center and all it represents put a powerful punctuation mark on all that we need to know.

Former President Barack Obama excoriated President Trump’s shocking ban of three media outlets from White House access — but glossed over his own history of trying to block Fox News from covering him.

Last Friday, Trump ignited a First Amendment firestorm by announcing a ban on CNN, Politico, and MS Now from accessing the White House to cover his administration, citing their “negative” coverage of him, a move that Obama panned.

“My imagination could not foresee some of the stuff that is going on right now,” Obama said during a discussion at Colgate University. “I’m trying to think what would have happened if I had said, you know what, Fox News, you’re out of here! It’s unimaginable!”

Former President Barack Obama on President Trump's White House press ban: "I’m trying to think what would have happened if I had said, you know what, Fox News, you’re out of here! It’s unimaginable!" pic.twitter.com/R1pmoVasEz

“If you have a certain cohort, let’s call it 30 to 35% of the country right now, which thinks that’s okay, what that means is that we have not developed the kind of understanding of what democracy requires, and we’ve got to shore that back up.”

However, the Obama administration had attempted to curtail Fox News’ press access — albeit at a smaller scale than Trump’s controversial ban on CNN, Politico, and MS Now.

In 2009, his team attempted to block Fox News’ pool reporters from interviewing his “executive-pay czar,” Kenneth Feinberg, while giving other outlets in the pool access. Obama and his administration openly questioned Fox News’ legitimacy as a news organization.

“We see Fox right now as the source and the outlet for Republican Party talking points,” then-White House Communications director Anita Dunn argued at the time.

“And it’s fine if that’s, you know, how they want to build their business model,” Dunn said. “But we don’t think we need to treat them as though they are a news organization the way other news organizations here are treated.”

Obama appeared to back the effort to cut Fox News out at the time, telling NBC News, “If media is operating basically as a talk radio format, that’s one thing. But it’s not something I’m losing a lot of sleep over.”

The top TV networks at the time, including CNN, ABC, CBS and NBC, protested the White House’s move, and ultimately the Obama administration backed down.

The Obama administration also faced criticism for secretly getting phone records of dozens of Associated Press phone lines, as well as those of other outlets.

Under former Attorney General Eric Holder, the administration slapped subpoenas and engaged in other aggressive tactics against the press during investigations into leaks. However, after backlash, officials carried out a comprehensive review and later made reforms, including new rules to protect reporters.

Obama has spoken out against Trump’s tough tactics against the press in the past. Last year, for example, he blasted Trump’s meddling in the White House press pool — the rotating group of reporters who get greater access to the president.

The Biden administration also repeatedly cut the New York Post out of access to various events and targeted other conservative outlets at times as well.

Trump’s ban on the three media outlets from getting access to White House grounds, a list he has floated the possibility of expanding, drew fierce backlash, including from some conservative scholars.

While the First Amendment doesn’t specifically mention reporters getting access to the White House, legal precedent in cases like Sherrill v. Knight has generally frowned upon government actions against press access that are the result of viewpoint discrimination.

“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably,” Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, who is president of the White House Correspondents Association, said in a statement.

Many adults who are obese have "indistinguishable" cholesterol and blood pressure levels compared to those with a healthy weight, according to a new study.

In the past, obese adults were more likely to have increased blood pressure and higher levels of unhealthy cholesterol.

But a study found differences in unhealthy cholesterol levels and blood pressure between older adults have "narrowed or disappeared" among those aged 40 and over.

The study, published in The Lancet, saw researchers examine data on almost one million adults aged 20 to 79 from England, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Finland and the USA.

They looked at data on blood pressure, cholesterol levels and body mass index (BMI) scores taken from 110 health surveys conducted from 1990 to 2024.

Experts say the findings are largely due to use of cholesterol-busting medications, such as statins, and drugs to lower blood pressure - both of which which are more commonly used among people who are obese.

They said the findings are important to "give a picture of the cardiovascular health" of people likely to be prescribed weight loss medications, which have rapidly increased in popularity.

Professor Majid Ezzati, from the School of Public Health at Imperial College London, said: "Our study suggests that, in high-income countries, taking medication to lower blood pressure and cholesterol has helped middle-age and older adults lower their cardiovascular risk to levels that are similar to people with normal BMI.

"At a time that weight-loss medications are becoming more widely used, our results give a picture of the cardiovascular health of people likely to be prescribed them, which allows the healthcare system to understand how blood pressure and cholesterol treatments benefit the population alongside weight-loss medications."

They also examined information on the use of cholesterol-busting drugs and blood pressure treatment - known as antihypertensives.

The team found unhealthy cholesterol levels and blood pressure "declined over time", especially among those age 40 and over.

The declines were larger among people with obesity "leading to a convergence of these risk factors between obesity and normal BMI in people older than 40 years."

Author Yse d'Ailhaud de Brisis, also from Imperial College London, said: "While good news for older adults with obesity, our results suggest that cardiovascular health risks remain higher for adults under 40 than for their counterparts with a normal BMI.

"Early lifestyle interventions, screening and, when appropriate, medication in this younger group should be considered to prevent long-term cardiovascular complications linked to obesity."

okanagan-sockeye-drought:
Warm rivers and streams are becoming a growing concern for salmon in B.C.’s Interior with another low sockeye return anticipated in Okanagan waters this fall.

According to the Syilx Okanagan Nation Alliance, the number of adult sockeye salmon returning to spawn is expected to be low for the second year in a row because of warm water and low stream levels.

It says current estimates suggest between 32,300 and 96,900 Okanagan sockeye will be counted at Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River — the largest river in the Pacific Northwest — which flows through B.C., Washington state and Oregon.

Of those, only about 4,800 to 14,500 are expected to reach spawning areas above Osoyoos Lake.

“For comparison, the spawning habitats have the capacity to support approximately 180,700 to 205,500 spawning sockeye,” the alliance said in a statement.

More stories from the B.C. Interior

To reach Okanagan waters, the salmon travel more than 1,000 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean. They swim upstream against the current of the Columbia River, passing through nine hydroelectric dams before reaching Syilx territory.

Last year, the alliance said, the vast majority of the run stayed in the Columbia River seeking refuge in cooler water.

Given the low projected return this time around, there will be no economic or recreational sockeye fishing this year. Members may still harvest fish for personal needs but the alliance is asking people to take only what they need to help conserve future returns.

Sockeye salmon return to B.C.’s Okanagan Lake

The Syilx Okanagan Nation Alliance is made up of eight First Nations whose territory spans from north of Revelstoke into Washington state.

According to the ONA website, salmon — or ntytyix — are sacred to the Syilx people.

In May this year, the Nation declared a state of watershed emergency because of drought conditions, stating that there wasn’t enough water in the creeks that made it harder for fish to swim.

New research from the University of British Columbia suggests increasingly warming rivers in the province’s Interior may be putting young salmon at greater risk than previously understood.

Two studies from UBC’s Pacific Salmon Ecology and Conservation Lab looked at juvenile Chinook salmon from the Nicola River and found that young fish had more trouble coping with heat when they were swimming, rather than resting in place.

Scott Hinch, a professor in UBC’s faculty of forestry and environmental stewardship, says most studies test fish at rest but young salmon in the wild are constantly moving to feed and avoid predators.

As fish struggle to swim in low streams, Syilx Okanagan Nation declares watershed emergency

“In the Interior ... the streams are really warm,” he said. “It’s not surprising that they're more adapted to dealing with warm conditions than the population along the coast.”

But he says researchers found 20 C was an important threshold for the Interior Chinook they studied. Fish acclimatized to warm water could cope around that level but above it their ability declined. Some fish even died after being forced to swim in water at 24 C.

“We're seeing streams in the interior right now that are getting up to 24 C quite, quite commonly and that's going to become more of a reality moving forward,” the researcher said.

Salmon Warriors restore spawning grounds as sockeye return to Okanagan

Warm water has already affected salmon migrations in B.C.

In July 2021, the B.C. Wildlife Federation reported that the Okanagan River reached more than 23 C, causing sockeye salmon to halt their migration.

In 2016, warm temperatures were blamed for the lowest number of returning sockeye in B.C.'s Fraser River on record, and two years later, officials warned that the river was so warm that migrating sockeye salmon might die on their journey.

“Salmon prefer to be in a particular temperature of water ... that might be between 15-17 C,” Hinch said. “If fish can't experience that … they'll go looking for it.”

Logging near streams in B.C. Interior is warming water and threatening coho salmon: study

Hinch says protecting trees along streams can help keep waterways cooler, creating areas where salmon can find relief during heat.

According to a 2023 study, decades of logging activities near rivers in the Interior have driven up temperatures of salmon habitat.

Hinch says it’s absolutely necessary that riparian trees are protected.

“They make a huge difference,” he said. “Temperatures can rise really rapidly in those streams when they are not there.”

American musician Oliver Tree, 32, is reportedly among six people who have died in a helicopter crash in Brazil.

Two helicopters collided over Rio de Janeiro on Sunday morning, crashing in the city's western zone and killing all six people on board, the Associated Press confirmed.

Tree, best known for his viral hits When I'm Down and Life Goes On, was in Brazil on a world tour.

He was scheduled to tour Australia in October with performances in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide.

Police said the alternative singer and online personality was listed on manifests handed to aviation authorities, alongside Gaspar Prim Díaz, also known as Argentine YouTuber Gaspi; independent filmmaker Lucas Vignale; Brazilian DJ and producer Lucas Brito Chaves; and helicopter pilots Alexandre Souza and Charles Marsillac.

Rio de Janeiro’s Military Fire Department at the site of the crash. (Supplied: Corpo de Bombeiros do Rio de Janeiro)

One of the helicopters was carrying five passengers and the other only the pilot.

Rio de Janeiro's Military Fire Department said one of the helicopters plummeted into the yard of a car dealership, setting ablaze at least 20 electric vehicles.

There were no survivors.

Police said an investigation was underway to determine the cause of the collision and officers had not been able to formally identify the bodies of the victims.

The singer, producer and content creator has more than 11 million monthly listeners on Spotify. (Supplied: Alien Boy Records)

With his wild fashion and distinctive hairstyle, Oliver Tree was known for blending satire, performance art and pop music.

His internet-savvy, meme-friendly music and persona often incorporated comedy and stunts into his marketing, music videos and content creation.

He was born Oliver Tree Nickell in Santa Cruz, California, on June 29, 1993, and took an interest in music from a young age.

In 2010, he began self-releasing music under the pseudonym Tree and in 2013, released his debut EP, Demons.

He signed to Atlantic Records in 2017 shortly after When I'm Down, a collaboration with producer Whethan, went viral.

He officially debuted as Oliver Tree with the single Welcome To LA, sporting his trademark bowl cut, purple-pink windbreaker and sunglasses.

His debut album Ugly Is Beautiful followed in 2020, and the same year he broke the Guinness World Record for the largest kick scooter standing at 4.16 metres tall and 3.13m long.

Tree's single Life Goes On from the Shorter, Thicker & Uglier deluxe album became one of his most popular tracks with over 700 million plays on Spotify.

He followed with 2022 album Cowboy Tears featuring another signature song, Miss You, and 2023's Alone In A Crowd.

Tree released his fourth album Love You Madly, Hate You Badly in April this year. It was his first via his own imprint Alien Boy Records and prompted a world tour scheduled to feature 70 shows across 30 countries, including Australia in October.

Oliver Tree performing at Laneway Festival, in 2020. (triple j: Russell Privett)

Tree's first Australian visit was as part of the 2020 Laneway Festival line-up.

He returned for festival performances at Splendour In The Grass (2022), Yours & Owls (2023) and, most recently Tasmania's Party In The Paddock (2025).

He performed in São Paulo, Brazil on June 6, and on Saturday shared a video on his Instagram playing football in a Brazilian neighbourhood.

It’s been a year since federal immigration authorities detained 76 employees at a meatpacking plant in Nebraska’s second-largest worksite immigration raid.

But the effects are still being felt.

South Omaha’s business district has not fully recovered from the negative economic effects of the raid on the Glenn Valley Foods meatpacking company, city officials and community leaders said at a news conference Tuesday.

Following the raid last June, federal authorities had touted the operation as uncovering “massive identity theft,” accusing the immigrant workers of using stolen Social Security numbers to obtain employment.

Yet, a year later, only one woman has been charged with the crimes federal immigration authorities said drew them to the meatpacking plant in the first place. The person pleaded guilty and was sentenced to a year in prison.

“If they’re meant to make our community safer, they’re not doing that,” Roger Garcia, chairman of the Douglas County Board of Commissioners, said at the news conference about the raid and other subsequent immigration actions in Omaha.

Meanwhile, the people who were detained, their families and the broader community are still dealing with the enforcement action’s ripple effects, leaders noted, as they try to mitigate the effect on local businesses. The community leaders encouraged participation in a “Day of Joy” event Wednesday to support the businesses in the predominantly Latino 24th Street corridor.

Two community surveys of the South Omaha business district show that business health and customer traffic remain low.

Forty local business owners surveyed by the Nebraska Hispanic Chamber of Commerce said uncertainty, misinformation about immigration enforcement actions and ingrained fears have affected consumer behavior so dramatically that it’s hurting businesses’ ability to bounce back.

The businesses surveyed include seven restaurants and food trucks, 18 retail establishments, three construction companies and a variety of other storefronts. Three business owners said they’re planning to transition to online operations to stay afloat.

Challenges in workforce retainment have caused six businesses to shut down, said Irma Villezcas, a grocery store owner and chair of the South Omaha Business Association.

The results echo some of the findings from recent nationwide workforce studies on the economic impact of last year’s immigration raids.

A Brookings Institution study found that last year’s immigration enforcement surge across the nation cost 668,000 jobs, and those losses affected both immigrant and U.S.-born workers. Another study from the University of Colorado Boulder found immigration enforcement didn’t expand opportunities for U.S.-born workers and instead reduced employment for some of them.

Of the 76 people immigration authorities arrested at Glenn Valley Foods, close to 10 self-deported, Garcia told NBC News on Tuesday. Others who were also detained were eventually granted bond and reunited with their families, though many of them are still facing immigration proceedings.

“They have this constant pressure of being tied up in that system that might ultimately lead to deportation eventually,” said Garcia, who is the first Latino commissioner of Douglas County, where Omaha is located.

Garcia’s family was also among those directly affected by the raids. His wife’s aunt was among the meatpacking workers taken into immigration custody.

The woman, a mother of three U.S.-born children, spent a couple of months in detention before she was released on bond. Garcia said his wife’s aunt was granted a temporary work permit — alongside others who had been detained — while they wait for their next immigration court hearing.

Luis Mejía, 20, said he went to work last June at Glenn Valley Foods “thinking it would be a normal day.” The Nebraska native who was raised in South Omaha said everything changed that morning when immigration officers entered their workplace.

As some ran away in fear, Mejía’s immigrant mother hugged him and told him to take care of his younger siblings. Then, she ran with the others.

Meanwhile, immigration officers asked Mejía to show proof of U.S. citizenship.

“I didn’t know how to do that since I’ve never been asked that before. I looked at the officer with confusion and told him I was born here,” Mejía recalled. The officers cleared him to go after looking him up in their system.

A couple of hours after authorities let him go, Mejía received a call from his mother, telling him she had been detained. After that, Mejía didn’t hear from her for a few days while she was in detention.

She was one of the at least 63 workers who were taken to the Lincoln County Detention Center, four hours away.

The situation forced Mejía and his older brother to provide for their two younger siblings while not knowing if they would get to see their mother again.

“What made this raid especially significant was what happened afterward. Many individuals were held for more than 60 hours before being processed. During those 60 hours, families did not know where their loved ones were being held and we legal service providers did not have access to them,” said Roxana Cortes-Mills, legal director at the Center for Immigrant and Refugee Advancement, an immigrant rights organization in Omaha. “It was unlike anything we had ever seen in Nebraska.”

Lina T. Stover, executive director of the Heartland Workers Center, agrees.

“One day a person may have authorization to work and remain with their family, the next day policy changes, processing delays or court decisions can place their future in jeopardy,” she said at the news conference.

Her organization supports workers in the meatpacking, construction, restaurant and cleaning industries. The group, alongside the Center for Immigrant and Refugee Advancement, was crucial in helping the families directly affected by last year’s raid.

Two other people were sentenced in connection with the events surrounding the raid at Glenn Valley Foods. One man who worked at the plant was sentenced to 14 months in prison after being convicted of wielding a box cutter while attempting to resist an immigration arrest. Another worker who protested the raid was sentenced to 22 months in prison for using a rock to assault and impede a federal officer.

“At the end of the day, only like two or three people were prosecuted with any kind of charge,” Garcia said. “It’s just really quite silly that this huge effort led to like two or three prosecutions.”

Even though Omaha police do not cooperate with ICE to enforce immigration, state police do. Garcia said he gets weekly calls informing him of individuals who have been detained by immigration officials.

“Immigration enforcement did not end a year ago,” Cortes-Mills said.

After the one worker from the Glenn Valley Foods raid was charged with identity fraud last year, Elhrick Cerdan, the assistant special agent in charge of Homeland Security Investigations who led the operation, told NBC News “that number could change.”

The Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Attorney’s Office-District of Nebraska did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the investigation and the workplace raid last year.

U.S. Attorney Lesley Woods said last year that a five-year statute of limitations had expired for much of the Glenn Valley workforce that otherwise would have been similarly charged.

Nicole Acevedo is a news reporter for NBC News.

"It's also not lost on us that this is the biggest state campaign in the party's history," he said, calling Victoria "the most fiscally and morally bankrupt state in Australian history".

"We are officially putting the major parties on notice.

"Polling says Victoria is on track for Australia's first Liberal-One Nation government," he said.

Pauline Hanson is hopeful her party can have a big impact at Victoria's election. (ABC News)

"We'll have a talented team of people intent on restoring Victoria and kicking out the tired and toxic Labor government which has run this state into the ground, getting away with it thanks to a weak Liberal opposition," she said in a statement.

"ABC were denied entry into here and The Guardian. I'm not putting up with their rubbish, I'm not putting up with their spin," Ms Hanson said.

The projected windfall comes as Adelaide Magistrates Court forces One Nation to repay a former candidate thousands of dollars in campaign spending. In a separate case, Hanson could be held personally liable for failing to lodge party financial statements over the past three years.

“You could fill a town hall with the people she has short-changed,” says former One Nation South Australia leader Jennifer Game, who won a $15,000 settlement on Thursday.

“I think people should know that there are two sides, ultimately, to Pauline. There’s a lot of positive qualities about her, you know, that I could talk about; but equally, the way in which candidates and others are dealt with is pretty grim.”

Game tells The Saturday Paper she was forced to sign a candidate contract that placed a range of restrictions on her and required her to source campaign materials centrally.

“In my case, for example, my contract said that for the 2025 election, I had to take 1500 corflutes,” Game says. “Well, they’re banned in South Australia. You can’t put them up, you can only use them at polling booths in the week of the election. So I said, ‘Look, I don’t need these, I don’t want them.’ But I had to buy them, otherwise they wouldn’t let me stand as a candidate. So I had 1500 corflutes just sitting in my garage that I then had to pay [for them] to be taken to the tip.”

Game is especially critical of a centralised party structure that essentially gives Hanson and her chief of staff, James Ashby, control of the entire party apparatus. It is to this structure that the projected $219 million in campaign funding will be paid over the next five years.

“Everything’s done centrally. It’s all highly controlled; it’s not an organisation you can scale up, like a normal party,” Game says. “You could go to the Labor Party now, and they’ve got the processes, they’ve got the checks and balances in place to handle money and policy committees … They all have people who have accounting and legal backgrounds, but none of these checks and balances exist in One Nation.

“There’s Alex Jones, who’s their treasurer. I mean, he was in his early 20s when he first came on board, he has no qualifications regarding the handling of money, and I say that as someone who has a tax law degree and practised for a long time. And then there’s Pauline and James, and until recently, of course, there was Sean Black, the convicted rapist.”

Jones pleaded guilty in 2022 to one count of attempting to defraud the Queensland Electoral Commission over campaign funding, although a conviction was not recorded. Black was jailed in 2018 for rape and assault.

“It’s a party legally, I guess,” Game says. “But it’s not a party in the traditional sense of the word, which is why it all fell apart back in 1998 or whatever, and it will fall apart this time, because at the end of the day, Pauline trusts no one and cannot delegate power to anyone outside that very tight inner circle.”

Ashby, Hanson’s long-time chief of staff, dismisses concerns over One Nation’s centralised structure, and rejected claims candidates had to choose a nominated supplier for campaign material.

“The reason we’ve steered candidates to use businesses vetted by the party is that we guarantee quality and price,” Ashby tells The Saturday Paper.

“Candidates are welcome to use other suppliers, but often they can’t match wholesale rates we’ve negotiated with larger suppliers.”

Ashby’s comments follow a secret 2017 recording, made at a meeting also attended by Hanson, where he raised the idea of doubling the price of candidate advertising packages on invoices to be claimed back from the Queensland Electoral Commission.

“There is an opportunity for us to make some money on this if we play this smart,” Ashby was recorded saying. “I will deny I ever said this, but what stops us from getting a middleman or gracing … I am happy to grace in cash, double the price of whatever it is.”

Ashby later said the comments were part of “a brainstorming session that has been taken right out of context”.

The latest, huge spike in projected funding for One Nation is made possible by the introduction of state and federal laws that increase public funding for political parties to reduce their reliance on private donations.

“You could go to the Labor Party now, and they’ve got the processes, they’ve got the checks and balances in place to handle money and policy committees … but none of these checks and balances exist in One Nation.”

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Electoral Reform) Act 2025, due to take effect on January 1, 2027, will raise the per-vote public funding rate to $5 for every first-preference vote, a 48 per cent increase on the $3.386 rate that applied at the 2025 election.

“A system, purportedly designed to increase trust in elections, has become a mechanism to exclude newcomers and protect the political establishment – of which One Nation is a member – from competition even as the major party vote is in permanent decline,” says Climate 200 convenor Simon Holmes à Court, who produced the modelling.

“It’s as if the winner of the grand final got to make the rules for the next season and gave first draft picks and the gate takings to just the final four. Everyone would lose interest in the game quickly – but politics is too important to us all to be a game, let alone a rigged game.”

The modelling is based on an aggregate across federal and state elections starting from this year’s South Australian election through to the expected 2031 federal election.

At the May 2025 federal election, One Nation received 991,814 first-preference votes, or 6.4 per cent of the total, in the House of Representatives, and 899,296, or 5.7 per cent of the total, in the Senate. Under the funding rules then in force, the party received $3.386 for every eligible first-preference vote for candidates who cleared the 4 per cent hurdle, yielding just over $6 million in public funding.

At the South Australian election on March 21, One Nation achieved a primary vote of 22.9 per cent, winning three Legislative Council seats and four House of Assembly seats. Under South Australia’s generous public funding laws, on which the new federal laws are largely based, One Nation banked $7.3 million.

Six weeks later, One Nation’s David Farley swept to victory in the Farrer byelection triggered by the resignation of former Liberal leader Sussan Ley, ending the Coalition’s 77-year hold on the seat.

In funding terms it was a modest result. The byelection saw One Nation receive $140,107 in public funding, paid at the current rate of $3.499 per vote, but its political significance was enormous, with One Nation winning its first federal lower house seat in 30 years.

“One Nation has reached the end of its beginning,” Farley told supporters in Albury that night. “We’re going through the ceiling from here.”

Labor’s electoral funding legislation, which passed with Coalition support last February, also introduces a new system of administrative assistance funding – $30,000 a year for each member of the House of Representatives, and $15,000 a year for each senator. It is paid in advance, with no cap on the number of parliamentary members a party holds.

With One Nation’s representation in Canberra already numbering six, that means from January 1 through to the next election, due in May 2028, One Nation will receive $183,000 in administrative funding alone.

Victoria, where voters will head to the polls in November and which has its own generous public funding arrangements, will represent the biggest opportunity so far for One Nation to increase its cut of electoral funding.

Based on the Freshwater poll from June 2026, the Climate 200 modelling estimates One Nation’s Victorian public funding entitlement at $38.5 million, which would represent the biggest state-level figure in the entire five-year window.

In New South Wales, where Labor Premier Chris Minns will ask voters to give his government a second term in March next year, Climate 200’s modelling uses the May Resolve poll data to project a funding entitlement of $33.8 million.

Together, Victoria and NSW account for more than $72 million of the $219 million total.

It is the 2028 federal election that has the potential to deliver One Nation the biggest windfall, however.

With the latest Newspoll, conducted from June 1-4, putting One Nation’s primary vote at 31 per cent, Climate 200’s model scales up the 2025 results and distributes the swing across all 150 lower house seats and the eight state and territory Senate contests, using the same preferential and proportional counts as the Australian Electoral Commission.

On that basis, the model projects One Nation winning 58 seats in the House of Representatives and 12 of the 40 Senate seats turning over at the next election, giving it a total of 15 senators.

Applied to its projected 2028 vote tally, the new $5 a vote rate would see One Nation entitled to about $50.7 million, about eight times One Nation’s 2025 public funding.

With a post-2028 election party room comprising 73 MPs and senators, One Nation would receive a further $6.3 million in administrative funding on top of its per-vote entitlement.

Queensland goes to the polls in October 2028, with the Climate 200 modelling projecting a funding entitlement of $14.2 million. Western Australia follows in March 2029, with public funding projected at $5.1 million. South Australia returns to the polls in March 2030, with public funding projected at $6.1 million.

In Victoria, where another state election will be due in November 2030, Climate 200 projects public funding worth $17.6 million. NSW taxpayers could kick in an extra $11.6 million at the March 2031 state election.

Looking ahead to the 2031 federal election, which, if this parliament and the next parliament both run the full three years would be due in May 2031, Holmes à Court’s modelling projects that if One Nation’s primary vote held at the current level of 31 per cent, it would generate a per-vote public funding entitlement of $57,294,880, calculated at the indexed $5 a vote base rate.

The huge increase in public funding is likely to present something of a dilemma for Hanson, who has previously signalled her strong opposition to political parties accepting public funding.

“If you are really serious about it, stop putting your hand out and taking the electoral funding every time an election’s held, because the people are fed up with it,” Hanson told the Senate in 2018.

“It’s take, take, take. That’s what people see from this house all the time, that you’re not prepared to be up-front and honest with the Australian people.”

Special Minister of State Don Farrell, the architect of the new federal funding laws, says the headline figure that could potentially flow through to One Nation disguises the onerous transparency obligations and other strict requirements that the new laws place on political parties.

“Under Labor’s reforms, everything is transparent and visible. The public will see who is funding election campaigns and where that money is spent,” Farrell tells The Saturday Paper.

“Under changes fought and won by Labor, you cannot claim public funding unless you can show that money has been spent appropriately – no politician or party should profit off taxpayer funds.”

Senator Farrell argues that the new laws make it much harder for wealthy individuals to exert oversized influence on political parties and their elected representatives. “This is a clear choice. We can have a robust system of public funding, or we can have campaigns flooded with donations from billionaires playing politics.”

Beyond the increased per-vote rate and new administrative funding, the Electoral Reform Act also introduces major changes to donations.

From January 1 donations above $5000 must be disclosed, with expedited reporting requirements kicking in during election periods, and as quickly as within 24 hours in the final days of a campaign.

Private donations are capped at $50,000 per person per recipient per year, with an overall cap of $1.6 million across all recipients.

Electoral expenditure is also capped, with a $90 million ceiling on total spending by a registered political party and its associated entities and an $800,000 limit per division.

“Australia has one of the best voting systems in the world – compulsory preferential voting, no gerrymandering and a trusted ballot – but our democracy is far from perfect,” says Holmes à Court.

“Over the last 15 years, the legacy parties have built a massive wall of advantage around themselves, almost impossible for outsiders to climb, and with the threat of newcomers, the legacy parties use public money to raise the wall and build moats … The upshot is less choice for voters, and a ballot paper where the only viable candidates are those chosen by those already in power.”

Jason Koutsoukis is The Saturday Paper’s special correspondent.

openai_chatgpt_teen_safety:
The maker of ChatGPT is rolling out a range of new safety features today for under-18s who use the AI chatbot.

Those with new teen accounts will be able to switch off the human voice response, in order to minimise the tech's ability to appear like a person.

OpenAI is also introducing regular reminders for young people to take a break from using the tool, reminding them ChatGPT is AI, and saying "it can wait".

The firm insisted this was not in response to a particular issue with children believing ChatGPT to be alive - but there are growing concerns about people becoming convinced that the AI tools they interact with are sentient.

Last year Mustafa Suleyman, the head of AI at rival firm Microsoft, said "seemingly conscious" AI products "kept him awake at night" because he was so worried about their impact on society.

In other areas, OpenAI seems to be loosely following the teen account model developed by the large social networks.

In a blog post announcing ChatGPT for Teens, external, the firm said teenagers' use of AI "should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time".

It said teen accounts would become the default for those who identified themselves as teenagers when they signed up, and others whom the firm itself identified as under 18.

But it did not elaborate on how it would identify these teens.

Under-13s are not allowed to use the product.

Last year, ChatGPT launched Study Mode for students, in which it talks through schoolwork without giving away the answers.

Young people will now be able to set Study Mode hours during which this will be the default setting.

They will also be able to activate "quiet times" when the tool will be switched off for them.

OpenAI says of the young people who use ChatGPT, nine out of 10 use it to help them with learning.

A report released yesterday, external by the Policy Exchange think tank claimed that the majority of UK universities are leaving themselves exposed to students enhancing their grades using AI by relying on online exams completed remotely.

It said 94% of the students it spoke to admitted to using the tech in assessments.

OpenAI is also adding eating disorder-themed prompts to a list of harmful user requests which will be flagged to parents with linked accounts.

The company said each alert would be reviewed by a human before it was sent, and it aimed to have them with parents within an hour of the request being made.

In its blog, OpenAI said it would focus on "moments when offline support may matter most".

OpenAI said it would alert teens not to share sensitive content with ChatGPT

So far, there is no bespoke AI regulation in the UK. The government under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer considered restricting AI chatbots for under-18s alongside its other reforms on social media use by children.

Anthropic's AI tool Claude is still for adults only. When Google first launched its Gemini AI tool, initially called Bard, it also did not allow children to use it.

Dr Susan Shelmerdine, a medical imaging doctor at Great Ormond Street Hospital and an AI academic, told the BBC last year that one day doctors may start asking patients how much they use AI, in the same way that they currently ask about smoking and drinking habits.

"We already know what ultra-processed foods can do to the body and this is ultra-processed information. We're going to get an avalanche of ultra-processed minds," she said.

Oracle has sent a force majeure notice to the developer of Project Jupiter, a Stargate data center campus in New Mexico, Bloomberg first reported Thursday.

Force majeure clauses, common in energy and commodities contracts, excuse a party from contractual obligations when events outside its control get in the way. Oracle is not seeking to exit as the campus’s main tenant, according to Bloomberg’s sources. Instead, the notice would allow the company to delay payments should the facility miss its 2028 target to come online.

The notice also comes as AI data center construction faces growing scrutiny nationally, and as developers take on steep costs to build capacity for customers like OpenAI.

Oracle maintains that it does not expect a delay. “Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule,” Oracle said in a statement to CNBC. “We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”

Blue Owl Capital, whose unit received the notice, said in its own statement to CNBC that “this notice does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project.”

Neither Oracle nor Blue Owl immediately responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

Still, the notice follows a string of setbacks at the site, many of them tied to its energy supply. The campus, designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts, is meant to run on gas-powered fuel cells from Bloom Energy, which makes a reliable gas supply central to its timeline.

An Energy Transfer pipeline intended to deliver gas to the site has also been delayed nearly six months, to February 1, 2027, after regulators repeatedly denied permits for the line. In August, Bloomberg reported that the pipeline’s route had been changed following those rejections. A separate air-quality permit for the fuel cell system that would power the campus is also pending. The state’s environment department faces a November 23 deadline to decide.

Project Jupiter is one of the flagship sites of Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative Oracle, OpenAI, and SoftBank announced with President Donald Trump early in his second term. The campus has drawn opposition from residents and environmental groups and has become a political flashpoint ahead of the midterm elections. Oracle has responded with a public outreach campaign in the state aimed at winning over the project’s critics, according to Bloomberg.

EXCLUSIVE: Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia is being criticized as a "hypocrite" and faces a challenge to return a sizable donation from a Jeffrey Epstein-linked billionaire or drop one of his main lines of attack on Republicans as representing the "Epstein class."

Ossoff has framed his re-election effort as pushing back on the influence of wealthy elites and getting big money out of politics. However, his campaign received the maximum legal contribution of $7,000 from Silicon Valley billionaire Reid Hoffman, a venture capitalist who previously admitted to visiting Epstein’s private island. Hoffman also donated $1 million to an Ossoff-linked political action committee, New Engagement PAC.

Hoffman has not been accused of any wrongdoing. But Ossoff’s Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, says that accepting donations from Hoffman shows Ossoff "has been nothing but a hypocrite the entire time."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Collins said he is giving Ossoff a very simple choice: return the Reid Hoffman donation or explain why the "Epstein class" does not include one of his own maximum-dollar donors.

out_of_office_etiquette:
You're finally about to head off on a well-earned break, but there's one more task to tick off your to-do list: composing an out-of-office reply.

Many will be all too familiar with debating how much information to include and how available you will be - and whether to inject some personality into your message, or even risk cracking a joke.

Experts say there are clear dos and don'ts when it comes to writing an out-of-office message (OOO) - and getting it wrong can have more serious consequences than you might think. Here are their rules to penning the perfect out-of-office reply.

Debretts, an etiquette consultancy, says a good automatic reply should be polite and concise, give a specific return date, and provide another point of contact if appropriate.

But you should avoid oversharing, for instance including the specifics of your holiday plans, or boasting about things like second homes or expensive hobbies.

Avoid sharing personal details about your holiday plans, says Debretts

"Virtue signalling" about why you are taking time off is another no-no. It could seem "smug" or like you are "trying too hard", says director Rupert Wesson.

"Some people will be delighted you are spending 'quality time with your family', but given that they are the ones emailing you and are hard at work, you could risk rubbing their noses in it."

That said, a bare message that simply states, "I'm out of office" with no details of a return date or alternative emails to try, can raise more questions than it answers.

"People don't know when to expect a reply or who else can help, and that uncertainty is what leads to the 'just-in-case' follow-ups," says Charlotte Davies, a career expert at Linkedin.

She believes a good OOO does two things: shares your dates and points people to a backup contact.

She also thinks it's worth briefing the person covering you about anything important before you go: "It helps whoever's emailing you, and it protects your break too."

Would you set an out-of-office reply like this one?

While the personal touch may work in OOOs if your team culture is informal, beware that humour doesn't always land well over email.

Overly glib or sarcastic messages can get you into trouble, even if they are funny, reckons Paul Fitzsimmons, head of sales and marketing at law firm Wilford Smith.

"'I'm currently out of the office pretending this company doesn't exist'... 'If it's urgent, call someone who cares'... 'Emails received while I'm away will be deleted unread,'" he gives as examples.

It is important to manage expectations around your availability

Adam Murfet, 41, a senior sales executive, says a former colleague lost a deal after a joke in an OOO angered a client.

But he thinks humour can help some people stand out at a time when communication is increasingly AI-driven.

"Always ask, would you put the same thing in an email?" he says, as a rule of thumb.

"Anything you send will be read and people will judge you on it."

Commentators often complain about the sender saying they will have "limited access to email" while they are away.

The risk is it invites people to keep contacting you as if you were still at work.

Wesson says that if you really need to check emails on holiday, then it's better to say, "I will be periodically checking emails," as it manages expectations.

Davies adds that if you want a proper break, "say so clearly - something like 'I won't be checking emails during this time'."

"Remember, in the UK you have a legal right to uninterrupted annual leave unless your contract says otherwise."

1. Be polite: Don't just launch in with "I'm on annual leave". Preface your message with a greeting, such as "Thank you for your email".

2. Give a specific return date and back-up contact if appropriate. Ensure all the contact details are correct

3. Be clear about your availability: Manage expectations and if you would prefer not to be contacted, say so

4. Don't promise instant replies on your return: A backlog is completely normal, so "within a few days" is a better promise to make

5. Tick both internal and external contacts if you use Outlook. It's an easy one to miss

6. Switch off your out of office when you return: A stale OOO can look disorganised.

Sources: Debretts, Linkedin
