By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA and ANDREW BROWN FOR AUSTRALIAN ASSOCIATED PRESS

Anthony Albanese has repeatedly declined to rule out changes to Australia's copyright laws covering artificial intelligence, despite insisting 'humans must remain in control'.

The Prime Minister met with former Apple head Tim Cook and other executives at the company's headquarters in Silicon Valley, California, on Sunday morning, Australian time.

Following the meeting, he spoke to ABC's Insiders host David Speers, who pressed him several times on whether Australia would dilute copyright protections as US AI firms seek greater access to books, music, articles and other creative works to train their models.

Albanese said creators should keep control over their intellectual property, but did not directly answer questions about whether copyright laws themselves would remain unchanged.

Speers noted that, in a speech earlier this year, Albanese said: 'No company should use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the artist's control. Anything less is theft.'

Asked if that was still his position, Albanese said: 'Absolutely, and that's our position.'

But when Speers asked whether that meant copyright laws would not be watered down, Albanese did not answer directly.

'They should still have control over whether their intellectual property is used and, if it is used, there should be proper monetisation of that use,' he said.

Anthony Albanese (pictured) declined to rule out potential changes to copyright laws covering artificial intelligence

Albanese (right) met with Apple chief executive Tim Cook (left) at the company headquarters

Speers pushed again, asking: 'Does that mean any watering down of the copyright laws or not?'

Albanese did not directly answer the question, saying: 'What it means is control and monetisation of it.'

He reiterated that creators should retain authority over how their work is used by AI companies.

'Artists need to keep control of their intellectual property. I think that's a very clear position,' he said.

When Speers asked whether creators might instead be required to opt out of having their content used to train AI models, Albanese pointed to what he described as two key principles.

'They will have control over their intellectual property, and the second principle is that any use needs to be monetised as well. That needs to be part of the equation,' he said.

Asked whether those protections would apply to independent creators as well as large media organisations capable of negotiating licensing agreements, Albanese said commercial deals should flow through to the underlying creators.

'If they do deals, then those deals will encompass the artists. One would assume that if they do a deal with the ABC then the ABC content will be available,' he said.

Albanese's comments on the policy came just days before he is due to meet with US President Donald Trump at the UN where AI is expected to be a major topic

'But to all other creative content makers who may not be part of a big organisation, I can't be clearer, David, than what I have said.'

Speers then raised the issue again, asking: 'So no change to copyright law?'

'Well, no change to the principles that I've outlined very clearly,' Albanese said.

Speers said: 'That's different to saying no change to copyright law. What might you change?'

But Albanese again would not specify whether legislative changes were being considered.

'I've said what the principles are, and we'll engage constructively on all of these issues,' he said.

While declining to provide a definitive answer on copyright laws, Albanese argued the rapid development of artificial intelligence posed significant risks and backed international efforts to establish safeguards, while warning Australia could not afford to fall behind.

'I certainly accept that there are risks and that's why we need to mitigate them,' he said.

ABC's Insiders host David Speers pressed Albanese several times on whether Australia would dilute copyright protections as US AI firms seek greater access to creative works

'There is a need for a discussion about what the global framework is for the rollout of AI, because it is moving very quickly. We need to make sure that humans remain in control.'

The federal government unveiled national AI standards in July requiring data centres supporting eligible projects to be powered by additional renewable energy.

The policy comes as the Prime Minister prepares for a meeting with US President Donald Trump at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, where AI is expected to be a major topic.

The push at the UN coincides with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei calling for a slowdown in the technology's development.

But Trump has rejected calls for further guardrails, warning America could lose the AI race to China as a result.

Asked by Speers whether the United States and China should work together on AI regulation, Albanese said: 'I certainly agree.'

'They're the big two giants here. We want to see cooperation.'

Albanese also expressed hope that a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this coming week might yield progress.

While avoiding direct criticism of Trump, Albanese emphasised the need for safeguards around AI development.

Speers noted Trump had previously dismissed concerns about artificial intelligence and questioned the need for stronger guardrails.

Asked whether he was concerned by that approach, Albanese said: 'There is a need for all of us to act in the interests of humanity.'

He cautioned there is a risk AI systems could develop beyond human control.

'The risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing,' he said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says tapering the fuel excise cut is a sensible measure that will provide certainty to motorists as fragile peace talks come under threat and Iran says it closed the Strait of Hormuz because of Israel’s continued attacks on Lebanon.

The prime minister said on Sunday that drivers would get 16¢ a litre off fuel for the month of July – an extra month of relief, but at half the rate of the 32¢ discount that had been applied since April. The announcement came after the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding last week to end hostilities.

By Sunday, Iran had accused the US of a clear breach of commitments by failing to end Israeli attacks on Lebanon, leaving the future of the region and the flow of oil out of the strait in doubt.

Albanese will convene national cabinet on Monday to discuss the excise cut with state and territory leaders, whom he expected to do “the right thing” and agree to continue forgoing GST windfall profits to help fund the relief extension. This is expected to cost an additional $400 million.

“A step-down is a sensible thing to do,” Albanese told Sky News. “We know that families are still under pressure, and we also know that the impact of this conflict on the other side of the world will have a long economic tail to it.”

NSW Premier Chris Minns said on Sunday that he would put his hand up for the state to drop its GST component.

Albanese said the government would continue to assess the circumstances in the Middle East, and respond to future shocks appropriately.

Asked whether the nation would join the US if it removed sanctions on Iran to get a peace deal over the line, Albanese said Australia would make its own decisions.

“Bear this in mind, that Iran orchestrated attacks on Australian soil. We don’t take it lightly – we expelled the Iranian ambassador from Australia, the first time an ambassador has been expelled since the Second World War.”

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the government would continue to ensure fuel supply to Australia while an agreement between the US and Iran hung in the balance.

“We know that the simple announcement of a peace deal is not implementation of a peace deal. We want to see the Strait of Hormuz open and open permanently and sustainably. We’re not yet there,” he said in Sydney on Sunday.

Opposition foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien blamed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah for undermining the agreement with attacks on Israel.

“If you think of it from an Australian point of view, if we actually had missiles raining down on our country, the expectation would be our government acts,” he told the ABC’s Insiders program.

“We’re dealing with a terrorist organisation – we’re dealing with Hezbollah again. This is a proxy of Iran, a despotic regime that kills not only their own people but other people around the world, and this is what makes it so complicated that I don’t think we can simplify it.”

O’Brien said Labor should be credited for gradually reducing the excise cut, while Opposition Leader Angus Taylor was more circumspect, saying he hadn’t seen all the detail.

“I understand the logic of having a graduated taper of this, and as I say, we’ll look at it, but we have been supportive of cuts to the fuel excise from the start,” Taylor said. “In fact, we proposed it in the first place, and Labor copied us.”

Taylor said the relief should be offset with cuts from other parts of the budget.

Greens senator David Shoebridge said the shrinking relief would do little to help Australians who were struggling in an ongoing cost-of-living crunch, and called for the government to show greater leadership.

“One of the reasons we’re seeing this one-month measure of reimposing half the fuel excise is because the world’s in chaos. The war that Anthony Albanese [and] Pauline Hanson supported, launched by Donald Trump in the Middle East, throwing everyone’s energy prices into chaos, doesn’t seem to be ending,” he told reporters in Canberra.

“When will our government call out the chaos-makers here?”

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said the decision to extend the cut to the fuel excise and the heavy-vehicle road user charge was welcome aid for freight operators and the businesses that depended on them.

“Transport costs flow through the entire economy. When those costs spike, it pushes up prices and adds to the pressure businesses are already facing from weak demand and rising operating costs,” McKellar said in a statement. “The government should remain ready to respond if conditions deteriorate.”

National Roads and Motorists’ Association spokesman Peter Khoury warned the lost revenue would have consequences for the nation’s infrastructure.

“We are absolutely delivering relief when you halve the excise, there’s no doubt about that, but then the flip side to that, of course, is we have roads that need to be maintained and upgraded,” he said at a press conference.

“We need this war to end, and we need the strait to open – otherwise, all we’re doing is really tinkering around the edges.”

Founders, employees and early investors in startup companies will get an extra capital gains tax discount as the federal government moves to stamp out the backlash to its budget.

Labor has been consulting with the startup sector and with small businesses, which have argued that the proposed overhaul to the capital gains tax would unfairly penalise them and stifle innovation.

More small businesses will stand to receive the 50 per cent active asset discount, which currently applies to those with an annual turnover of up to $2 million.

That will be expanded up to $10 million under the proposal.

That discount applies in addition to the regular 50 per cent capital gains tax discount when businesses or business assets are sold.

Labor wants to replace the regular 50 per cent discount with an inflation-linked discount.

The details of the carve-out for startups will be subject to consultation, but the initial suggestion is a choice between a 50 per cent discount and an inflation discount, applying to “new, innovative” businesses.

Founders, early stage investors and employees granted shares as part of their remuneration will be included.

“The next steps that we announce today are all about providing more clarity and confidence to investors, more support for small businesses and more incentives for innovation,” Treasurer Jim Chalmers said.

“We understand that there’s never a unanimous view about economic reform and particularly about tax reform.

“It’s always contested, it’s always contentious. But it will be worth it. We are delivering real change here.”

Testamentary trusts to be exempt

The government has also moved to quell concerns about the inclusion of discretionary testamentary trusts in a new 30 per cent tax.

Discretionary trusts allow their owners some flexibility to move income around between different beneficiaries, holding companies, and across different years for tax purposes.

Several types of discretionary trusts are exempt from the new 30 per cent minimum, including deceased estates and farms.

But testamentary trusts, which activate when a person dies and can be used by their beneficiaries, were not.

That had prompted accusations the government was creating a “death tax”.

Labor’s argument was that the trusts needed to be included for integrity purposes, but Mr Chalmers said on Thursday this concern would be addressed through anti-avoidance rules as well.

The government will also reduce the amount of discretion it had proposed to give Mr Chalmers to vary key definitions in the law, including the definition of new homes, which are treated differently, and those who are exempt from tax changes.

Concerns had been raised about this discretion by Greens economic spokesperson Nick McKim, whose support will be essential to passing the tax changes through the Senate.

Mr Chalmers had said the discretion was important to avoid unintended consequences in the application of the law, but that the government would move to put as much as possible into the legislation, with several amendments to be moved in the upcoming sitting fortnight.

“It’s not unusual for big, ambitious tax reform like this to involve a lot of consultation, to involve primary legislation for the core element, subsequent pieces of legislation as well,”

he said.

“We have seen that in the past with governments of both political persuasions, and that’s what is taking place as well.”

It has, in short, had to restructure core revenue-raising measures because of a widespread public backlash. This is a major capitulation for an administration that initially dismissed criticism of the legislation as partisan scaremongering.

The timing raises questions about political strategy and transparency. Only 48 hours before the backflip, Treasurer Jim Chalmers ruled out any imminent carve-outs or exemptions during a media conference. He insisted ongoing consultations with the tech and small business sectors were genuine and incomplete.

Thursday's volte-face suggests that was either a deliberate effort to obfuscate the government's intentions or a swift intervention by a Prime Minister determined to halt a severe slide in political fortunes.

Labor, tellingly, chose to announce the retreat from its unpopular policies in the wake of a controversial speech by Pauline Hanson; a classic deployment of the political tactic known as "taking out the trash".

Under the reworked package, the government lifted the turnover threshold for the 50 per cent small business capital gains tax reduction from $2 million to $10 million. This concession brought an estimated 98 per cent of active businesses into the exemption zone, effectively reversing the Treasurer's earlier insistence that the original boundaries were already adequate.

Furthermore, the government has exempted income distributed through discretionary testamentary trusts from a proposed 30 per cent minimum tax rate, a policy critics branded as a death tax by stealth. The government also removed nine separate discretionary powers originally granted to the treasurer, which would have allowed ministerial control over housing definitions and asset discounts.

Despite the scale of the concessions, neither the Coalition nor major industry bodies see them as a complete fix to what they say is a toxic budget. Angus Taylor has declared the budget is "in tatters" and demanded the scrapping of the entire bill, not just piecemeal carve-outs.

Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox argued that the amendments lessened but did not eliminate the broader economic harm. Mr Willox pointed out that the core legislation still raised taxes to punitive levels for medium and large enterprises, applied rates retrospectively, and penalised investment and innovation.

Because official consultations on various tranches of the tax package remained open, the frantic policy rewrite resembled a firefighting exercise rather than an orderly legislative process. The hasty adjustments indicate further amendments are likely as the government quietly finalises decisions behind closed doors.

Labor has paid a heavy price for what voters viewed as blatant electoral overreach. The bruising retreat does not erase the political stigma stemming from the Prime Minister's pre-election assurances that a Labor government would not alter negative gearing or capital gains tax frameworks.

Hanson's "fire the liar" campaign has achieved significant cut-through since the budget, reportedly raising millions of dollars for her One Nation party.

By overestimating its mandate and attempting what many people see as an ideologically driven tax hike on the back of a lie, Labor misjudged the electorate, suffered a severe political blow and has handed its opponents an effective weapon ahead of the next election.

Pauline Hanson has hit the road to campaign as her party pulls ahead in the polls.  (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

As Anthony Albanese stood in front of a Medicare banner and Pauline Hanson put her hand out for donations, voters could be forgiven for thinking the election was two months, not two years, away.

The prime minister wanted to get back on territory where the government feels most comfortable fighting, laying down the challenge for One Nation to outline its plans for health and education.

But the minor party had other ideas. Buoyed by overtaking Labor for the first time in several opinion polls as the most popular political party, it launched an appeal of its own.

“Fire the liar,” the message read in all caps. The call out was to donate so One Nation could spread the message. It amassed over $2 million in 48 hours – a number anyone who’s tried to sell a Freddo frog or raffle off a meat tray for a local club could only wish for.

The three-word slogan wasn’t even a line One Nation dreamed up itself. Hanson’s chief of staff, James Ashby, got the idea from Sky News host Peta Credlin.

"I was watching her show and I stole it off her. Nothing quite like a borrowed line," he told 2GB.

Credlin was part of the team that brought us some of former prime minister Tony Abbott’s most memorable slogans. She later admitted the lines used in the attack against the carbon tax helped bring down the Gillard government weren't entirely true.

“That was brutal retail politics, and it took Abbott six months to cut through and when he did cut through Gillard was gone,” she said in 2017.

Pauline Hanson is hoping her liar line will cut through to voters.  (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

It’s clear the while the election proper is two years away, the campaign has already begun. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has done his best to attack the budget and the prime minister. His slogan is all about “toxic taxes”.

The government has conceded the most recent budget included broken promises. Of course, it argues the circumstances have changed and that’s why it acted. But it also acknowledged that doing so carries a political risk.

The Albanese government is paying an economic and political toll for Donald Trump's actions.

That risk is opening the door to the question of whether a broken promise is a lie. Hanson and Ashby will hope the recent press about the unprecedented donation drive, paired with whatever advertising that is funded by that, will cement that idea in public consciousness like Abbott and Credlin did with the carbon tax.

She wants to use the money to target Labor seats, including ministers such as Chris Bowen and Tony Burke – who hold suburban Sydney seats.

While Albanese questioned the legitimacy of the donations, Hanson argued she had no reason to claim otherwise.

“It would destroy me,” she said.

As One Nation begins to take up more time and space in the political consciousness, Abbott reportedly floated that a preference deal between the two parties should be considered. It’s what the Greens and Labor do, he argued, so why not the Coalition.

Abbott’s own relationship with Hanson has ebbed and flowed over their 30 years of political life. The now-federal Liberal president was behind a trust fund set up to fund civil cases against One Nation in the 1990s.

In a documentary a decade ago, Hanson said it took her a long time to get over Abbott’s involvement in a case that led to her brief imprisonment for electoral fraud (a conviction that was later quashed). Hanson was emotional as she repeated the sentiment while in the West on Thursday.

"It just broke my heart ... it was a very hard time for me and it was a very hard time for my children," she said.

Elsewhere, Liberal MPs are genuinely concerned about what One Nation means for their re-election prospects. Tony Pasin, who represents the South Australian seat of Barker, put forward the idea of carving out the electoral map so the Coalition and One Nation don’t go up against one another.

Angus Taylor has yet to stop the slide in voters switching their support from the Coalition to One Nation.  (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

That idea was promptly shut down by Taylor, although he’s more open to the idea of a preference swap. Senior Liberal frontbencher James Paterson went further when asked this morning, declaring the whole discussion was premature. The focus needs to be on rebuilding trust with the voters it's lost, he said.

“Who knows what policies One Nation is going to come out with between now and then, who knows what candidates they’re going to endorse. Who knows how many of their MPs are going to defect or found to be invalidly elected between now and then,” Paterson told Radio National Breakfast.

Friday marks four months since Taylor toppled Ley. The opposition leader hasn’t stemmed the bleeding of support to One Nation. Ley was given nine months in the top job.

Outwardly though, the Coalition is declaring the Taylor-Abbott leadership has the party going in the right direction. Nationals leader Matt Canavan thinks there is a “revolutionary fervour in the air” and the electorate is “waking up”.

But whether voters are open to hearing what they have to say is another question entirely.

Meanwhile, the government has some hard decisions ahead of it. A resumption of strikes in the Middle East adds another level of complexity around whether the halving of the fuel excise will be extended beyond June 30.

Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

As with everything, it comes with a trade-off and a three month extension would cost the budget $3b in foregone revenue. But deciding to extend could help dampen inflation (as it did in April). Keeping it around would also have the added benefit of people not talking about their petrol prices for that little bit longer.

Elsewhere, questions about the government’s approach to data centres are starting to crop up after rush of private investment in the infrastructure helped prop up Australia’s sluggish GDP figures.

Fresh off the gas tax campaign that had extraordinary cut through; independent David Pocock has taken up the issue. He’s concerned Australia won’t get a fair return from the boom and unsurprisingly linked it to the gas producers.

On the other side of the coin, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton, will use a speech tonight to again argue the government's fix on gas (the reservation scheme) is correct, albeit years late. And the same should be applied early on to data centres.

“That is the real lesson from gas for data centres: it’s far better to get the rules right at the outset than to try to put them right a decade later.”

Millions of Australians could be caught in a surprise superannuation tax trap despite Treasury assuring voters retirement savings would be exempt from Labor's controversial capital gains tax overhaul.

Anthony Albanese's government has been accused of burying a new tax on super after analysis by the Financial Services Council found superannuation assets worth $372billion could be exposed to an additional $55million a year in tax costs, potentially reducing returns for members whose retirement savings are invested through managed investment trusts.

The finding appears to contradict a Budget explainer released by Treasury in May, which promised superannuation, including self-managed super funds, would be shielded from the government's capital gains tax changes.

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson seized on the analysis, accusing Labor of laying 'yet another tax landmine' in its Budget.

'The Albanese Government has been caught laying yet another tax landmine in its Budget to feed its spending addiction, and this time it's targeting superannuation,' he said.

The Financial Services Council, which represents retail superannuation funds, said assets worth billions held within superannuation structures could be affected by the change.

Under current tax rules, super funds can use capital losses in a way that preserves as much of their valuable capital gains tax discount as possible, helping to minimise tax and maximise returns for members.

Under Labor's proposed changes, that treatment would continue for assets held directly by a super fund.

Anthony Albanese's (pictured) government has been accused of burying a new tax on super

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson (pictured) seized on the analysis, accusing Labor of laying 'yet another tax landmine' in its Budget

But if the same assets are held through a managed investment trust, different loss-ordering rules would apply before gains flow back to the fund, reducing the available tax discount and potentially increasing the tax paid on members' retirement savings.

The industry group argued those additional costs would ultimately flow through to super fund members in the form of lower investment returns, despite Treasury's assurance that retirement savings would be exempt from the changes.

Colonial First State Superannuation chief executive Kelly Power said the finding showed super funds had not escaped Labor's tax changes and urged the government to close the loophole.

'Super members should not be worse off because of how their investments are structured,' she told The Australian.

'A targeted adjustment is needed to ensure members receive the same tax outcome whether assets are held directly or through a managed investment vehicle.'

The industry warned the hit would fall hardest on Australians in smaller super funds and self-managed super funds, which are less able to hold assets directly.

Financial Services Council chief executive Blake Briggs said the rules risked pushing money out of managed funds, increasing costs across the super system and ultimately eroding members' returns.

'Unless corrected, the rules could drive money out of pooled managed funds, fragment investment structures and increase costs across the superannuation system, with members ultimately footing the bill,' he said.

Mr Briggs said the issue went beyond a technical tax quirk, noting the government had explicitly promised on Budget night that superannuation would be unaffected by the changes.

'The final design must deliver on that promise, rather than leave some Australians paying more tax through a technical back door,' he said.

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that sanctions against Francesca Albanese, an Italian human rights lawyer and UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Palestine, will remain in place while her legal challenge continues.

In July 2025, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions under Executive Order 14203, citing Albanese’s calls for International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and her efforts to hold global companies accountable for their alleged involvement in atrocities in the occupied Palestinian territories. These actions were part of her broader advocacy condemning Israel’s military operations in Gaza, which she and other human rights experts have described as genocidal.

Rubio alleged that Albanese attempted to prompt the International Criminal Court to “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute nationals of the United States or Israel, without the consent of those two countries.” As a result, the Office of Foreign Assests Control listed Albanese as a specifically designated national, freezing her credit cards, bank accounts, and other assets while barring US persons from engaging with her. The sanctions have also made it difficult for her to travel, preventing her from visiting her daughter—a US citizen—in the United States. Her daughter now faces potential criminal consequences for remaining connected to her mother—a sanctioned individual under US law.

Albanese’s husband, Massimiliano Cali, along with their daughter, filed a lawsuit alleging that the US sanctions violate her First Amendment rights. While a district court granted a preliminary injunction, the US government appealed the ruling.

In a per curiam opinion, the appellate court partially stayed the injunction pending appeal, allowing the sanctions to be enforced again.

In a concurring opinion, Judge Gregory Kastas suggested that Albanese’s free speech argument may fail, stating that First Amendment protections do not apply to the speech of “non-resident aliens” abroad, as “foreign citizens outside US territory do not possess rights under the US Constitution.” Judge Kastas also noted that “equitable considerations,” such as foreign policy and national security interests, favored granting the stay.

UN Watch, a non-governmental organization that monitors the UN, reported that the concurring opinion indicates that “Albanese’s core First Amendment theory may fail altogether.”

A luxury resort backed by the US president’s family may be built on a wildlife-rich nature reserve in one of Europe’s poorest nations

If the real estate dreams of a billionaire political family come true, an island in one of Europe’s poorest countries will become a luxury hotel complex, sweeping up stretches of the wildlife-rich nature reserve that sits across the water.

No public consultation has taken place, but there are signs the idea is on the way to becoming reality. Albania has been rocked by nearly two weeks of fierce protests after fences and heavy machinery came to a sensitive wetland and preparatory work began on the tourism vision of Ivanka Trump and her husband, Jared Kushner.

Domestic anger at the government’s corruption and global interest in the business dealings of the US president’s family have inflamed the unrest. But at its heart, the fight is driven by the same tension between environmental protection and short-term economic growth that is playing out across Europe.

The area’s status as a wildlife sanctuary was “something that amid all of this probably gets forgotten, but it’s what sparked the big outrage”, said Aleksandër Trajçe, the executive director of PPNEA, Albania’s largest conservation group. “If you want to see the Mediterranean as it used to be, before it was wrecked by tourism, this is one of the last – if not the last – spots where you would find it.”

Marshes, dunes, lagoons and salt pans stretch across the dynamic delta of the free-flowing Vjosa River, which was declared Europe’s first wild river national park in 2023. It sits on a major migratory corridor, hosting about 12% of the country’s wintering waterbirds, and is home to Eurasian otters, loggerhead sea turtles, bottlenose dolphins and Albanian water frogs. Flamingos add bright shocks of pink to striking blue shallows.

Unpublished conservation data shared with the Guardian shows 279 of the 2,529 species in the delta are internationally threatened. Aleko Miho, a biologist at the University of Tirana, who monitors the area with his students each year, said: “These are important habitats. It doesn’t matter who is behind it. What matters is the pressure it puts on a protected area.”

Machines have been seen in the Pishë Poro–Nartë protected area – which sits within the Vjosa-Narta protected landscape inside the delta – but it is unclear how much of the ecosystem would be affected by the proposed development.

The project has not received planning permission or an environmental impact assessment, and the Albanian government, which has welcomed the scheme, said the continuing works were for technical surveys and environmental measurements rather than construction.

“In the meantime, the bulldozers are really progressing,” said Trajçe. “They’re destroying the dunes. They’re opening new roads. The area has been fenced off … it’s really a wild west situation.”

Albania is among the poorest countries in Europe but boasts some of its wildest landscapes. The combination has drawn in holidaymakers seeking cheap getaways – a record 12 million tourists visited Albania in 2025 – but the government has also successfully enticed elites. In May, Ivanka Trump said she was “just captivated” when she swam up to Sazan Island and hiked barefoot to the top.

“It’s not even a business for me, despite the scale of it,” she told the podcast host David Senra about her plans to turn the area into a vast resort. “It feels like a challenge more than anything else: the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live, how I think people increasingly are wanting to live, and trying to really build something that’s a tangible manifestation of that.”

But many fear that Albania’s tourism push has led the government to disregard nature protection. It redrew the borders of the protected area in 2022 to allow the construction of Vlora airport, which had hoped to see its first commercial flight this month but is still awaiting an operating permit. In 2024 it loosened conservation laws to allow the construction of five-star hotels even in protected areas.

Albania is under pressure to tighten its environmental laws to meet the requirements of the EU, which it hopes to join by 2030. On Tuesday the European Commission said it should refrain from actions that undermine its bid and urged it to “act without delay” in complying with environmental rules. The same day, 96 civil society organisations wrote to the Albanian parliament to demand they repeal the 2024 amendment to the environmental protection law, citing the risks it posed to joining the EU.

The office of Edi Rama, the prime minister, said the fencing of private property was the lawful right of its owner and disputed having reduced the size of the protected area to build the airport.

A spokesperson said projects should not be condemned before they existed. “No European country, including Albania, operates on the principle that development and environmental protection are mutually exclusive,” they said. “The challenge is not exclusion but balance.”

Affinity Partners, Kushner’s investment firm, referred a request for comment to a PR agency, which said Affinity was not involved in the project and “investors are involved in their personal capacity”. A spokesperson for the partners involved in the project said he could not comment on the scale because it was still in the planning phase.

Sazan Real Estate Development LLC, the developer, said it respected continuing public and institutional processes. Asher Abehsera, the chair, said: “Our focus remains on responsible stewardship, environmental enhancement, job creation and creating long-term value for local communities.”

Arup, a global engineering firm that consulted on the project, said its scope was to provide “technical advice on the initial masterplanning” but that it had completed its work last year and was no longer involved.

The Vjosa-Narta ecosystem is not as unspoiled by human activity as Ivanka Trump or some protesters claim. A defunct oil-fired power plant sits beside the lagoon, while the beaches are home to dozens of guest houses, restaurants and even a music festival. However, scientists say it has been spared much of the pollution that plagues other parts of Albania’s coast, as well as the overcrowding that characterises much of the Mediterranean.

The planes, cars and construction that come with a large resort would disturb a special ecosystem that is “relatively untouched” compared with other dunes and lagoons in the Mediterranean, said Miho. “The birds will fly away, for sure.”
alberta_library_restrictions_deadline:
The Alberta government has given libraries around the province until the start of next year to introduce new policies restricting access to materials with sexually explicit images.

The province updated its Libraries Act earlier this month to set a Jan. 1 deadline for libraries to comply and ensure they're not allowing anyone 15 years old or younger to use or borrow materials containing a visual depiction of a sexual act, without a parent or guardian's authorization.

The new restriction applies to books, periodicals, comics and graphic novels, films, TV programs and video games.

Library boards also have until Jan. 1 to determine which materials should be restricted, how to regulate access to them, and where to store them separately from other resources.

Boards must also meet the same deadline to establish how to determine a person's age, and whether a parent or guardian has authorized their access to restricted materials.

The province is calling on boards to introduce policies about issuing library cards to people 15 years old or younger, and on allowing people in that age group to use library computers to access the internet or play video games.

Boards are also required to consider how the same age restrictions can be applied to digital resources like e-books.

The restrictions are a result of Bill 28, which was passed in May.

The Coalition of Alberta Public Libraries said this week it's still reviewing the new restrictions.

The Calgary and Edmonton public libraries said they are still reviewing the impact of the new restrictions, too.

Earlier this month, the Canadian Federation of Library Associations said it's working with colleagues across the country to address concerns other provincial governments could introduce similar restrictions.

Jack Alarie, press secretary for the Ministry of Municipal Affairs, said no content will be removed from libraries due to the new restrictions. Instead, he said the province wants to ensure libraries continue to be family-friendly, without affecting adults' access to them.

Bill 28 gives inspectors, appointed by the Municipal Affairs minister, the ability to look at any matter related to a library's management, administration or operation. Alarie said this is an expanded scope for inspectors, after they were previously limited to board records.

“It is reasonable that there be accountability for public institutions that are governed by provincial statute and funded by tax dollars,” said Alarie.

Rob Miyashiro, the Alberta NDP's shadow minister for municipal affairs, said the new rules are likely to cost more money for libraries and put extra stress on their staff. He highlighted that it will be especially difficult for small libraries with only a couple of employees.

Why the Alberta government is telling libraries to put some books out of sight

“It’s something that wasn’t necessary, and the libraries were never asking for this. In fact, the vast majority of public libraries in Alberta already had policies and practices that did what this government wants as an outcome,” said Miyashiro.

"Local decision-making is going to be minimized in favour of a centralized approach by this government."

The province is also requiring library boards that operate a location inside a school to set up a process for the public to ask the board to review whether restrictions are needed on specific materials in these libraries.

Reviews can be asked for by students, parents or guardians, staff and school council members, other members of the public with a connection to the school, and library card holders.

Boards have until Jan. 1 to establish these processes, and must regularly review their resources to ensure they comply with the Libraries Act, and provide reports, on request, to the minister.

Reporter

alberta_pipeline_referendum:
Standing alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney, Premier Danielle Smith unveiled Alberta's official proposal for an oil pipeline to the West Coast on Thursday, a project she's pointed to as proof her province can work with Ottawa.

But while one pollster said the project could move some "soft separatist" voters to instead support remaining in Canada, some Albertans supporting independence are still skeptical the pipeline will ever be completed.

Let Alberta Decide, a third-party advertiser advocating for Albertans to vote in an October referendum in favour of exploring separation from Canada, said the announcement “proves the problem with Confederation.” The group argued a year of negotiations only led Alberta to an “uncertain starting point.”

"It feels a little bit like a promise that at some point there will be a pinky swear that this will happen, and I just don't place a lot of weight on it,” said Tanya Clemens, co-chair of Let Alberta Decide.

Alberta pitches new West Coast oil pipeline to B.C.'s South Coast

Smith’s announcement on Thursday included a proposed pipeline route to British Columbia’s southern coast to export oil to Asian markets. The federally-owned Trans Mountain Corporation is partnering on the project, with Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline acting as the private proponent.

Early work on the project could begin in 2027, with its completion projected for between 2032 and 2034. More detailed funding and the cost for taxpayers “remains to be negotiated,” Smith said on Thursday.

The federal government also announced a multibillion-dollar deal with British Columbia, which included a commitment to maintain an oil tanker ban on the province’s north coast.

Clemens argued too many federal conditions still plague the deal, including Ottawa calling for a proposal to be coupled with a carbon capture agreement.

But on Friday, Smith said the announcement signalled Alberta and Ottawa can co-operate constructively.

“The demonstration that Canada and Alberta can work together is the proof point in itself. Canada and Alberta were not working very well together for the last 10 years,” said Smith on CBC Radio’s Calgary Eyeopener on Friday.

“It's demonstrated that we can take a different path that can not only support Alberta's economic prosperity, but also be good for the country."

Taxpayers could be on hook for West Coast pipeline, but it's a 'good investment': Energy minister

But Christopher Scott, CEO of Let’s Talk Alberta, argued the deal still has too many hurdles that could drag out a pipeline deal.

“There’s lots of talk, lots of hype, and I think it’s a means by which the federal government and the provincial government are trying to extinguish the independence movement,” said Scott.

“I’ll believe it when I see it.”

Scott's organization hosts conversations on Alberta independence. He said he’s not a separatist, but he believes Alberta should have more authority over its own resources, which can currently only be achieved through seeking independence.

To some federalism supporters, Smith's announcement signalled Confederation can still work.

That’s how former Progressive Conservative deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk sees it. Lukaszuk, who spearheaded the Forever Canadian petition last year, said Thursday's announcement shows why separation should not be supported.

He argued that for some voters “hell-bent on separatism," nothing is likely to convince them to change their vote. He argued they cannot support the pipeline proposal, because it undermines their argument that Canada cannot work.

But to more open-minded voters who are weighing evidence, Lukaszuk said the pipeline proposal could push them to support remaining in Canada.

"This will serve as an evidence that if they ever wanted to send a message to Ottawa, the message has been sent and it has been heard,” said Lukaszuk.

Most Albertans were not confident the memorandum of understanding Smith and Carney signed last year would actually result in a new pipeline, polling by Janet Brown Opinion Research for CBC News showed.

On Friday, Brown said a private proponent being involved in the project, a carbon capture deal, and British Columbia not opposing the project all together ticked a lot of boxes for skeptical Albertans.

A guide to the (many) groups running Alberta's separatist and remain camps

Why expansion of Delta, B.C., container port is going hand-in-hand with Alberta pipeline

She said while polling has consistently shown about 20 per cent of the population is locked into supporting separation, there is a narrow band of nine to 11 per cent of Albertans whose votes are up for grabs. Brown referred to this group as “soft separatists."

If any of those voters are driven by economic concerns, Brown said the pipeline proposal is likely to give them more confidence in Confederation.

"This could be proof to them that Canada can work, that Alberta can make headway [in] the things the premier has said about trying to make progress within the federation rather than without,” said Brown.

“I think this should give soft separatists pause."

Reporter

alberta_senate_referendum:
It was in the pages of a 1985 issue of the Alberta Report newsmagazine where conservative Alberta writer Ted Byfield proposed a “triple-E” vision for the Canadian Senate.

In Byfield’s view, a triple-E Senate — equal, elected and effective — offered a salve if Alberta again faced something like Pierre Elliott Trudeau’s controversial 1980 National Energy Program, seen as evidence by Byfield and others that Ottawa unfairly treated the West.

In addition to being equal and elected, a triple-E Senate would also see senators having more legislative power.

“The task of selling this to Canada is awesome, but not impossible,” Byfield wrote in his 1985 column.

“There is an obvious first step. Triple-E supporters — the revolutionaries — wear a triple-E symbol on their lapels.

“It denotes the opposite of separatism. It does not declare, we want out. It declares we want in. If a million westerners and a half-million Maritimers began wearing it, the politicians would soon be listening.”

Though the idea predated Byfield (the Canada West Foundation proposed the idea in 1981), the “triple-E” catchphrase was adopted by scores of Alberta leaders, from Preston Manning and his Reform Party to former premier Don Getty.

Speaking in 1987, Getty said “Senate reform along the triple-E lines is the only hope for westerners who are loyal to both their region and their country.”

Various reform attempts followed, but none matched what Byfield and Manning and Getty envisioned. The Senate reform movement, as Alberta conceived of it, stalled.

This October, Albertans will be asked to ponder the Senate’s future once again.

Unlike the triple-E movement of decades past, Albertans will be asked to consider a more dramatic gambit: abolishing the Red Chamber entirely.

“The unelected Senate is a waste of taxpayer dollars, is entirely undemocratic, doesn’t represent the interests or will of the province they represent, and should have been abolished years ago,” wrote Ryan Fournier, a spokesperson for the premier's office, in an email.

A “yes” vote prompts Alberta to partner with “other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate.”

That would be no easy feat.

“I think it’s a dead end, myself,” said Gary O’Brien, a former clerk of the Senate.

That’s not to say O’Brien doesn’t understand the frustration. The author of The Senate of Canada was clerk in the Senate from 2009 until 2015, when he retired.

Much pessimism has been tied to a 2014 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, in O’Brien’s view.

That ruling stated the federal government doesn’t have the power to enact reforms on its own. Instead, reform takes the support of seven provinces representing half the population, while abolishment requires the support of all 10 provinces.

“The chances of this happening are almost nil,” O’Brien said.

In O’Brien’s view, eliminating the Senate would weaken provincial representation in Ottawa and remove a key institutional check on the House of Commons.

“I give credit to Alberta for … putting it on as a very important issue facing them and facing Canada,” O’Brien said. “I think their solution is the wrong one, but at least they're putting the Senate on the map.”

O’Brien argued past efforts at reform failed by being too broad. In the future, reform could concentrate on individual problems, starting with Senate seat allocation.

He noted Alberta has six seats out of 105 with a population of five million, while New Brunswick has 10 seats for less than a million.

“Why not correct the way seats are distributed to give a better balance of fairness?” he said. “I think if people enter into that debate with a sense of compromise, there could be a chance of success.”

On its referendum website, Alberta lists its grievances with the Senate. Along with seat counts, it states five of Alberta’s senators were appointed by the current federal government “with zero consultation, entirely ignoring the Senate election process in place in Alberta.”

Unlike other provinces, Alberta elects Senate nominees. Between 1989 and 2012, Alberta held elections that resulted in 10 nominees, half of whom were appointed. The process was revived under former premier Jason Kenney in 2021.

There’s nothing on the books to stop provinces from holding such elections, but the results are non-binding. The Governor General appoints senators on the prime minister’s recommendation, following input from an advisory board.

Gerard Kennedy, an associate professor in the faculty of law at the University of Alberta, said the province’s process can’t trump the clear constitutional purview of the federal government to recommend appointments of senators.

“The federal government is entitled to arrange an alternative process. Moreover, the Supreme Court of Canada has held that the non-elected nature of the Senate is a key characteristic of it,” Kennedy wrote in an email. "While the government can choose to appoint an elected Senator, they cannot be obliged to do so."

In a 2021 letter to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, Kenney wrote provincial nominee elections “could work in conjunction with the federal nomination process to ensure alignment of our respective processes.”

Provincial Senate nominee Erika Barootes on Alberta's frustrations

Erika Barootes was one of three provincial Senate nominees from 2021.

Under Trudeau, Barootes said there was “not an expectation” she would be called to service right away.

“Would I say I fell off my chair when I found out that he had appointed other Albertans to those vacancies? No,” said Barootes, a former principal secretary to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. “But it is, I think, still frustrating and insulting to know that I've put in lots of work. I travelled the whole province.”

Though Barootes views abolition as a “throwaway” question on the referendum ballot, she believes talk may have moved in that direction given long-standing frustration over reform.

“I think that’s where we’ve seen the triple-E idea of seat counts shift towards — just get rid of the darn thing … because it’s not working,” she said.

Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, the government recently announced it intends to recruit candidates “with enhanced focus and expertise in key Canadian strategic industries, regulatory frameworks, and emerging social and economic affairs,” while also removing the non-partisanship criterion for Senate appointments.

Sen. Scott Tannas was elected as an Alberta senator-in-waiting in 2012 and was appointed to the Senate by former prime minister Stephen Harper the next year.

“Honestly, when I first went, I said, if we can't make the changes, we should abolish it,” Tannas recalled.

Sen. Scott Tannas on why he changed his mind on the Senate

But Tannas, who is the former president of the insurance services company Western Financial Group, said his thinking flipped after spending time on various committees.

“I got an appreciation of the committee work that senators do, the studies that they do, where their expertise and whatever area of experience they have come to bear,” he said. “And that was humbling.”

Sen. Scott Tannas on what would be lost should the Senate be abolished

Gary Mar, a former Alberta cabinet minister who is president and CEO of the Canada West Foundation, said the idea of an elected, equal and effective senate is still central to the foundation's "legacy on co-operative federalism today."

"Abolishing the Senate requires constitutional reform, and history shows that this is neither easy nor simple. Renewed engagement and discussion are perhaps the more realistic path towards Senate reform that can benefit all of Canada and especially the West," Mar wrote in an email.

The idea of affixing triple-E symbols to one’s lapel never really seemed to catch on in Alberta.

As to whether Albertans feel ready to throw in the towel on the whole institution? Clarity on that point is only months away.

america-slamming-brakes-alpr:
(Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Officials across party lines are moving to dismantle the growing network of cameras tracking American drivers.

Several state and federal officials are calling to restrict automated license plate readers (ALPRs), artificial intelligence-powered cameras that scan the plates of passing cars. Pushback to this technology — specifically Flock Safety cameras — has brought together Republicans and Democrats who say these tools amount to warrantless mass surveillance, while law enforcement warns that restricting them would hinder their ability to solve crimes.

At the state level, Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott blocked agencies from spending money on the cameras on Aug. 27, according to the Texas Tribune. Similarly, Florida’s Department of Transportation revoked permits for the devices on state highways on Aug. 31 and ordered them removed within 30 days, according to The New York Times.

A total of 201 local communities have canceled or not renewed ALPR contracts since the start of 2025, according to the Institute for Justice’s cancellation list.

“The growing opposition from local city councils to Congress and state legislatures is the direct result of communities across the country standing up against mass surveillance,” Rindala Alajaji, Associate Director of State Affairs at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

She added that opposition to these cameras “crosses every political line because people recognize that turning our streets into a warrantless tracking grid violates fundamental civil liberties.”

Among them was Knox County, Tennessee, where local officials unanimously voted to remove the cameras on Aug 31, according to Knoxville News Sentinel.

“The big issue is that when these cameras are deployed in large numbers … [they] can determine your movements based on this network of cameras,” Mayor of Knox County, Tennessee, Glenn Jacobs said in an August interview with the DCNF, prior to his county’s removal of its Flock cameras.

WATCH:

In Pennsylvania, lawmakers have introduced at least nine bills to restrict or ban the cameras, most of them in a matter of weeks.

“These tools can serve legitimate law enforcement purposes, but Pennsylvanians should not have to choose between public safety and their constitutional right to be free from unreasonable government surveillance,” Republican Pennsylvania state Rep. David Rowe, chairman of the House Republican Policy Committee, told the DCNF. “We can—and should—protect both. I believe these bills strike that balance by protecting Pennsylvanians’ privacy while ensuring that police have access to critical information in dire situations.”

Rowe, along with Republican Pennsylvania state Rep. Josh Bashline announced a two-bill package to place “guardrails” on ALPR cameras, according to a July 24 memo from the representatives. One of the bills would establish a local moratorium on the use of ALPR cameras.

The most recent legislation proposed in the state’s senate, sponsored by Democratic state Sens. Nick Pisciotto and Patty Kim, would enforce oversight, accountability for bad actors and protect personal data, according to a joint memo.

This bill would act as a companion to a bipartisan House package led by Democratic Rep. Tarik Khan that would set rules for who can access ALPR data and create civil penalties for misuse, according to an Aug. 10 memo. (RELATED: Dozens Of Towns Reject AI Cameras That Track Your Every Move)

Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said Flock cameras are “not something in the public interest,” he told the Center Square on Aug. 28.

Legislators in California failed several times to pass legal guardrails for ALPR cameras in the state since 2022, according to CalMatters.

The most recent of these attempts involved Democratic state Sen. Sabrina Cervantes’s bill, SB 1013, which called for specific safeguards on the technology. The bill was removed from the assembly floor on the final day of the legislative session by Democratic Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, and a vote never took place, CalMatters reported.

“It’s unfortunate that Senate Bill 1013 did not get the chance to be voted on before the deadline passed, but I look forward to continuing to fight for the privacy rights of Californians next year,” Cervantes told the DCNF.

The senator said this legislation would ensure privacy for Californians, immigrants and other “vulnerable communities,” according to an Aug. 13 press release.

“We need to take action to protect Californians’ personal information when it comes to license plate cameras,” Aguiar-Curry told the DCNF.

She said the holdup was a normal procedural move, and the bill was supposed to be voted on later that day.

“My motion to pause, where I stated we would, ‘come back to the measure later,’ had nothing to do with my personal position on the bill,” Aguiar-Curry told the DCNF, clarifying her position on the legislation. “I do support the policy in SB 1013 and am hopeful the bill is reintroduced in the next legislative session.”

Defenders of the cameras in the state say privacy concerns are overblown and warn that stripping the tool away would cost law enforcement its most effective means of solving crimes.

Riverside County sheriff Chad Bianco, president of the California State Sheriffs’ Association, serves in the same jurisdiction as Cervantes and supports ALPR technology. His sheriffs’ association is among the list of groups opposed to Cervantes’ ALPR bill.

“I am probably one of the biggest proponents of ALPRs. Yeah, I would never employ this type of technology if it was even remotely violating somebody’s constitutional rights, and it’s nowhere close,” Bianco, a former Republican candidate for California governor, told the DCNF.

He argued that claims against these cameras are completely unfounded and are the result of the Left’s “love affair with criminals.”

Youtube Screenshot Riverside County Sheriff’s Department

“[T]his is a massive negative campaign that was created by a very pro-left, pro-criminal agenda that is that has spent a decade removing tools that work in arresting and prosecuting criminals,” the sheriff told the DCNF.

The International Association of Chiefs of Police concurs with Bianco stance on the technology.

“The [IACP] strongly supports the lawful, ethical, transparent, and accountable use of Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) technology when it advances legitimate public safety objectives,” The International Association of Chiefs of Police said in an Aug. 20 press release.

The IACP added that these cameras can identify vehicles associated with violent crimes, locate missing and vulnerable community members, and locate stolen property, when used “properly.”

“[E]very single argument for the opposition of these cameras is based on emotion [and] has no factual basis whatsoever,” Bianco claimed. “None. It’s like, well, what if? What if? What if? What if the sky fell tomorrow and we all blew up and died? No one would care anymore.”

He claimed law enforcement failed to step up and present the accurate facts about this technology. Because so few law enforcement officials are willing to speak up about the issue, he argued, a nationwide “misinformation” campaign has spread.

Bianco’s solution is legal repercussions for officers who abuse the technology.

“[M]akes it life in prison if a law enforcement officer does that. I’ll be all for it,” he told the DCNF.

At the federal level, Republican Reps. Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Eric Burlison of Missouri introduced the Flock-Off Act, which would bar federal funds for buying or operating ALPRs and give recipients 180 days to shut existing systems down.

“The federal government shouldn’t provide ‘security’ grants to cities and police departments that have gone beyond the pale and turned their communities into a version of 1984,” Massie stated in a Sept. 2 press release.

”Public pushback has hit a fever pitch because of a toxic mix of heightened awareness and corporate tone-deafness,” James Czerniawski, head of emerging technology policy for Consumer Choice Center, told the DCNF. “People are genuinely concerned about being trapped in a dragnet of constant government surveillance.”

Republican Texas Rep. Keith Self has separately pushed the PRIVACY Act, which would require federal agencies to obtain a warrant prior to using ALPR data.

Flock, which have received the majority of public criticism for this technology, defended its cameras.

“Flock’s technology is an important public safety tool for law enforcement agencies across America, helping officers solve serious crimes and find missing people,” a Flock spokesperson told the DCNF.

“We support thoughtful, bipartisan legislation that puts strong privacy, transparency, and accountability guardrails in place while preserving law enforcement’s ability to use technology responsibly to keep people safe,” the spokesperson added.

Critics argue the problem extends well beyond any single company.

”Flock gets the spotlight because they are a market leader, but the underlying issue isn’t tied to just one ALPR company; it’s the business model itself,” Czerniawski told the DCNF. “Any ALPR company building mass-tracking infrastructure faces the same fundamental questions and critiques.”

While Flock Safety is the largest ALPR vendor in the U.S., police departments also partner with Axon, Motorola Solutions’ Vigilant unit, and Rekor for these services, according to the ACLU.

None of the other major vendors are any better, said Alex Marthews, national chair of Restore the Fourth.

“Though Flock Safety is a bad actor in the ALPR space, that doesn’t mean that Axon or Vigilant/Motorola or other providers is better from a privacy perspective,” Marthews told the DCNF, adding that “the whole business model of ALPR firms rests on profiting off of violating your privacy.”

american_parents_backpack_school:
We do not make the child fit the backpack. We keep looking until we find the one that fits the child. Education deserves at least that much imagination.

Toward the end of every summer, my family makes what has become a small back-to-school hajj to the western suburbs of Chicago. We hit Oakbrook Center, then the outlet mall nearby, and spend a day acquiring the things our children try to convince us they need to become well-educated Americans.

This year my son got an L.L. Bean backpack, and my daughter, a pink patterned one from Pottery Barn. Water bottles, teal unicorns, sketchbooks, chapter books. My son will read almost anything with a credible risk of dismemberment. Then shoes: He wanted something that made him look a little more like James Dean, whom he reported on last year. I doubt Dean bought his shoes at an outlet mall with his father, but we worked with what we had.

This is what American parents do in August. Using survey projections and K-12 enrollment data, Deloitte estimated the back-to-school market at $30.4 billion this year, or about $557 per child. We comparison-shop, chase sales, and adjust according to price, taste, and the lobbying power of the child standing beside us.

Somewhere between Pottery Barn and L.L.Bean, it struck me that we were exercising extraordinary discretion over everything surrounding school.

Except, mostly, the school.

I conduct focus groups with parents about education, and one of my favorite questions is meant to get them outside the school they already know: If you could build a school custom-tailored to your kid, what would it look like?

The first response is often dead air. Eventually come the safe answers: good teachers, safety, strong academics. Leave it sitting there long enough, and people start wandering. Maybe school happens mostly outside. Maybe the kids build things every day. Maybe it looks like a laboratory or a garage full of cars and go-karts to pull apart and, with luck, put back together again.

Once I let myself do the same thing, I have no trouble at all. For my son, I can imagine museums and national parks, robotics labs, and workshops where roller-coaster engineering and animatronics count as perfectly serious subjects. Maybe a year on the Great Loop with American history passing just above the bowline.

Then I look at what we actually choose from. Even a good school is built for scale, not for my son. The calendar, subjects, age groups, classrooms, and shape of the day are largely fixed before anybody meets the kid who has to live inside them.

For most of American history, there wasn’t much alternative. The school was where the school was. You took the package. Eventually, necessity hardened into habit, and we stopped expecting much of the education itself to be ours to decide.

Psychologists stumbled onto something useful here in the late 1960s. Martin Seligman and Steven Maier found that dogs exposed to shocks they could not control eventually stopped trying to escape, even when escape became possible. The finding became famous as “learned helplessness.”

Parents learned something similar about school. You could request the teacher, hire the tutor, pack the lunch, fill the afternoons. But the big decisions were already made: where, when, what, how, with whom, for how long. We got very good at choosing around school because choosing much about school itself rarely seemed possible.

Then Seligman and Maier went back to their own work and found the more interesting lesson.

Helplessness, they concluded, wasn’t really learned. When nothing you do changes anything, passivity comes naturally. Control is what has to be learned. You act. Something changes. So you act again.

Agency needs reps. Fortunately, by then we needed lunch.

We wandered into a restaurant hilariously embedded in the middle of Crate & Barrel, where my daughter ordered buttered corkscrew pasta and my son ordered tonkotsu ramen with chili oil and an extra soft egg. Same parents, same house, much of the same genetic material. Apparently none of it reached lunch.

Parents get absurdly good at this. We know who needs advance warning before plans change, who regards sauce touching pasta as an act of aggression, who is prepared to die over the precise shade of pink. We acquire an almost embarrassing amount of knowledge about the peculiar human beings assigned to our care.

Then, every August and September, millions of those peculiar human beings become third-graders and fifth-graders and seventh-graders.

Formal schooling cannot operate at that level of particularity. It was built to move enormous numbers of children through the same buildings, on the same calendar, according to the same clock. Schools have since developed a generous vocabulary for individuality: gifted, exceptional, differentiated, personalized. The language has changed much faster than the machinery.

What makes this moment different is that the machinery is no longer the only option. Charters, microschools, hybrid programs, co-ops, and online courses have made the landscape more varied than it has ever been. In a 50CAN survey of 23,000 parents published earlier this year, 70 percent said they feel they have a choice in where their children go to school. Yet only 26 percent had reviewed information comparing their school’s performance with others.

The choices are arriving faster than the habit of choosing.

After lunch, we resumed the hajj. Hours later, the bags exploded across the floor at home. My daughter’s teal unicorn bottle fit perfectly into the side pocket of the pink backpack. My son tried on the shoes one more time.

The James Dean effect remained modest.

Looking at the pile, I realized this was what reps looked like: small judgments made so often they become instinctive. This fits him. She’ll actually use this. He hates those. She needs that. Try something. Watch what happens. Adjust.

We already know how to do this. We just rarely think to do it with education.

Take the hour. Pull your kid out early because the robotics lab is open and he cannot stop talking about it. Take the day and go to the museum. Take three days and build the go-kart. Take the week and see the Tetons or Gettysburg, or follow some obsession farther than the school calendar finds convenient. Hell, take the semester and let him study somewhere that treats a roller coaster as a legitimate physics problem. Take the year, if you can, and build the strange little school you keep waiting for somebody else to invent.

Nobody needs to homeschool everyone or burn down the neighborhood school. Just choose something, then choose again, until taking some authority over your child’s education feels less like rebellion and more like what it has been all along: parenting.

The backpacks will disappear. The shoes will be outgrown. The unicorn bottle has, if history is any guide, a fighting chance of vanishing before Christmas. The hours are harder to replace. We gave a whole day to choosing the small stuff because nobody would dream of handing us the standard fourth-grade-boy bundle and insisting it ought to fit.

We do not make the child fit the backpack. We keep looking until we find the one that fits the child. Education deserves at least that much imagination.
